ideas.title: Lot-Lender
ideas.one_liner: A chattel lender that lends only inside land-lease communities that sign a three-party agreement, so the park's lot-rent ledger becomes the credit file and the collection channel.
ideas.customer: Households buying or replacing a home in a land-lease community (the 4.3M-homesite base per MHI) and the regional operators who need 1970s-80s homes replaced and pads filled.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Borrower pays about 9-10% gross interest (FHFA average chattel rate 9.24%). Operator signs the master agreement: COO or VP Home Sales of a regional owner with 20-300 communities (budget line is occupancy and home sales). Funding side: warehouse lender, then ABS investors.
ideas.problem: The home is the only collateral but the park controls the land under it. The lender cannot see the lot lease, rent increases or park approval; the park cannot see loan status. A repossessed home becomes a liability to both (unpaid lot rent, vacant pad, resale only the park can approve). Lenders price that blind spot into 9%+ rates and FHFA reports 65.6% of chattel applicants denied (vs 8.8% site-built).
ideas.solution: Master lender-park agreement: lot-lease approval is part of underwriting; lot rent and loan payment drafted together with a waterfall; park shares 12-60 months of rent ledger as thin-file credit data; park gives 30 days notice and a cure right before eviction; pre-agreed voluntary surrender and in-place resale so a default becomes a new sale on the same pad. Operator gets filled pads and old homes replaced.
ideas.why_now: Capital just began flowing into chattel (Zippy $20M Series C from Saluda Grade on 14 Oct 2026, Forum Markets' up-to-$150M loan purchase commitment, Apollo's $850M MH fund first close). REIT occupancy is already 94-98% (ELS 94%, Sun 97.8%, UMH 95%), so the growth lever for operators is replacing aged homes. FHFA's June 2026 proposal puts chattel on the policy agenda.
ideas.wedge: Purchase and replacement loans in 10-20 communities of one regional operator in 2-3 states chosen after counsel reviews repossession and park-tenancy law (e.g. Minnesota caps a repossessing lender's park-rent liability under some conditions). First 10 customers: ten regional owners with 20-100 communities each; one REIT pilot later.
ideas.path_to_100m: About $1.0B average receivables x ~10% gross yield (9.24% market average + fees) = ~$100M. At a 7-year effective life and 0.6 balance factor (my assumptions) that needs ~$250M originations a year at maturity = ~3,000 loans a year = ~6% of the ~52,000 HMDA chattel loans a year (366k home-only loans 2018-24 per Pew / 7), or 2.5-5% of $5-11B of annual originations. Ramp to $350M/yr reaches $1B in ~5 years. Capital ~$150M equity at 85% advance. Sanity check: Zippy's announced money ($20M equity + $150M purchase commitment over five years) is about one-sixth of what this needs, so funding is the binding constraint. Revenue is not profit: with funding ~6-7%, opex ~2% and losses 2-4%, profit exists only if park integration really cuts losses.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Clayton's 21st Mortgage and Vanderbilt (~$29.5B loan book at 31 Dec 2025, Berkshire-funded; no park contracts found), Triad (Champion JV), Cavco's CountryPlace (memory), Cascade, Zippy (27 states), credit unions such as PremierOne (chattel program launched Aug 2025). Operators sell homes themselves (UMH home sales ~$50M a year) and use third-party lenders. Free substitutes: seller financing, contract for deed, personal loans.
ideas.why_they_lose: No incumbent has a contract with the park; their channel is dealers. Honest caveat: they do not lose on price, because Clayton's funding is the cheapest in the industry. The bet is lower losses and higher approval rates, which are untested.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (exclusive operator agreements plus the rent-ledger data) and switching costs (ledger/draft integration). Weak until a loss-rate edge is proven.
ideas.earned_secret: Hypothesis, not interviewed: a park manager knows on day 3 of a late payment whether a household will default; the lender learns 60-90 days later. Both want the same outcome (household stays and pays) and no contract aligns them, so the best credit signal in the industry sits unused.
ideas.first_90_days: Letters of intent from three operators. Get 24 months of anonymised lot-rent ledgers plus loan performance on 5,000+ homes from one operator and test whether 60-day rent history predicts default better than FICO. Counsel drafts the master agreement in two states. Obtain one warehouse term sheet.

ideas.title: Open Lot
ideas.one_liner: A multi-brand retail chain built by buying independent dealers, with every lender competing for each buyer, in-house set crews, and the finance and insurance economics kept inside the chain.
ideas.customer: Home buyers (~104,000 new homes a year) and the plants that depend on brand-locked retail.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Buyer pays home price and finance charges. Signers: dealer owners who sell (about 1,200 dealer companies, undated source) and plant sales VPs who give volume terms. Capital: acquirer equity plus floor-plan lines.
ideas.problem: The three integrated players (Clayton, Cavco, Champion) sell their own brands through captive or affiliated lenders (Champion via a JV with Triad). Independents borrow floor plan from, and send buyers' files to, a lender owned by their biggest competitor: 21st Mortgage calls itself the largest floor-plan lender (22,000+ units, ~$1.6B floored in 2023). Champion grew factory-direct stores from 18 (2022) to 73 (2024), showing manufacturers are buying distribution because independents are weak.
ideas.solution: Buy 15-25 independents in 3-4 states over three years. Sell several brands. Route every application to 4-5 lenders at once so approval and price compete. Keep F&I reserve in a captive structure where state law allows. Add in-house set crews and warranty. Attach the Park Shield insurance program.
ideas.why_now: Shipments are -7.3% YTD, so weaker independents are for sale and plants want volume. Chattel capital is entering (Zippy, Forum, Saluda), creating more lender choice. Champion's retail push proves the distribution fight is on.
ideas.wedge: Three to five dealers in one state to prove same-store approval rate and margin. First 10 customers are the first 10 dealer sellers.
ideas.path_to_100m: Average dealer revenue ~$9M ($11B / ~1,200, undated source). $100M = ~11 average dealers = ~760 homes a year at $131k blended = 0.7% of shipments. Capital $30-70M including inventory (assumes low acquisition multiples). This is the easiest path to $100M of revenue in the pool and has the thinnest moat; it is revenue, not margin.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Clayton Homes retail with 21st Mortgage; Cavco and Palm Harbor stores (memory); Champion Homes (73 factory-direct locations in 2024, bought Iseman, agreed to buy 11 Homes Direct stores); independent regional chains (memory). Free substitute: the independent dealer as it exists today.
ideas.why_they_lose: A brand-locked retailer cannot be neutral: Clayton cannot send its buyer to a rival's lender or sell a rival's home first. The independent's flaw is scale.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in wholesale terms if plants are underused (assumption); little else. Honest verdict: a distribution roll-up, worth building only if lender and insurance attach economics are retained.
ideas.earned_secret: Hypothesis, not interviewed: at a dealership the sale is decided by which lender approves, not by the home. The independent dealer feeds buyers' credit files and prices to a competitor who rations approvals.
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 20 dealer owners on lender approval rates and floor-plan terms; get approval data from five; test whether a four-lender waterfall raises approvals. Sign LOIs with two dealers in one state. Ask two plants for volume pricing.

ideas.title: Park Shield
ideas.one_liner: A manufactured-home insurance program underwritten community by community, enrolled through the lease and paid in the monthly rent draft, so the insurer is paid first and the park enforces the mitigation that makes the risk insurable.
ideas.customer: Households in land-lease communities (~3.5-3.9M homes: 4.3M sites at an assumed 80-90% owner-occupied) and operators who bear fire and wind loss from uninsured homes.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Homeowner pays $1,000-1,300 a year through the rent draft (consumer-site estimates, low authority). Operator signs the program via a lease addendum (VP Operations or CFO of a regional owner). Lenders already require cover.
ideas.problem: Standard policies are priced per home from age, location and construction; they ignore what the park controls (tie-down certification, skirting, lot spacing, hydrant access, old wiring and gas lines). Premiums are rising (Massachusetts residents reported hundreds of dollars more, Jan 2026, anecdotal) and lapses are common.
ideas.solution: MGA on a fronting carrier with reinsurance, later a carrier, writing one program per community with rating credit for mitigation the park enforces and verifies. Default enrollment with opt-out and a proof-of-other-coverage path. Premium collected on the rent invoice. Claims data feeds next year's community rating.
ideas.why_now: Insurers are repricing; Foremost, American Modern and CoverTree are individual-policy businesses. Straight-through MGA tooling now exists (CoverTree claims 92%). Operators are in a rent-increase fight and a bundled lower premium helps them.
ideas.wedge: One operator with 30-60 communities in one state plus its claim history. First 10 customers: its first 10 communities.
ideas.path_to_100m: Premium pool for homes in communities ~3.5M x $1,100 = ~$3.9B (my arithmetic on assumed counts and consumer-site premiums). $100M of gross written premium = ~91,000 policies = ~2.6% of that base. If revenue means MGA commission (15-20%, assumed), $100M needs $500-650M of premium = 13-17% share, which is heroic, so the idea meets the bar only as a risk-bearing program carrier (surplus $50M+ with reinsurance, assumed).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Foremost (Farmers), American Modern (Munich Re, memory), Assurant lender-placed (memory), State Farm and Progressive for some homes (memory), CoverTree (MGA; $10M seed 2022, $13M Series A 2024). Free substitute: no insurance, which is why parks care.
ideas.why_they_lose: Agent- and lender-sold carriers cannot see the park, cannot collect through rent and cannot enforce mitigation. A park program needs a lease addendum that only the operator can sign.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (exclusive park programs plus community claims data) and switching costs (premium rides the rent bill).
ideas.earned_secret: Hypothesis, not interviewed: the park knows which homes are tied down, skirted and rewired, and the lease can force it. The insurer's pricing treats them all as the average, so the best homes subsidise the worst.
ideas.first_90_days: Collect three years of claims and mitigation data from one operator. Counsel memo on licensing, referral-fee limits and opt-out enrollment in two states (a park must not act as an unlicensed agent; I found Oregon ORS 90.527 allows required tenant liability cover only under conditions and no statute barring a named insurer, but did not check all states). Term sheets from a fronting carrier and reinsurer. Pilot in three communities.

ideas.title: Park Utility Co
ideas.one_liner: A water and sewer utility for manufactured-home communities that buys or operates the failing private systems under the parks, rebuilds them with state and federal money plus rate-based financing, and bills a utility charge instead of a lot-rent spike.
ideas.customer: Owners of 1960s-80s communities with private wells, septic and sewer lines; resident-owned co-ops; state agencies that run park-infrastructure grant programs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Park owner or co-op pays a monthly utility charge (assumed $60-110 per site). Signers: owner, co-op board president, or the state housing/environment agency that awards the grant.
ideas.problem: Aging water, sewer, electrical and road systems are common and owners cannot fund fixes without big rent increases. State grant demand far exceeds supply: Minnesota awarded $43.9M of $84.8M requested since 2020 and funded 21% of 2024 requests. Two small Maine co-ops cost about $50k and $67k per home (n=2). In Delaware, 98 of 170+ communities use on-site wastewater, many beyond a 30-year life.
ideas.solution: Standard assessment, design and construction packages; grant and revolving-fund applications written by the same team; long-term O&M contract; option to transfer to the town once the system meets standard. The utility is a separate asset from the land, so it can be financed on its own cash flow.
ideas.why_now: ARPA and infrastructure-law money is being spent now and is one-time (Vermont put $26M+ of ARPA into parks); owners face political fire over rent increases; private-equity buyers price deferred maintenance into rent.
ideas.wedge: Design-build and grant packaging for 10-20 mid-size parks in two states with active programs (Minnesota, Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine, Delaware). First customers: resident-owned co-ops that already have technical-assistance partners.
ideas.path_to_100m: Route 1, EPC: a 100-home park at ~$25k a site = $2.5M, so 40 parks a year = $100M; the one state with data requested ~$17M a year of grants, so this needs about a dozen states plus private financing and the one-time money fades. Route 2, utility revenue: $100M / ($90 x 12) = ~92,600 sites = 2.2% of 4.3M sites; if Delaware's 58% on-site ratio held nationally (one state only), ~2.5M sites are on such systems and the need is ~3.7% of them. Rate base for 92,600 sites at $25k = ~$2.3B, so route 2 needs an infrastructure-fund sponsor. No national backlog estimate exists; the first job is sizing it from a 50-park sample.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Park owners themselves (RUBS billing firms such as Conservice, memory); Nexus Water Group (ex Corix) and Essential Utilities for small systems (memory); municipal annexation; nonprofits (ROC USA and technical-assistance partners) for co-ops; state grant programs.
ideas.why_they_lose: Small-system utilities want towns, not 90-home parks with a 70-year-old network and a landlord dispute; nonprofits are capital-constrained; owners will not sell the pipes unless the deal lowers their rent-increase risk.
ideas.moat: Process power (standard designs and packaging) and, for route 2, scale economies in operations. Thin unless the utility asset is regulated or contracted for decades.
ideas.earned_secret: Hypothesis, not interviewed: owners defer what residents cannot see; the pipe is a separate business from the land, and splitting it out is the only way to finance it without a rent hike.
ideas.first_90_days: Sample 50 parks across three states for system type, age and condition; map the funded programs and annual size; get a utility-commission memo on jurisdiction in two states; sign one design-build partner.

ideas.title: Covenant Parks
ideas.one_liner: An owner-operator that buys manufactured-home communities under a recorded covenant (capped rent growth, pre-granted resident right to buy, resident equity glide path), financed with agency tenant-protection loans.
ideas.customer: Retiring owners of small and mid-size communities (most of the 43,000 are small), residents, and impact and pension capital that wants yield without a rent-gouging label.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Residents pay lot rent (~$9.0-9.4k a site a year). Signers: the selling owner (or broker in a right-of-first-refusal state) and the investment committee of a pension, insurer or impact fund. Debt: a Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac MHC lender.
ideas.problem: Residents own the home but rent the land, so rent increases (ELS core MH rent +5.6% in Q2 2026; UMH same-store rental +8.7%) compound against fixed incomes (~70% of ELS's MH communities are senior-oriented). States respond with right-of-first-refusal laws (NY 2023, Maine 2025-26; PA and MI bills in committee; federal bill Apr 2026). A court has held a resident association's right ended when it missed a statutory deadline, so sellers also want a clean process.
ideas.solution: Buy at market and record a covenant enforceable by a residents' association: rent growth capped at CPI or a fixed percent for 10 years, a pre-agreed formula price and 90-day path for residents to buy, and an equity credit funded from NOI above a threshold that converts toward resident ownership in years 7-10. Fannie's own tenant-protection terms (one-year renewable lease, 30 days' notice of increases, 5-day late grace) are the floor; the covenant goes beyond them.
ideas.why_now: Political pressure on private-equity owners is rising; agencies already price tenant-protected communities (Fannie financed 122 properties and 19,808 pads in 2024); owners in right-of-first-refusal states need a buyer who will not get litigated.
ideas.wedge: Two to four communities of 50-150 sites in a right-of-first-refusal state (NY or Maine) and two in a state without one, bought from owners aged 65+. First 10 customers: ten sellers found through brokers and the state manufactured housing association.
ideas.path_to_100m: $100M / $9,000-9,400 per site = ~10,700-11,100 sites = ~110 communities of 100 sites = ~0.26% of 4.3M homesites. Assets: Fannie's 2024 deliveries average ~$47.6k UPB per pad (mission-adjusted), so ~$70k value per pad at 65-70% LTV (assumed) = ~$0.75B of assets and ~$230-270M equity. Six to eight years at 15 communities a year. Share is trivial; capital and sellers' price expectations are the constraints.
ideas.who_does_it_today: ELS, Sun, UMH (public REITs); Havenpark, Yes! Communities and Apollo-backed funds (memory/pool file); ROC USA (nonprofit, ~346 resident-owned communities, $450M+ financed since 2008, $47M acquisition pool). Free substitute: owner sells to whoever pays most.
ideas.why_they_lose: REIT guidance and exit values depend on 5-6% annual rent growth, so they cannot promise caps or equity to residents. ROC USA cannot deploy more than its grant and CDFI capital. A for-profit covenant owner is neither.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (REITs cannot copy it without cutting their own rent growth); cornered resource in right-of-first-refusal states (seller trust).
ideas.earned_secret: Hypothesis, not interviewed: in a leased-land community the rent schedule is the largest driver of what a resident's home is worth on resale, so a recorded cap should raise home values; that is something the owner can sell.
ideas.first_90_days: Draft the covenant and a residents' association charter with a landlord-tenant lawyer in NY and one other state. Ask a Fannie/Freddie MHC lender whether a covenant earns tenant-protection pricing. Underwrite five parks. Line up $50M of impact capital.

ideas.title: Deposit Bridge
ideas.one_liner: A credit-union service organization that gives member credit unions a turnkey chattel program (origination, underwriting standard, servicing, repossession and title in every state) and a participation market, so deposit funding finally reaches manufactured-home loans.
ideas.customer: Credit unions, especially rural and community ones whose members live in manufactured homes.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Credit union pays an origination fee and servicing fee out of loan yield. Signers: CU chief lending officer and CEO, with ALCO and board approval; each founding CU commits capital to the CUSO.
ideas.problem: Banks have been leaving chattel; the three largest lenders (~76%, undated) are non-depository and one is funded by Berkshire, not deposits. Credit unions already originate and lobby for these loans (America's Credit Unions letter 24 Jul 2026; PremierOne program Aug 2025) but each originates a handful and cannot staff repossession, title perfection and servicing across states.
ideas.solution: A CUSO owned by credit unions: dealer and direct origination channel; one underwriting standard; sub-servicing plus repossession and in-place resale in all states; a participation market where the originating CU keeps 80-90% and sells the rest; later a securitization shelf for members.
ideas.why_now: Chattel is on FHFA's agenda; credit unions say they want secondary-market infrastructure; outside capital has just arrived (Zippy, Forum, Apollo), showing the loans are bankable at ~9%; deposit costs are lower than warehouse and ABS costs (assumed, not quantified).
ideas.wedge: Servicing, repossession and title as a shared service for 10-20 credit unions that already make some chattel loans, in Texas, the Southeast, Michigan, Washington and similar states.
ideas.path_to_100m: Managed book ~$6B (~10% of an inferred $45-65B stock). Servicing 0.55% x $6B = ~$33M; origination 1.25% x $1.2B a year = ~$15M; retained 10% slice of $600M at 9.5% = ~$57M gross interest; total ~$105M. That is 11-24% of annual originations ($5-11B) and is heroic: it needs credit unions to go from a small share to a large one within about eight years.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Triad markets chattel to credit unions (program terms not read); individual credit unions (PremierOne and others); Cascade and Zippy sell to investors, not credit unions. No CUSO for manufactured housing found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Triad, Clayton and the others earn on the spread and have no reason to arm deposit-funded scale; they also cannot use deposits. Credit unions alone cannot cover 50 states of repossession law.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in servicing and repossession; owners are the customers (cornered resource).
ideas.earned_secret: Hypothesis, not interviewed: a credit union's compliance officer is less afraid of chattel credit than of running a repossession in a state where they have 12 loans; the missing piece is operations, not capital.
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 25 credit unions on volume, losses and appetite. Get five founding CUs at $2-5M each. Counsel on the CUSO structure under NCUA rules (12 CFR Part 712, from memory) and participation rules. Sign one sub-servicer and one repossession/remarketing vendor.

ideas.title: Title I Reborn
ideas.one_liner: A Ginnie Mae manufactured-home MBS issuer that aggregates FHA Title I chattel loans from credit unions, banks and non-Berkshire lenders, giving the roughly half of the market Berkshire does not fund a government-guaranteed funding path now, and a GSE exit later if the pilots happen.
ideas.customer: Originators outside Berkshire (credit unions, community banks, Triad-type finance companies, new lenders) and, through them, chattel borrowers.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Originators pay a gain-on-sale discount and a servicing strip; borrowers pay the FHA premium inside the loan. Signers: originator CFO or treasurer (funding is their budget line) plus Ginnie Mae and HUD approvals.
ideas.problem: Private chattel funding is expensive: a Fitch-rated Cascade deal (likely 2024) carried 36.6% credit enhancement on collateral with a weighted FICO of 637, so lenders price at 9%+ and deny 65.6% of applicants. FHA Title I can insure up to 90% of loss on each loan and Ginnie can wrap the pool, but the program is dormant (Pew 2024: no loans made in recent years).
ideas.solution: Make Title I the standard product of a new issuer: closed-loan purchase from correspondents, a Title I underwriting and claims desk, and pooling into Ginnie Mae manufactured-home MBS. Target a borrower rate below the 9.24% market average (depends on FHA premium rates I did not find).
ideas.why_now: HUD indexed Title I limits to $105,532 single-section / $193,719 multi-section in Mar 2024 with annual review; Ginnie cut MH MBS issuer requirements in Feb 2024 (old rule: net worth $10M + 10% of outstanding MH MBS); FHFA's June 2026 proposal and S.4804 (17 Jun 2026) push chattel onto the policy agenda; a House Title I modernization bill was circulated in May 2026. All pending items are not law.
ideas.wedge: Buy Title I loans from 10 credit unions and small lenders in two states; the origination base can be shared with Deposit Bridge. First 10 customers: those credit unions.
ideas.path_to_100m: Gain on sale 2-3% (assumed) x $2.0B a year = ~$50M; retained servicing book ~$6B x 0.6% = ~$36M; warehouse carry and fees ~$14M (assumed). $2.0B a year is 20-40% of annual chattel originations ($5-11B) and is heroic; it only works if Title I becomes the default box for the roughly half of the market not funded by Berkshire.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Effectively nobody at scale: Pew reports few participating lenders and no recent loans. Private-label chattel ABS (Cascade, Clayton, Cavco deals) is the substitute.
ideas.why_they_lose: Berkshire's lenders do not need Ginnie (cheapest funding in the industry) and would cannibalise their own spread. Others had a barrier (net worth, low limits) that fell in 2024.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (HUD and Ginnie approvals plus a working Title I claims process) and process power.
ideas.earned_secret: Hypothesis, not interviewed: the binding constraint on chattel pricing is funding liquidity, not borrower credit. A guarantee converts an asset that funds at 36.6% enhancement into one that funds at a Treasury-linked spread.
ideas.first_90_days: Find out why the program is dormant: ask HUD's Title I desk for claim approval rates and processing times, interview two former Title I lenders, read Ginnie's MH MBS guide for current net worth and G-fee. Model the all-in borrower rate including the FHA premium; if it is not below about 8.5% (assumed threshold), stop.

ideas.title: Keyring
ideas.one_liner: A fund-backed landlord that buys new HUD-code homes at fleet prices, places them on vacant pads in other people's communities under a three-party agreement, and offers a rent-to-own path to residents the lenders denied.
ideas.customer: Households denied chattel credit (about 66% of applicants) who can afford about $1,000 a month for the home, and small and mid-size park owners who have pads but no capital to replace old homes.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Resident pays home rent plus lot rent in one monthly bill (park keeps lot rent, remits home rent). Signers: the resident (lease), the park owner or manager (placement agreement), and the credit committee of an institutional fund.
ideas.problem: FHFA reports 65.6% of chattel applicants denied, roughly 100,000 rejected applications a year (my arithmetic: 52,000 funded / 34.4% approval x 65.6%; an upper bound since one household can apply more than once). The pads exist (REIT occupancy 94-98%) but old homes in small parks are not replaced because owners lack capital and lenders do not lend.
ideas.solution: Buy single- and double-section homes from plants running below capacity (shipments -7.3% YTD), set them on vacant pads in partner communities, rent under a true lease with an option to buy at a fixed formula, report on-time rent to credit bureaus, and refer the resident to a Lot-Lender-type lender after 24-36 months. The lease and the lot lease are the lock.
ideas.why_now: Institutional capital has started to flow to the pool (Apollo $850M first close, Zippy, Forum); plants have empty capacity; the denial rate is documented in the FHFA proposal; REITs prove the model works (UMH ~11,400 rental homes at 95% occupancy). The ROAD Act chassis change and HUD's pending rules may lower home cost later (not final).
ideas.wedge: 100-200 homes in 10-20 partner communities of one regional owner in one state. First 10 customers: ten park owners with 10+ vacant or obsolete pads.
ideas.path_to_100m: At $1,000 a month for the home (assumed) one home yields $12,000 a year; $100M needs ~8,300 homes = ~$0.8B of assets at ~$95k all-in (Census retail prices $88-91k single-section, $161-164k double-section excluding setup; fleet pricing is my assumption). That is ~8% of one year's rejected applicants, ~2% a year over four years, or ~2% of annual shipments a year. Capital ~$0.8B with 70-75% debt (assumed).
ideas.who_does_it_today: UMH (~11,400 rental homes in its own parks), Sun and ELS in their own parks (rental counts from memory), Apollo-backed funds, local rent-to-own operators. No one found placing homes in third-party parks at scale.
ideas.why_they_lose: REITs place homes only in parks they own and do not buy small ones that lack scale; lenders do not lend to this customer; rent-to-own retailers do not do homes.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (fleet purchasing from underused plants) and switching costs (resident and park); weak on its own.
ideas.earned_secret: Hypothesis, not interviewed: the constraint on a small park is the home, not the pad; its owner will give up part of the first year's rent for a filled pad and a new home.
ideas.first_90_days: Counsel memo on rent-to-own and installment-sale law in the first two states (general rent-to-own statutes often exclude manufactured homes; New York has a 2019 manufactured-home-specific law; a 2022 North Carolina complaint alleges a park operator's used-home installment contracts were disguised contracts for deed); structure as a true lease with no equity forfeiture. Sign three park owners. Quote fleet pricing from two plants. Pre-wire one lender for the 24-month take-out.

ideas.title: Seam Map
ideas.one_liner: A fee-only service and data product that reconciles every policy's actual wording, the company's real AI deployments, and the insurance and indemnity clauses in its customer contracts, then turns the gaps into carve-back asks backed by wordings carriers already granted peers.
ideas.customer: US operating companies with $100M-$5B revenue and a full tower (GL/umbrella, cyber, tech or professional E&O, D&O). Beachhead: tech-enabled services, healthcare services, financial services and engineering firms that have signed AI addenda with uncapped indemnities.
ideas.payer_and_signer: VP Risk or Treasurer (General Counsel where there is no risk manager); CFO signs above $50k. Budget: risk-management advisory and legal operations, today spent on coverage counsel at hourly rates (a $30-100k per-program anchor is my assumption).
ideas.problem: ISO CG 40 47/40 48/35 08, Berkley's absolute exclusion and AI sublimits arrive differently on each line, and summary letters miss it (Fenwick: narrowing comes via base forms, definitions and carve-backs, not headline exclusions). The same AI incident can be excluded on GL, E&O and cyber at once, and customer contracts still demand cover that no longer exists. Peer carve-backs sit in brokers' private files.
ideas.solution: Parse every policy/endorsement into a clause graph; ingest customer MSAs' insurance and indemnity schedules and an AI-use inventory (SSO/OAuth, procurement, AI addenda); output a seam map by AI use x loss type showing which policy responds, which excludes, which contract demands cover; supply a carve-back kit (peer wordings plus the governance evidence pack underwriters want: human override, human-in-the-loop inventory, data provenance, accountable executive); negotiate at renewal, fee-only. Phase 2: place residual gaps into Mirror Policy or a carrier's affirmative endorsement with disclosed fees. Every outcome feeds a benchmark.
ideas.why_now: Exclusions attach through the whole 2026-27 renewal cycle; no admitted replacement product exists; carve-backs are being granted where governance is documented (design-industry example); Aon says documented governance improves terms.
ideas.wedge: Ten companies in an active renewal with an uncapped AI indemnity outstanding, sourced via 3-4 policyholder coverage-counsel referral partners; $35-60k diagnostic plus renewal support. First 90 days: 40 real tower sets under NDA, parse and have counsel hand-mark the same sets, sell five paid diagnostics before building the benchmark.
ideas.path_to_100m: About 28,000 US firms with a real tower (A: ~20,000 with 500+ employees (U, from memory) plus ~8,000 of $100M+ revenue below 500 employees) x $40k a year (A) = $100M at 2,500 customers, ~9% of reachable firms, year 5-6. Share is not heroic; the risk is the sales cycle against a free broker service. Benchmark sales and placement fees are extra and uncounted.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Brokers' internal analytics (Marsh, Aon, WTW, Gallagher, Lockton) bundled into commission; coverage counsel (Fenwick, Reed Smith, Haynes Boone, Shumaker) via alerts and hourly work; Haven Safety AI (niche workplace-safety paper); Coverwatch (flat-fee AI broker, $4.5M pre-seed Jul 2026, serves HOAs/VC-backed tech/contractors); AI carriers (Armilla, AIUC, Corgi) assess only to sell their own policy; GRC vendors build AI inventories but hold no insurance corpus.
ideas.why_they_lose: A broker is paid by premium and carrier contingents and cannot criticise those carriers' forms or be seen pushing premium down; law firms bill hourly and have no cross-client data; Coverwatch targets small buyers and starts from placement, not reconciliation.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (corpus of wordings, contract clauses and negotiated outcomes that big brokers hold privately), counter-positioning (fee-only, incumbents can't copy without cutting income), and switching costs (becomes the system of record for program documents).
ideas.earned_secret: The exclusion is rarely what hurts you; the seam is. Carriers deny by pointing at the other policy, and carve-backs are available to anyone who arrives with governance evidence and the wording a peer got. The mid-market never sees peer wordings.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign three coverage-counsel partners; collect 40 tower sets plus top-20 customer contracts under NDA; build the parser against CG 40 47, CG 40 48, CG 35 08, Berkley's absolute exclusion and the Beazley/QBE sublimit wording and validate against counsel's hand-marking; sell five paid diagnostics.

ideas.title: Warranty File
ideas.one_liner: Turn the signed AI and cyber application into an evidence-backed, time-stamped file, and get carriers to agree by endorsement not to rescind on verified answers: a contractual incontestability clause for commercial cyber, tech E&O and affirmative AI cover.
ideas.customer: Mid-market and enterprise buyers of cyber, tech E&O and AI cover ($10k+ premium), their brokers, and the carriers and MGAs underwriting them.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Two payers. Carrier/MGA pays per verified file (head of cyber or underwriting; budget: underwriting expense and claims leakage). Insured pays an annual subscription (VP Risk or CISO, CFO signs) priced against the premium it protects.
ideas.problem: Claims die by exclusion and by rescission/misrepresentation. Travelers v. International Control Services (C.D. Ill., 2022) sought to rescind a $1M cyber policy because a CEO-signed application said MFA covered privileged access and it only covered the firewall. AI answers (human override, HITL inventory, data provenance, accountable executive) are now on every application, given by IT, signed by a CEO who never saw the config, and different per carrier supplement. Underwriters ask more questions because they cannot trust answers.
ideas.solution: Connectors (identity provider, agent permission scopes, gateway logs, policy docs, org chart) collect evidence behind each answer, hash and timestamp it at signing; one standard File accepted by many carriers replaces bespoke supplements; accepting carriers add an endorsement that verified answers are conclusive absent fraud (life-insurance incontestability adapted); continuous attestation between renewals and a claim-time packet. Legal premise to verify: state rescission law, filing of the endorsement, anti-waiver rules.
ideas.why_now: Affirmative AI underwriters converge on a common evidence set (CSA, Aug 2026); carve-backs are conditional on governance; 4.4M US cyber policies in force, 55% endorsement-type (NAIC, 2024); carriers want faster quoting and fewer rescission suits.
ideas.wedge: Two mid-size cyber MGAs that want to quote AI-supplemented risks without a call, plus 50 insureds they write; start with the five AI answers underwriters ask most; 25-file pilot with counsel drafting the endorsement.
ideas.path_to_100m: Carrier side (A): ~400k policies/yr with $10k+ premium (my assumption, ~10% of 4.4M) x 35% verified x $250 = $35M. Insured side (A): 25,000 insureds x $3k = $75M (~6% of mid-market-and-up insureds). Total ~$110M by year 6-7. Heroic parts: 35% verified share and carriers actually signing the incontestability endorsement.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Outside-in scanners (Coalition, At-Bay, Cowbell, Bitsight, SecurityScorecard) see the perimeter, not agent permissions; GRC automation (Vanta, Drata, Secureframe) serves auditors with insurer discount partnerships; AIUC-1 certifies and insures but is tied to its own capacity; Armilla runs assessments for its own policies; trust-center vendors (SafeBase, Whistic) package evidence for customers, not underwriters. Searched for rescission protection: none found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Scanners can't see inside the firm; GRC tools are built for auditors and carry no carrier commitment; a single carrier can't waive rescission on answers it can't verify, and a certifier owned by one insurer won't be accepted by rivals. A neutral file lets competing carriers agree on the same clause.
ideas.moat: Network effects (carrier acceptance and insured adoption feed each other), switching costs (evidence history), a cornered legal asset (the filed incontestability endorsement), and data on which answers fail verification.
ideas.earned_secret: Rescission and misrepresentation, not exclusions, are how a clean-looking claim dies. The carrier doesn't want to rescind; it just has no way to trust the answers except by asking more questions. Make answers trustworthy and you remove both the questions and the fight.
ideas.first_90_days: Interview ten underwriters and five claims counsel on their last rescission files; map six carriers' AI supplements into one schema and measure overlap; build connectors for the top three identity providers and one gateway; get an LOI from one MGA for a 25-file pilot with counsel drafting the endorsement.

ideas.title: The Mutual
ideas.one_liner: A Bermuda-domiciled, member-owned excess liability mutual for independent frontier AI developers and the largest AI deployers, writing the $50M-$1B layers commercial markets will not, with training-data copyright carved out as uninsurable legal-regime risk.
ideas.customer: About 10-15 independent frontier and near-frontier developers (big tech groups self-insure) plus 200-400 large deployers (banks, insurers, health systems, retailers) needing excess above the $25-50M dedicated AI products.
ideas.payer_and_signer: General Counsel and CFO/Treasurer of each member, with board approval of the capital contribution. Budget: insurance and legal reserves. OpenAI reportedly holds ~$300M of cover via Aon and is weighing a captive/self-insurance from ~$60B of investor funds (FT via secondary summaries; Reuters could not verify).
ideas.problem: Insurers fear correlated losses from one upstream model; Aon's cyber head says the sector lacks capacity for model providers. 60+ P&C insurers filed AI exclusions for 2026 and dedicated AI products top out at $25-50M (one analysis, unverified). Anthropic's $1.5B authors' settlement was reported as funded from its own resources. Self-insuring from the cap table is capital-inefficient and signals unmanaged risk to investors.
ideas.solution: A mutual (Bermuda Class 3A/3B or a sponsored cell on an existing platform) owned by members who contribute capital plus premium; layered limits (e.g. $50M xs $50M to $500M) with reinsurance/ILS above retention; scope is idiosyncratic incident risk (wrongful death/BI, defamation, privacy, agent-caused financial loss, regulatory defence); training-data copyright excluded as one correlated legal regime that cannot be pooled; membership requires published safety practices and incident reporting; retrospective assessments for the tail and a seat at the table for any federal backstop (Stetler 2025 and a May 2026 arXiv paper describe pool plus government reinsurance; no bill exists).
ideas.why_now: First reported capacity shortfall at the top of the tower (OpenAI $300M vs multibillion claims); reported captive/self-insurance talks; carrier exclusions; the labs' investors (hyperscalers, chip makers) benefit when customer indemnities become credible.
ideas.wedge: Three or four labs plus 20 large deployers; $150-250M initial capital (A) from members, strategic investors and a reinsurer anchor, on a sponsored-cell platform so licensing does not gate launch.
ideas.path_to_100m: Premium (A): 12 developers x $30M (anchored on ~8-10% rate-on-line for a $300M tower) = $360M, plus 250 deployers x $1.2M = $300M, ~$660M total. Sponsor/manager revenue 10-15% fees plus profit commission = $80-110M (if it owns the paper, gross premium is revenue). Share check: $660M is ~14% of Deloitte's ~$4.8B 2032 global AI premium, heroic if Deloitte is right, though one company's reported $300M tower suggests the forecast is low.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Aon-placed towers (OpenAI), Marsh, Lloyd's syndicates, Munich Re (aiSure since ~2018), Armilla ($25M limits), AIUC, Corgi (Technology RRG, ~$4B reported valuation), Testudo ($10M); OpenAI discussing a captive; Anthropic pays settlements from its balance sheet. No lab-owned mutual found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Commercial carriers price for diversified books and can't hold multibillion single-name limits with no loss history; start-up carriers are capped at $10-50M by their capacity partners; a captive per lab can't diversify or buy reinsurance as cheaply; members who own the mutual share incident data and set safety conditions, which a seller of cover cannot require.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (capital depth is the product at the top of the tower), cornered resource (member incident data, reinsurance relationships, founding capital), switching costs (member equity and retrospective liabilities), counter-positioning against stock carriers. 7 Powers path reached via the 1985-86 ACE/XL and OIL/AEGIS/EIM precedent (dates from memory).
ideas.earned_secret: Capacity isn't short because AI risk is unpriceable; it is short because losses are correlated through one model and one legal regime. Split them: incident risk is poolable, legal-regime risk is not and shouldn't be insured. Mutuals that endured wrote the layer members could share and left the rest on balance sheets.
ideas.first_90_days: Interview GCs at five labs and ten large deployers on tower structure and renewal dates; retain Bermuda insurance counsel and a reinsurance broker to price a $50M xs $50M layer; draft the incident taxonomy and membership safety standard; line up one anchor reinsurer and one strategic investor.

ideas.title: Gate Meter
ideas.one_liner: Usage-based AI liability cover sold as a toggle on the model gateway or cloud marketplace: premium is a few basis points of the metered AI bill, priced from runtime telemetry the gateway already sees (tool scopes, spend caps, guardrail hits, human-override rates, model versions), never from content.
ideas.customer: Enterprises running production agents through a gateway or model platform (Portkey, LiteLLM, Cloudflare AI Gateway, Kong, cloud model platforms), with those vendors as distribution partners sharing the premium.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Head of AI platform or CISO turns it on; CFO or VP Risk approves; charge appears on the AI cost line, billed through the cloud marketplace; gateway/cloud takes a share (assumed, mirrors marketplace resale terms).
ideas.problem: Affirmative AI cover is priced from questionnaires and point-in-time tests, and testing costs more than a mid-market premium can carry. Exclusions force purchase but not at a price reflecting actual agent behaviour, and no loss dataset links behaviour to claims.
ideas.solution: An MGA on Lloyd's or admitted paper with a gateway SDK/proxy recording minimal telemetry; premium = metered usage x risk multiplier with credits for controls (spend caps, scoped tools, human approval on money movement), like a driving score; billed on the same invoice so premium is collected first and cannot lapse; evidence pre-captured for claims; an exclusive incident-level loss dataset grows with each deployment.
ideas.why_now: Enterprise agents now route through gateways; cloud marketplaces make resale billing standard; sublimits and exclusions create demand; 55% of US cyber policies are endorsement-type with little underwriting data (NAIC).
ideas.wedge: One gateway vendor and one MGA partner; 10 enterprises already paying for the gateway that have a customer contract demanding AI cover; price a $1-5M limit as a percentage of monthly AI spend.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assumption-heavy. Enterprise gen-AI spend tens of billions (Menlo ~$37B in 2025, from memory, unverified); suppose $60-100B by 2029 with a quarter metered via gateways = $15-25B insured base (A); premium 1.5-3% = $225-750M; MGA take 25-30% = $55-225M. $100M needs ~$350M premium, the upper half of the range, so it works only if cover attaches to a large fraction of gateway traffic.
ideas.who_does_it_today: No telemetry-priced AI cover found (searched; low-confidence negative). Adjacent: Armilla, AIUC, Corgi and Testudo sell questionnaire-and-test cover; Coalition's AI endorsement (Mar 2024) clarifies cyber triggers but isn't usage-priced; gateways and clouds sell guardrails, not insurance; hyperscaler copyright indemnities are narrow and limited.
ideas.why_they_lose: Gateways and clouds aren't licensed and won't carry third-party liability on a balance sheet; broker-sold MGAs can't see runtime behaviour; question-based underwriters can't price at usage granularity. Race-the-bundle risk: a hyperscaler could embed an insurer partner, so the MGA must own the loss dataset and a multi-gateway position.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (telemetry-to-loss dataset), switching costs (embedded in the billing path), process power in continuous pricing, scale economies in reinsurance terms. Pattern transferred: control the repayment channel plus usage-based auto insurance (Snapshot/Root).
ideas.earned_secret: Progressive and Root learned that observed behaviour at the control surface beats the application. For AI the control surface is the gateway or identity provider, not the insured's questionnaire, and a premium collected on the usage invoice never lapses.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign a design-partner letter with one gateway vendor; define the minimal telemetry schema and have privacy counsel confirm it excludes content; build a pricing prototype from public incident cases and have two underwriters challenge it; get an indicative reinsurance quota-share quote; check file-and-use rules for usage-based commercial rating in five states.

ideas.title: Waive List
ideas.one_liner: A per-policy generative-AI footprint score plus an exclusion rules engine that lets a carrier waive CG 40 47 (or attach only CG 40 48, or a sublimit) for the ~60-70% of its book with little AI in the causal chain, and tells the reinsurer why.
ideas.customer: Chief underwriting officers and commercial-lines product heads at the top ~50 US commercial groups and ~200 MGAs writing GL, E&O, cyber and D&O; wholesalers; reinsurers scanning cedent portfolios.
ideas.payer_and_signer: CUO or head of commercial product (for growth and retention, not compliance); reinsurers' portfolio-management heads for portfolio scans. Budget: underwriting data and portfolio management.
ideas.problem: Carriers are stuck in a blanket-attach equilibrium: ISO makes the exclusion optional, but they can't tell AI-light insureds from AI-heavy ones, and Verisk sells the uniform form to all and the data to both sides. A policyholder with no AI exposure pays the same for less cover and can shop. Hypothesis (unverified): treaties may require the exclusion on all cedent policies, so waivers need reinsurer permission. APRA (2026-04-30) and a June 2026 trade-body report are pressing insurers to quantify silent AI, giving the tool a second buyer.
ideas.solution: Footprint score from outside-in signals (public AI features, chatbots, job postings, tech stack, SDK strings, app stores, filings, vendor lists) plus consented inside-out signals (identity/SaaS inventory), with confidence band and renewal change alerts; a rules engine deployed as an API into policy-admin systems deciding full exclusion / advertising-injury only / sublimit / waive, with rationale recorded for the treaty file; portfolio scans for reinsurers and regulators; filed as a rating variable where required.
ideas.why_now: The 2026-27 renewal cycle is deciding who gets the exclusion; 2,369 filing records (one analysis) show carriers moved together; carve-backs are granted for documented governance.
ideas.wedge: Two or three regional commercial carriers and five wholesalers wanting to market 'no AI exclusion for verified low-AI businesses', at $4-8 a policy (A).
ideas.path_to_100m: Policy scoring (A): ~8M GL/E&O/cyber/D&O policy-terms a year (no sourced count; NAIC shows 4.4M cyber policies alone) x $6 = $48M at full share; portfolio/reinsurer scans (A): 60 x $0.5-1M = $30-60M; total $80-110M only if most large writers adopt. Honest ceiling for the exclusion decision alone is $40-70M; it reaches $100M only if the footprint becomes a filed commercial rating factor across lines. Path is heroic.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Verisk and Moody's (commercial analytics), LexisNexis Risk and Dun & Bradstreet (firmographics), cyber raters (Bitsight, SecurityScorecard, Coalition scan, Cowbell Factors, CyberCube, Kovrr), underwriting-ingestion start-ups (Cytora, Kalepa, Sixfold with $30M raised Jan 2026). None found selling an AI-exposure score or selective-exclusion engine.
ideas.why_they_lose: Verisk is conflicted: it licenses the uniform exclusion and benefits from uniform adoption. Cyber raters measure security posture, not AI use in the causal chain. Ingestion tools read submissions but don't decide exclusions. The carrier alone lacks the data and possibly the treaty room to act.
ideas.moat: Regulatory position (a filed rating variable is sticky), counter-positioning against Verisk's uniformity, data (renewal-by-renewal footprint history), switching costs via the policy-admin integration.
ideas.earned_secret: The exclusion is a data problem dressed as a wording problem. Carriers attach it to everyone because they can't see usage; the first carrier that can sells the same policy without the exclusion to the people who don't need it.
ideas.first_90_days: Pull 2,000 public and 2,000 private companies, build the footprint model from public signals and back-test against known AI incidents and announced deployments; ask three CUOs and two reinsurance heads whether treaties require blanket attachment; draft a rating-variable filing for one state to learn what regulators ask for.

ideas.title: Mirror Policy
ideas.one_liner: An exclusion-triggered difference-in-conditions (DIC) policy sitting beside a company's GL and umbrella program: it pays what the primary would have paid but for the gen-AI exclusion, priced as a percentage of the primary premium so the primary underwriter's pricing does the heavy lifting.
ideas.customer: Operating companies with real AI in the causal chain of physical or advertising harm: construction/engineering (scheduling, safety, estimating), healthcare operators, logistics/dispatch, manufacturing QC, retail, and product makers embedding gen AI (CG 35 08). Concrete case from the Reed Smith/Haven paper: AI in workplace-injury investigations and corrective-action programs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: CFO or VP Risk; budget: the GL/umbrella program as an incremental line; signer is whoever signs the renewal.
ideas.problem: The GL carrier can't sell the buy-back (its own filed form excludes it, adverse selection, no AI data); ISO can't file an affirmative form without loss data; surplus-lines AI start-ups sell financial-loss cover to AI vendors, not BI/PD/advertising-injury cover to operating companies. Review of state filings found no admitted replacement; I found no CG 40 47 buy-back. 'AI need not be the proximate cause', so the exclusion removes cover for the core risk of the business.
ideas.solution: A Lloyd's coverholder/MGA on surplus-lines paper issues a DIC mirroring the primary's limits, terms and defence obligations with the AI exclusion as trigger; price = percentage load on primary GL+umbrella premium (A: 5-12%), adjusted by control evidence (Warranty File) and the seam map; quota-share reinsurance with per-insured sublimit and annual aggregate; causation appraisal clause (Causation Desk); audit denials made on the exclusion without causation analysis to guard moral hazard; scale path: same wrapper for any ISO optional exclusion (PFAS, cyber-in-GL, abuse/molestation, silica, communicable disease).
ideas.why_now: Exclusions attach through the 2026-27 renewal cycle; buyers have nowhere to go for BI/PD; reinsurers still want casualty diversification.
ideas.wedge: Ten mid-cap operating companies in construction, healthcare operations and logistics with agentic workflows live, recruited via Seam Map customers and 2-3 wholesalers.
ideas.path_to_100m: Base (A): ~20,000 firms with 500+ employees (U) at $600k GL+umbrella, ~110,000 mid-market firms at $50k, ~4,000 very large at $4M = ~$31B. AI-only: 30% with material exposure by 2028 = $9B x 8% load = $750M at full take-up; 40% attach = $300M premium; MGA at 25% = $75M. AI alone cannot reach $100M of MGA revenue even at 100% share. As a general exclusion-wrap (add non-AI exclusions at 3% load, 25% attach = +$230M) total ~$530M premium and ~$130M revenue by year 7-8; if it writes own paper, $100M is ~20% of that premium.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Armilla (Lloyd's, up to $25M, model error/financial loss), Testudo (up to $10M), AIUC, Corgi (Technology RRG plus new admitted carrier aimed at small business), Coalition and AXA XL (cyber endorsements), Beazley/QBE (10% sublimits). Coverage counsel advise on carve-backs. No BI/PD buy-back or liability-wrap DIC for AI found.
ideas.why_they_lose: The primary carrier can't undercut its own filed form and fears adverse selection; AI start-ups price AI-model risk and distribute to AI companies, not through the operating-company renewal; the mirror borrows the primary's underwriting so it needs no AI loss model to start.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against form-bound carriers, cornered resource (loss dataset across many primaries' AI-excluded claims), scale economies in reinsurance, switching costs once the mirror sits inside the program.
ideas.earned_secret: Coverage counsel know the pollution precedent: ISO's absolute pollution exclusion in the mid-1980s was followed by a separate environmental-liability market (from memory), not a better primary. The exclusion tells you where the standalone market will form, and pricing as a percentage of the primary is how you start without data.
ideas.first_90_days: Collect 30 GL and umbrella loss runs and test the 5-12% load with two GL underwriters; interview three wholesalers on surplus-lines placement of a follow-form DIC; draft the form with counsel including trigger on denial or probable denial under CG 40 47/40 48/35 08; ask two reinsurers for an indicative casualty quota share with an AI cap; check state DIC and surplus-lines eligibility.

ideas.title: Causation Desk
ideas.one_liner: A pre-agreed neutral panel that decides within 30 days whether a loss 'arose out of' generative AI, written into policies as an expert-determination clause like the appraisal clause in property policies.
ideas.customer: Carriers and MGAs (claims), insureds and their counsel. First: AI-native carriers and the Mirror Policy and Mutual structures, which can write the clause into their own forms; then mid-size GL and E&O carriers wanting to avoid declaratory-judgment suits.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Chief claims officer, from loss adjustment expense: a declaratory-judgment fight costs $250-600k (A) vs $12-35k for a determination (A). Where the insured wins on causation the carrier pays the fee; otherwise split.
ideas.problem: Exclusions trigger on an AI connection, 'not how much of the work AI touched', and some say 'in any way involving'. From 2027 the central fact in contested claims is whether gen AI was in the causal chain, and evidence perishes (AI logs sit with vendors; retention windows unverified). Carriers fear a published adverse ruling on a form filed ~2,369 times so prefer quiet denial; insureds can't afford declaratory actions; forensics firms (Surefire Cyber and others) work for one side.
ideas.solution: Neutral panel (ex-ML engineers, digital-forensics examiners, coverage lawyers) with a published protocol. Clause: on first notice an evidence-preservation protocol starts (log-collection templates and standing arrangements with model vendors' compliance APIs) and the panel issues a written finding of fact on causation (AI absent, incidental, contributing, dominant), binding on facts not on how the policy wording applies. Fixed fees; cooling-off bar for panelists; a determination corpus becomes the industry's cross-claim record.
ideas.why_now: Exclusions attach through the 2026-27 cycle; disputes arrive 2027 onward (denied-claims client alerts already exist); AI logs are short-lived; vendors are building compliance APIs.
ideas.wedge: Ten claims from AI-native carriers or any carrier willing to pilot the clause; $15-25k per determination.
ideas.path_to_100m: NAIC counts nearly 50,000 cyber claims in 2024. Assume 8% involve AI by 2030 (A) = 4,000; assume 1.5M third-party GL/E&O/D&O claims a year (A, unsourced) with 2% AI-involved = 30,000; 20% go to determination (A) = ~6,800 x $18k = ~$122M. Fragile assumptions: AI-involved rates and carriers adopting the clause; if not adopted this is a $10-20M expert practice. Path is heroic.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Nobody as a neutral. Digital-forensics firms (Surefire Cyber, Kroll, Mandiant) serve one side; forensic engineers (Exponent and others) handle physical failure; AAA/JAMS lack AI forensic capability; the AI Incident Database, OECD monitor and MIT tracker are free but carry no loss or causation findings.
ideas.why_they_lose: A firm retained by the carrier or insured is conflicted; courts and ADR bodies lack the forensic skill; carriers can't build a neutral themselves. The clause makes the neutral part of the contract before the dispute.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (neutrality accrues with each finding, like AAA's), switching costs (clause sits in forms), cornered resource (determination corpus), process power (evidence-preservation protocol).
ideas.earned_secret: In coverage fights the expensive part is not the law but the fact of what the tool did, and the fact perishes. Evidence preserved neutrally on day one is worth more than any brief.
ideas.first_90_days: Interview five coverage litigators and five claims heads on their last AI-related denial; draft the clause and protocol with counsel; recruit a nine-person panel; ask two large model vendors what log export is available and for how long; pilot on any open dispute.

ideas.title: Trigger
ideas.one_liner: An independent model-provider incident index and calculation agent, built on continuous probing of frontier-model behaviour, that serves as the trigger for parametric covers, industry-loss warranties and cat bonds on systemic AI events.
ideas.customer: Reinsurers and carriers/MGAs of AI risk (to buy systemic capacity), insurance-linked-securities funds (to hold it), and enterprises dependent on one provider (contingent BI cover plus a monitoring service).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Chief reinsurance officer or head of ILS pays index and calculation-agent fees; enterprise CFO/CRO buys parametric cover; ILS fund manager buys notes. Budget: reinsurance spend, which already exists.
ideas.problem: Carriers and reinsurers are pulling capacity over correlated risk through one upstream provider (Aon on capacity; CSA). A May 2026 arXiv paper says an 'AI-using cedent pool' is hard to define, an AI cat bond lacks a trigger metric, and recommends a named provider-incident trigger. No investor will take systemic AI risk without a trigger they trust; property has PCS, cyber took years to get one.
ideas.solution: Define provider-incident events with objective thresholds (availability, integrity via behaviour regression on fixed probe suites or a compromised/poisoned model, provider-disclosed security breach, sudden deprecation/ban); run a probe network of thousands of canary tasks across providers, regions and versions plus status feeds and signed attestations; act as independent calculation agent with published methodology and annual third-party audit; fund it from an enterprise 'model weather' monitoring subscription (SLA tracking, drift alerts); later add a parametric MGA and structuring partnerships with reinsurance brokers.
ideas.why_now: Frontier providers are few and concentrated; agent deployments are creating dependence; insurers cite correlated risk; ILS investors want uncorrelated returns; the paper names the gap.
ideas.wedge: Sell the monitoring product to 200 enterprises with agent workloads ($20-40k, A) and give two AI-risk MGAs a pilot index for their reinsurance conversations.
ideas.path_to_100m: Three streams (all A): monitoring 1,500 enterprises x $30k = $45M; index and calculation-agent fees 0.5-1% on $5B of referenced limit = $25-50M; parametric MGA margin ~$30M; total ~$100-125M by year 6-7. Heroic pieces: $5B of referenced limit (cyber cat bonds are a much smaller market today, unverified) and 1,500 paying enterprises.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Parametrix (parametric cloud-outage cover, from memory), Verisk's PCS (property and, I believe, cyber designations), CyberCube and Moody's cyber models, Swiss Re/Munich Re parametric products, Downdetector/ThousandEyes/Datadog for outages, public leaderboards (Artificial Analysis, LMArena) for performance. Free AI incident trackers carry no thresholds or dollar impact. No insurance-grade provider-incident index found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Reinsurers can't calculate their own trigger (investors want independence); Verisk is conflicted as seller of exclusions and data to both sides; outage monitors don't measure integrity or tie to a contract; leaderboards aren't independent of the providers.
ideas.moat: Credibility as independent calculation agent (hard to earn, slow to lose, network effect among investors), a cornered longitudinal dataset of provider behaviour, switching costs once contracts reference the index.
ideas.earned_secret: Cat-bond markets exist only because an index investors trust exists first. The trigger design is the product and capital follows; whoever writes the definition of a provider incident writes the market.
ideas.first_90_days: Interview five reinsurance structurers and three ILS fund managers on what a trigger must look like; draft event definitions and test them against known provider incidents and public outage/regression events since 2024; build the first probe suite for three providers; ask Lloyd's AI-risk managing agents which of their events could not be settled with such an index.

ideas.title: National ESA provider network (Forage + CAQH + Headway for ESA vendors)
ideas.one_liner: A payer-agnostic provider credential, one-invoice billing to every ESA/scholarship wallet, and two-day payout for the tutors, therapists, pod leaders and curriculum sellers who get paid from choice dollars in every state.
ideas.customer: Independent tutors, OT/SLP therapists, music/art teachers, learning-pod leaders, online course and curriculum vendors working in ESA states; the family-facing verified directory is a by-product.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Provider pays a $29-99/month subscription plus about 1.5% for two-day payout (A); states, SGOs and wallet platforms pay $10-25 per credential check (A). Signer: the provider owner; at state level the ESA program director or treasurer.
ideas.problem: Every program keeps its own vendor list (Tennessee via Student First Technologies, NC state portal, Florida MyScholarShop, others via ClassWallet/Odyssey) so a provider re-enrolls state by state (S). Indiana providers do a state credential check then a separate ClassWallet onboarding (S). EdChoice reports vendor payment takes 7-30 days and admin approval up to 21 days (S). States do not know who their vendors are: Arizona deactivated 900+ tutors for accreditation in 2023 and a 2025 report found no cross-check against disciplinary records (S); Texas touted 2,400 vendors at launch but its marketplace listed about 1,200 on 7 July (S).
ideas.solution: (a) A reusable provider record (licence, background check, disciplinary cross-check, accreditation, W-9); (b) adapters to every wallet/portal so the provider sends one invoice and gets one remittance; (c) the network pays the provider in two days and collects from the wallet (small factoring spread on state-backed money); (d) a verified-status directory for families.
ideas.why_now: Texas ($1B), Tennessee, Alabama and Indiana launched or expanded in 2025-26; from 1 Jan 2027 the federal credit adds 600-700 SGOs, each of which may pay non-school vendors directly only if 'verified' and unrelated to the student (S, proposed regulation REG-117199-25), creating a credentialing need at every SGO.
ideas.wedge: Therapists, tutors and pod leaders in Texas and Arizona with $50k-$500k/year of ESA revenue; ask two state ESA offices to accept the network credential as a pre-check (Texas says it rarely rejects vendors, S). First 10 customers: 10 multi-state or high-volume providers who feel the re-enrollment pain.
ideas.path_to_100m: Non-tuition vendor spend is about 41% of Arizona ESA dollars (tuition and fees 58.7%, ADE via House testimony, S; EdChoice's older cohorts show 83% tuition, S) so I use 35%. ESA-type flows ~60% of $16B state programs by 2029 (A): $16B x 60% x 35% = $3.4B, plus ECCA vendor-paid scholarships ~40% of a $5B central case = $2B (A) => ~$5.4B of provider billings. At a 5% take that is a $270M pool, so $100M needs ~37% of it (heroic). Cross-check: 40,000 active providers x $2,500/yr. In Treasury's $26B ECCA case the pool is ~$690M and the share needed is ~14%.
ideas.who_does_it_today: ClassWallet marketplace/directory, Odyssey vendor marketplace, Student First Technologies (Tennessee), MyScholarShop (Step Up, Florida), state portals (NC, IN) (S). Outschool and Varsity Tutors sit inside ClassWallet's NC marketplace (S). Forage (YC, $40M Series B, SNAP/WIC/HSA/FSA acceptance API) has no ESA product I could find but is built to expand to other restricted-spend categories (S). Headway/Alma credential therapists for insurers, not ESAs (U). No national ESA directory found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each platform is paid by one state and wants an exclusive vendor list; none will export a credential that makes a rival's job easier, and states cannot share across their own statutes. A neutral network paid by providers gets the whole supply side.
ideas.moat: Network economies on the supply side plus switching costs (billing history, payout advance).
ideas.earned_secret: As a state ESA director with 15+ years you learn the binding constraint is willing, credentialed supply, not family demand or money, and that you cannot fix it because you are bound to one platform vendor and one statute while the platforms are rivals. That directors want a portable credential is an insider hypothesis (U); the fragmentation facts are sourced (S).
ideas.first_90_days: Onboard 200 providers in Texas and Arizona; build adapters to ClassWallet and Odyssey vendor flows; measure days-to-paid against the 7-30 day baseline; get one state office to accept the credential; stand up a small payout float.

ideas.title: School payments and capital OS (Toast for private schools and microschools)
ideas.one_liner: Multi-payer tuition acceptance with automatic reconciliation, next-day payout, and working-capital advances repaid by sweeping scheduled ESA/SGO payments through a wallet partner.
ideas.customer: Private schools and microschools that take ESA, voucher and SGO money (about 29,730 private schools and about 75,000 microschools exist, S; the number taking choice money is not sourced).
ideas.payer_and_signer: School pays 0.5-0.8% on volume plus $150-300/month SaaS plus a fee on advances (A). Signer: head of school or business manager; microschool founder.
ideas.problem: Choice money does not arrive on the payroll calendar: Texas private-school awards pay 25% on 1 Jul, 25% on 1 Oct and 50% on 1 Feb 2027 (S). A school with 100 TEFA students at $10,474 (S) is owed ~$524k that lands six months after teachers start. Arizona stopped authorizing payments in Nov 2022 and later released ~$22M overdue, including to a small school shopping for a bank loan (S). Banks will not lend against a family-controlled, audit-exposed state account; the proposed rule also makes schools return any SGO payment in excess of the student's costs (S).
ideas.solution: (1) Accept ESA wallets, SGO, voucher, 529 and parent ACH/card on one invoice with mid-year withdrawal and refund handling; (2) pay the school next day; (3) advance against scheduled payments underwritten on payer calendar, enrollment contracts and payer history, repaid by payment direction through the wallet partner; (4) later, family gap loans and facilities loans.
ideas.why_now: TEFA, Alabama, Indiana and Florida expansions; 31% of Catholic schools already take choice money (S); federal-credit wallets arrive in 2027.
ideas.wedge: Ten Texas private schools/microschools with TEFA students (an Alpine school said it was listed as a vendor but unsure what is required, S) plus a $2-3M warehouse line (A) for advances.
ideas.path_to_100m: Platform handles ~$5B of choice-funded tuition (~30% of $16B state flows, A) x 0.6% net = $30M; 6,000 schools x $2,400 SaaS = $14M; advances on 30% of that volume for ~4 months = ~$500M average outstanding x 14% = $70M. Total ~$114M. Needs ~6,000 schools and ~30% of choice-funded tuition volume: heroic.
ideas.who_does_it_today: FACTS/Nelnet (~12,000 schools, $9B tuition managed in 2018, S) and its new Compass for SGOs; Building Hope Lending Lab (ESA bridge loans for microschools up to 100 students) and a $675k Stand Together/Building Hope microschool loan fund that needs a signed lease (S); Charter School Capital (receivable sales for charters, S); ClassWallet/Odyssey pay vendors but do not lend.
ideas.why_they_lose: FACTS earns on family-paid fees and card processing and sells SIS lock-in; diverting volume to payer-side lockbox rails runs against that model. CDFIs are grant-capped; banks cannot underwrite; platforms cannot lend against state money they administer. FACTS is the competitor most able to copy this; the edge is risk pricing off payment calendars and speed.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (billing + payments + capital in one login), process power in underwriting (payer behavior data), scale economies in cost of funds.
ideas.earned_secret: A 25-year school business manager knows the loss event is not a family defaulting but a payer freezing, clawing back, or paying six months late, and that the job is chasing four to six payers per family. A lender that sees the payment calendar and the wallet can price that; a bank cannot. The 'spreadsheet of remittances' detail is an insider hypothesis (U); the payment schedules are sourced (S).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign ten schools; negotiate payment direction with one wallet partner; stand up a $2-3M facility from a specialty lender; run the first advances against Texas Oct 1 and Feb 1 tranches.

ideas.title: K-12 education wallet and custody (HealthEquity for scholarship dollars)
ideas.one_liner: A bank-partnered wallet for the 600-700 new SGOs: they move scholarship dollars into it on day one (counted as 'spent' for the 90% test), it holds them until families spend, pays vendors directly, and shares the yield.
ideas.customer: SGOs, including dioceses, school networks and community foundations that become SGOs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: SGO pays a wallet fee from its 10-15% overhead room; vendors pay for fast pay and interchange; provider keeps a negotiated share of yield. Signer: SGO executive director with the board treasurer.
ideas.problem: New SGOs must meet a 90%-of-income spending test by the end of the year after receipt, must verify spending, prevent duplication, pay tuition directly to schools and keep a segregated account per state (S). Donations cluster in Q4 while scholarships are paid Aug-Jun. Most SGOs are small nonprofits with no treasury or payments capability.
ideas.solution: FBO accounts at a sponsor bank (pass-through insurance), ACH/direct pay to schools, debit and marketplace for non-tuition items, receipts/reimbursement controls the rule requires, SKU-level eligibility checks (the HSA/FSA IIAS model, S), a vendor network (idea 1), a published yield-sharing schedule, later 529 K-12 and family top-ups.
ideas.why_now: The 1 Oct 2026 proposed regulation defines a 'qualified digital wallet' and says funds moved to it count as spent if the SGO keeps no ownership (S); comments close 1 Dec, hearing 15 Dec, final rules likely 2027; credit starts 1 Jan 2027.
ideas.wedge: Three early SGOs (including a Missouri-style EAO), then dioceses and school-network SGOs; sponsor bank signed before launch.
ideas.path_to_100m: Central ECCA case $5B/yr (A): ~60% of gifts arrive in Q4 so average balance ~$2.9B x 3.5% yield (HealthEquity's cash yield, S) x 60% kept = $61M; plus 0.5% servicing on $5B = $25M; plus 1.7% interchange on 25% card/marketplace spend = $21M. Total ~$107M, which needs essentially all of the central case. In Treasury's $26B case the same math is ~$560M, so $100M needs ~18%. Analog: HealthEquity earns ~$36 custodial revenue per account on 17.8M accounts and $36.5B assets (S). Highest ceiling, least certain volume.
ideas.who_does_it_today: ClassWallet (runs Missouri's privately funded EAO programs on a shared wallet; one EAO reports $26.2M to 57 schools, S), Odyssey (ACH after proof of delivery + marketplace, S), FACTS Compass (fundraising and enrollment first, more in 2027, S), ACE Scholarships (services), banks/BaaS (U).
ideas.why_they_lose: State-contract SaaS vendors price per account, cannot keep yield on state money (Idaho ended Odyssey's contract in Oct 2024 after reports of non-educational purchases and interest earned, S) and sell through RFPs; serving 600 small nonprofits needs self-serve KYB, a sponsor bank and a treasury product they have not built (U, contracts not visible).
ideas.moat: Scale economies in cash and cost of funds, switching costs (SGO records, vendor network), bank relationship as a cornered resource.
ideas.earned_secret: Structural, not anecdotal: the proposed rule says funds moved into a qualified wallet are treated as spent at transfer if the SGO does not retain ownership (S). Any SGO that wants to clear its 90% test early has every reason to move cash in at once, so the wallet operator becomes custodian of the whole float. Float on state money is politically toxic; float on private SGO money is a contract term.
ideas.first_90_days: File a comment letter by 1 Dec asking Treasury to confirm wallet-transfer treatment and clarify who owns interest; sign a sponsor bank; pilot with three SGOs; draft the yield-sharing schedule.

ideas.title: SGO host (Fidelity Charitable for scholarships)
ideas.one_liner: A registered multi-state SGO that hosts branded affiliate funds for dioceses, school associations and networks that want their own donors but cannot run 25F compliance.
ideas.customer: Affiliates: diocesan and Catholic-school foundations (5,829 Catholic schools, S), Christian-school associations, day-school federations, school networks, community foundations.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The host SGO (nonprofit) contracts a service company at fair market value for marketing, donor care, awarding, verification and compliance, paid from the host's overhead room (10% of income, up to 15% of activities under the 85% safe harbor, S). Signer: host board; on the affiliate side, the foundation director.
ideas.problem: Each SGO must be a 501(c)(3) public charity, keep a segregated 25F account per state, pass annual audits, register in the IRS portal, send donor acknowledgments by 31 Jan and IRS reports by 28 Feb, avoid earmarking and give 10+ scholarships to students not all at one school (S). Small affiliates cannot carry that load but want to keep their donors.
ideas.solution: A multi-state host (using the multistate safe harbor, S) with affiliate funds that have their own donor pages and branding while the host holds the legal duties, runs awards, income verification (idea 5), wallet (idea 3) and filings; a service company operates it under a fair-market contract.
ideas.why_now: The credit starts 1 Jan 2027 and the comment window runs to 1 Dec 2026; vendors sell software to SGOs, not a legal wrapper.
ideas.wedge: Three affiliates: a diocesan foundation, a Christian-school association, a day-school federation. Get a legal opinion on branded funds first.
ideas.path_to_100m: Service-company revenue of ~8% of hosted gifts (marketing plus operations, inside the overhead cap, A): $100M needs $1.25B hosted = 25% of the $5B central case or 5% of Treasury's $26B. Net margin is thin; the digest's caution on gross versus net take applies.
ideas.who_does_it_today: FACTS Compass (120+ SGOs and group programs, S), Odyssey SGO suite, ClassWallet, ACE Scholarships (all-in-one services), LearningSpring, Vouchive, AwardSpring (600+ organizations), Foundant (S); statewide nonprofits such as Step Up (3% admin cap in Florida) act as SGOs themselves. I found no white-label host.
ideas.why_they_lose: Software vendors cannot be a charity; incumbent SGOs will not host rivals' donors; affinity groups will not give up brand control.
ideas.moat: Regulatory status in 30 states (cornered resource), scale economies in compliance, affinity-brand switching costs.
ideas.earned_secret: Giving to school scholarship funds is affinity-driven (parish, school, denomination), not cold-digital, and every affiliate needs identical compliance. Arizona individual giving fell ~23% in a year despite 28 years of habit (S), which is why affinity matters. That affinity thesis is an insider hypothesis (U); the compliance list is sourced (S).
ideas.first_90_days: Recruit three affiliates; obtain counsel's opinion on earmarking and same-school tests for branded funds; file a comment asking Treasury to bless affiliate funds; pick a state of formation; draft the service-company contract.

ideas.title: Neutral eligibility and anti-duplication clearinghouse (National Student Clearinghouse for K-12 scholarships)
ideas.one_liner: A consent-based ledger of who was awarded what for which expense across SGOs, state ESAs and vouchers, plus a reusable eligibility credential verified once.
ideas.customer: SGOs, wallet/platform vendors and state agencies.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Per-recipient annual fee of ~$12, per-credential fee of ~$10, plus a state integrity-analytics subscription (A). Signer: SGO CFO or compliance lead; state ESA director. Budget line: the proposed rule's required 'reasonable procedures' (S).
ideas.problem: The proposed rule requires every SGO to run systems to detect duplicate awards to the same student for the same expense; stakeholders name duplicates and misuse as the main fraud sources (S). Treasury prices income verification at ~$100 per household (S) and every SGO and state repeats it. No platform can see another platform's awards.
