ideas.moat: Neutral position (counter-positioning against every translator) that works like a rating agency or auditor, valuable once examiners and Big 4 audit partners accept the format (cornered resource); a library of per-language and per-platform gotcha test packs; process power from repeated cutovers.
ideas.earned_secret: Every failed cutover fails on a behavior nobody wrote down (a sort tie-break, a month-end-only rounding rule, a restart that reruns a half-posted file). Production data, not specifications, is the only complete spec, and it exists only in the system being replaced (background knowledge).
ideas.first_90_days: Build a replay harness around a z/OS batch emulator and a DB2 snapshot differ; partner with one integrator running AWS Transform and one mid-size insurer; run an equivalence report on one batch suite; show the certificate format to the insurer's internal auditor and a Big 4 audit partner. Legal: no US rule found that mandates independent equivalence certification, so demand is for defensible evidence; keep independence clean (never paid by the translator for the same program).

ideas.title: The Middle: a sponsor-level AI-native maintenance utility for PE portfolios
ideas.one_liner: A private-equity sponsor signs one framework agreement and every portfolio company gets fixed-unit-price AI-native application maintenance and development from a shared pod, below the big Indian firms' minimum ticket and clean to carve out at exit.
ideas.customer: PE-owned US companies with $50M-1B revenue. S&P Global counts 82,927 US private companies owned by PE (Aug 2025); I assume about 8,000 fall in this band (my estimate).
ideas.payer_and_signer: The sponsor's operating partner or head of portfolio operations signs the framework (value-creation-plan cost take-out is the budget line); each portfolio CIO or CFO issues work orders.
ideas.problem: A $200M-revenue portfolio company spends roughly 3-5% of revenue on IT (my estimate), a fifth on offshore-deliverable maintenance and development bought one company at a time from tier-2 vendors with no leverage and no standard security pack. The majors will not take sub-$5M tickets. Few sponsors built shared outsourcing, historically because it complicates exits; AlixPartners now says portfolio teams are warming to low-touch shared services and Zinnov says PE increasingly centralizes vendor management.
ideas.solution: A shared delivery utility with unit prices (per ticket resolved, per accepted story, per application-year), 40% below current tier-2 spend on common stacks (Salesforce, NetSuite, Dynamics, Workday, .NET, Java), a sponsor-level pre-approved security and data pack (30-day onboarding), 90-day exit rights and a portable runbook so a buyer at exit gets a clean data room. AI-native pods in India with a US account lead, measured by the Meter.
ideas.why_now: Cost take-out pressure with AI deflation visible (clients seek 25-30% cuts); the H-1B/onsite model is unreliable; delivery agents are good enough for common-stack maintenance with human oversight (Infosys announced a Devin-based hybrid-pod model in Jan 2026).
ideas.wedge: One mid-market sponsor with 25+ companies on overlapping stacks; first 10 customers are ten of its portfolio companies, starting with the most repeated cheap work (Salesforce/NetSuite administration and enhancements, tier-2 application support).
ideas.path_to_100m: About 8,000 companies x roughly $1.2M offshore-deliverable spend = about $9.6B pool (my estimate). $100M is 1.0% of the pool, about 83 companies, e.g. six sponsors with 14 companies each. Revenue is delivery revenue as principal, not a fee on spend.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Tier-2 Indian and US vendors and boutiques (Endava, Perficient, Slalom, Globant, EPAM at the upper end); PE-focused IT support firms; EY and Zinnov selling shared-service platforms as consulting (EY claims 50-60% five-year savings from labor arbitrage, plus 10-15% centralization and 12-18% automation; vendor claim); AI-native single-platform entrants (Tessera Labs, $60M Series A, SAP first; AppFactor, $4M seed).
ideas.why_they_lose: Tier-2 vendors have no sponsor-level standard and no incentive to ease exits. Consultancies sell a design, not the running service. AI-native startups sell one platform and one buyer at a time with long enterprise cycles; the sponsor channel compresses that.
ideas.moat: Scale economies on shared runbooks and prompts across a portfolio; switching costs inside each company; an exclusive sponsor framework (cornered distribution).
ideas.earned_secret: An operating partner can mandate a vendor across the whole portfolio within the first 100 days after a close and reports cost take-outs to investors; what stops them is fear of a tangled carve-out. Sell clean carve-out, not savings (background knowledge).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign one sponsor and three pilot companies; stand up a 40-person pod; get SOC 2 Type 1; publish the unit price card and exit-transfer runbook. Legal: portfolio-company data-protection agreements, each company contracts separately so the sponsor takes no liability.

ideas.title: Clawback: an IT-services contract recovery factory with claims financing
ideas.one_liner: A recovery-audit factory for IT-services contracts: find money vendors owe under rate cards, escalator caps, volume tiers, service-credit clauses and AI pass-through terms nobody enforces, take 20-30% of what comes back, and advance cash against signed credit memos.
ideas.customer: The same roughly 1,500 enterprises as the Meter, plus mid-market firms with $2-20M contracts that cannot afford a measurement project.
ideas.payer_and_signer: No budget line needed: the fee is contingent on recoveries, so the CFO or Controller signs with the CPO co-signing. This removes round 1's no-budget failure.
ideas.problem: Contracts leak after signature. An outsourcing consultant says line-item review yields at least 1% of contract value per unchecked year and about 5% of line items cannot be explained; a recovery vendor claims 3-7% (vendor claim); Forrester reports earn-back clauses mean many providers never pay service credits. Contingent recovery audit is a proven model (bids of 13.5-40% of recoveries; PRG-Schultz bid 20% flat in a 2004 state procurement).
ideas.solution: A rules library built for IT-services contracts (named-resource billing, FTE-to-ticket mismatches, volume tiers not applied, escalators above caps, benchmarking rights never used, service-credit earn-back traps, regulatory-change pass-through surcharges, duplicate and shared-resource billing). Look-backs on 24-36 months of invoices; recoveries land as credit memos; Clawback advances 50-70% of agreed credit memos from a credit facility and keeps the spread. A monitoring subscription bridges into the Meter.
ideas.why_now: Vendors fighting to hold revenue are more willing to settle legacy claims inside renegotiations (about 25% of contracts a year); AI-clause deals create new rights with no enforcement; any visa surcharge billed while the H-1B fee was in force and then vacated is a refund claim (a hypothesis to test, not a fact found).
ideas.wedge: Contracts renewed in the last 36 months that carry an escalator; look-backs on ten clients sourced through procurement-association members and PE operating partners.
ideas.path_to_100m: At 3% leakage of the $100B pool and a 25% fee the annual fee pool is $750M, so $100M needs 13%. At 1% leakage the pool is $250M and it needs 40% (fails); at 5% it is $1.25B and 8%. The idea works only if the first ten audits show at least 3% recoverable. No independent leakage study exists; the audits are the test.
ideas.who_does_it_today: PRGX (recovery audit; has an IT-contract-labor case study); Vaudit/VendorAudit (claims $1B+ of vendor spend audited); Cotiviti in healthcare; telecom-expense and freight-audit firms in adjacent categories; ISG and law firms at renewal; internal audit.
ideas.why_they_lose: Generic AP auditors lack IT-contract logic (FTE pools, resource units, earn-backs); advisers do not work on contingency for old invoices; neither can match a ticket to a login. Specialization is the only wedge and it is thin.
ideas.moat: Process power (a rules library that improves with every audit) and, with financing, a balance-sheet edge. Honest verdict: the weakest moat of the eight; its value is as the no-budget entry that funds the Meter.
ideas.earned_secret: Earn-back clauses let a provider avoid a credit by hitting a target for two consecutive months, so credits go unpaid even when quality is bad; the unpaid-credit pool is largest in contracts older than 24 months.
ideas.first_90_days: Run five contingency look-backs to measure the real recovery rate; build the rules library from them; set up a $10M receivables facility with a specialty lender; decide at day 90 whether the measured rate clears 3%.

ideas.title: Run-Base Shrinker: an energy-services company for the application estate
ideas.one_liner: We cut the run bill your offshore vendor is paid to maintain (repeat incidents, zombie applications, dead custom code), fund the engineering ourselves, and keep 30-50% of verified savings for three years.
ideas.customer: CIOs and CFOs of US enterprises with $20M+ of annual run spend with offshore application-management vendors; first wedge SAP ECC shops that have not yet released conversion budget.
ideas.payer_and_signer: CIO (budget owner) and CFO sign; Internal Audit signs the savings method. Budget: the run-cost line being reduced, so it is self-funding. The structure is the ESCO model: LBNL puts US ESCO revenue at $10.7B in 2024 (85% energy-savings performance contracts); no equivalent exists for IT run costs.
ideas.problem: Offshore maintenance is billed on volume (tickets, FTE pools, applications supported). The highest-return work, permanently fixing the few causes behind most tickets and deleting what nobody uses, shrinks the vendor's own revenue, so it sits in a problem-management clause and never gets done. Rimini Street argues publicly that time-and-materials structures have no provision for root-cause problem management. Zombie applications are common (an old CIO survey found about 15% underused).
ideas.solution: Four levers, each measured by the Meter: repeat-incident elimination (AI root cause, patch PR, regression, deploy); zombie application retirement from authentication and network logs with compliant read-only archives; dead custom code removal (first SAP custom Z objects before S/4 conversion; mainstream ECC maintenance is said to end 2027, not re-verified); licence and infrastructure right-sizing. Fees: 30-50% of audited run-cost reduction for 36 months; we fund the engineering.
ideas.why_now: AI makes root-cause fixes and code deletion cheap enough to fund on spec; clients demand 25-30% cuts; the SAP deadline gives CFOs a date; unit-priced and fixed-price deals pass reductions through. Contract check: volume bands and reduced-resource credits can leave a 20% ticket cut worth only 8-12% of fees unless the baseline resets, so target unit-priced or soon-to-renew contracts.
ideas.wedge: Ten SAP ECC enterprises: retire custom code before paying an integrator to convert it. Second wedge: zombie-application retirement for companies consolidating vendors.
ideas.path_to_100m: About $30M offshore run base per client x 12% reduction over 3 years x 35% share = $1.26M per client-year, so 79 clients (my estimates; the first audit tests the 12%). Pool view: if run-related offshore spend is about $40B, 12% is $4.8B/yr of savings and our 35% is $1.68B, so $100M is 6% of the shared-savings pool.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Rimini Street (third-party support for packaged software, about $430M revenue, background knowledge; sells cheaper support, not shared-savings shrink); the AMS vendors themselves (never); consultancy portfolio rationalization billed as projects (Deloitte, Accenture, TCS); app-retirement software (OpenText InfoArchive, Solix, Informatica; about $2.2B software market in 2025 per a vendor-style report); AI-native maintenance startups: AppFactor ($4M seed), LogicStar (pre-seed), DataAgent ($10M pre-seed, Sep 2026), Kodesage ($6.6M seed), Tessera Labs ($60M Series A, SAP upgrades).
ideas.why_they_lose: Vendors lose revenue by doing it. Retirement software sells licences, not outcomes. AI-native maintenance startups sell a cheaper replacement for the same volume, not a smaller volume with shared savings. Consultancies bill time for analysis and leave before the savings.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (the incumbent cannot copy it without cannibalizing); a cross-client root-cause and retirement library; a 36-month contract tail; an Internal-Audit-approved savings method (process power).
ideas.earned_secret: In a typical account a short list of applications and defects generate most tickets and stay unfixed because the billing unit is the ticket. No published repeat-ticket share was found, so the first deliverable is measuring it (delivery-practice knowledge, unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Three design partners on unit-priced or soon-to-renew contracts; instrument their ITSM for a repeat-ticket heatmap; retire the first five zombie applications; agree the savings method with each client's Internal Audit; line up a working-capital facility to fund engineering ahead of savings.

ideas.title: Evergreen Release Utility: flat-price release remediation, Guidewire first
ideas.one_liner: A flat price per release per instance that keeps an evergreen platform estate current: predict what each vendor release breaks, patch the customer's extensions and integrations, regression-test and deploy, starting with Guidewire in P&C insurance.
ideas.customer: Guidewire reports more than 570 insurers in 43 countries; then enterprise tenants of Salesforce, ServiceNow, Workday, Oracle Fusion and Dynamics.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Insurer CIO or head of core systems signs; COO co-signs. Budget: the recurring upgrade, regression and application-management program now paid to integrators.
ideas.problem: Evergreen platforms force releases on a fixed calendar (Guidewire documents say three updates a year; other sources say two upgrades with at least one mandatory; sources conflict). Each carrier pays an integrator separately for near-identical regression and remediation; Deloitte runs a dedicated migration factory. Guidewire's Aug 2026 Qusar release sells AI agents for claims and underwriting, not release remediation. Platform vendors cannot sell upgrade services against their integrator channel, integrators bill time and materials, test-tool vendors sell seats.
ideas.solution: For each release, diff release notes against the tenant's configuration and extension inventory, predict breakage, generate patches, run an AI-maintained regression suite and deploy through the customer's pipeline, for a flat fee per release per instance with a defect-escape guarantee. Learn fix patterns across tenants that permit it (no customer data crosses tenants).
ideas.why_now: AI code and test generation is good enough for extension code; onsite certified-consultant labor got scarcer and dearer while the visa fee was in force (the fee is now vacated; whether the scarcity persists is unverified).
ideas.wedge: Ten mid-size P&C carriers (premium $1-10B) on Guidewire Cloud that are not tied to a single large integrator.
ideas.path_to_100m: Guidewire: 60 carriers (10.5% of 570) at about $1M/yr = $60M (release-driven regression and remediation spend assumed $1.5-3M/yr per carrier before a 35-50% discount; my estimate). Other platforms: 200 enterprise tenants at about $200k = $40M. Total $100M; needs roughly 10% of Guidewire's base, high for a first vertical.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Integrators (Deloitte, Cognizant, Accenture, Capgemini, Endava, TCS, Infosys, Wipro); release/test tools (Tricentis, Panaya, Opkey, Provar, Copado); Tessera Labs (SAP first, says it also covers Salesforce, Workday, Oracle); FurtherAI (Guidewire technology partner with insurance AI agents); Guidewire's own agent framework; AppFactor.
ideas.why_they_lose: The structural blockers above. But this is the most contested of the eight: Guidewire can ship the same agents, Tessera has $60M, and the cross-tenant learning claim is arguable because customers will not share configuration.
ideas.moat: Weak and honest: repeated-release data and a flat-price offer; strongest only if the platform vendor certifies the utility as a partner (a Guidewire or ServiceNow co-sell relationship would be the real moat).
ideas.earned_secret: Hypothesis to test: most breakage per release sits in a small set of extension points (integrations, custom fields, forms, rating and reporting code) that vendor release notes already list; the customer-specific part is a long tail.
ideas.first_90_days: Get Guidewire partner status; instrument one carrier's last two releases retrospectively and show predicted breakage matches actual defects; price the first flat-fee release.

ideas.title: The Foundry: wholesale AI-native delivery for the incumbents
ideas.one_liner: Sell accountable, per-unit, AI-native delivery to the IT-services firms themselves, so they can meet 25-30% price cuts with variable cost instead of a pyramid they cannot restructure.
ideas.customer: Mid-tier IT-services firms (Persistent, Coforge, Mphasis, Hexaware, LTIMindtree, Zensar, Birlasoft, Cyient, Sonata and US mid-tier peers; roughly $10B+ combined revenue for the first five, background knowledge) and delivery units of the majors.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Chief Delivery Officer or COO with the CFO. Budget: cost of revenue, replacing subcontractor spend (4% of revenue at TCS, 8.1% Infosys, 11.3% Wipro, 12.6% HCLTech in the June 2024 quarter) and bench cost.
ideas.problem: Persistent's CEO reports clients want the same work for 25-30% less; top-5 Indian firms' headcount fell 7,389 in FY26. Delivery heads' P&Ls are tied to headcount and utilization and the fresher-to-lead pyramid is a social contract. Tools exist (Devin, Copilot, internal platforms) but a tool does not change the price card or the acceptance risk, and mid-tier firms often lack integration and verification capacity.
ideas.solution: A supplier that takes whole units of work (L2/L3 tickets, regression suites, migrations, change requests) at a posted unit price with written acceptance criteria. AI-native pods plus human verifiers (displaced mid/senior engineers with pod-profit participation) return accepted outputs. The vendor keeps the client relationship and margin spread; the Foundry carries the acceptance warranty. White-label, with client flow-down for AI use and subcontracting.
ideas.why_now: Repricing wave; the new buyer is the incumbent itself (Infosys announced a Devin collaboration with Cognition on 2026-01-07 including hybrid pods and managed service inside client environments); the mid and senior layers are shrinking and available (TCS cut about 12,000 mostly mid/senior roles; senior attrition 16%); a unit that can be audited (the Meter) is now possible.
ideas.wedge: One mid-tier vendor; one unit type (L2/L3 tickets on Java, .NET, Salesforce); five of its client queues in shadow mode for 90 days, priced 35-45% below that vendor's fully loaded internal cost.
ideas.path_to_100m: A vendor with $1.5B revenue routing 5-7% of delivery ($75-105M) through the Foundry, or five vendors at 1.5-2%. One signed mid-tier anchor reaches the target, which is the speed argument; the cost is customer concentration.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Cognition (Devin) sells agents to Infosys (no evidence found of Cognizant, Wipro or HCLTech deals); Factory and others (not verified); the majors' internal platforms (TCS WisdomNext, Infosys Topaz, HCL AI Force); tier-2/3 subcontractors priced by headcount; Turing/Andela-type staffing networks; AI-native integrators selling direct (Tessera Labs).
ideas.why_they_lose: Tool vendors sell seats and leave the price card and acceptance risk with the buyer. Direct AI-native integrators compete with incumbents for the same clients so incumbents will not feed them data or queues. Internal platforms stall on headcount KPIs. Subcontractors are paid by head.
ideas.moat: Cost curve (unit price falls as the verified library grows), switching costs inside the vendor's delivery workflow, a cornered resource in senior pod partners. Honest risks: Cognition and the incumbents can move to outcomes themselves; client consent clauses can block subcontracted AI delivery; one anchor customer is one point of failure.
ideas.earned_secret: A delivery head cannot cut their own pyramid, but can sign for a subcontracted unit, because subcontracting is already 8-12% of revenue at three of the four largest firms. The supplier line is the only place in the P&L the pyramid does not defend (percentages sourced; the rest is inference).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign a letter of intent with one mid-tier vendor; define three unit types and acceptance tests; run 500 tickets in shadow; line up three senior verifiers per pod; check client consent and data-residency clauses on the five queues.

ideas.title: Hot Spare: shadow-sourcing as a service
ideas.one_liner: Pay a second, AI-native provider to shadow-run 5-10% of your live application tickets so your exit plan is tested, your price is benchmarked, and a challenger already has a foothold on the day you rebid.
ideas.customer: Regulated enterprises with critical outsourced applications: banks, insurers, asset managers, payments firms, healthcare payers. First EU-exposed US financial groups (DORA applies to EU entities including subsidiaries of US parents), then US institutions under the 2023 interagency third-party guidance (expects contingency planning; verify), then any CPO wanting price leverage.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Head of Operational Resilience or COO and the CRO sign; CIO and CPO co-sign. Budget: operational-resilience testing and vendor-risk management, plus a share of the application-management line moved to the shadow vendor.
ideas.problem: About a quarter of contracts reopen each year and clients are cutting vendor counts (Google cut $50M from HCLTech), while DORA Art. 28(8) and RTS 2024/1773 Art. 10 require documented exit strategies, tested for critical functions (secondary summaries; verify at EUR-Lex). Exit plans are paper: sample termination-for-convenience clauses run 40-85% of estimated remaining value on declining schedules plus unamortized investment, and a second vendor who is not paid to be there cannot test anything. Without a credible exit, a 25-30% price demand is a bluff.
ideas.solution: A neutral orchestrator sets up read-only copies of the client's own ticket queue, assigns 5-10% of tickets to a pre-qualified challenger in shadow (the incumbent's answer is the control), captures knowledge artifacts, and reports cost per ticket, reopen rate and time to resolve for both. After a quarter the challenger writes on low-risk tickets. Annual outputs: a DORA-style exit test report with evidence and a price-comparison pack. Revenue: orchestration/evidence fee plus margin on the shadow vendor's work.
ideas.why_now: Renegotiation wave, vendor consolidation, DORA in force since Jan 2025, and a wave of funded AI-native challengers (Tessera, AppFactor, Cognition-powered pods) that lack a way into incumbent accounts.
ideas.wedge: Three EU-exposed US banks or insurers with an operational-resilience program already testing exit; then seven more through Big 4 operational-resilience practices that need an execution partner.
ideas.path_to_100m: Per client: a 10% shadow slice of a $20M application-management contract is $2M of shadow work; at a 25% orchestrator margin plus $0.2M evidence/orchestration fees, net revenue is about $0.7M, so 143 clients; as principal on gross billings (about $2.2M per client) it is 46 clients. Addressable base roughly 750-1,000 regulated enterprises with $20M+ outsourced critical-application spend (my estimate): net view needs 14-19% share (high), gross view about 5%. Warning on paper-only exit products: NCC Group's escrow arm Escode earned only about GBP 66.5M in FY2025, grew 2%, and is being explored for sale.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Third-party-risk platforms (OneTrust, ProcessUnity, Prevalent, Archer) provide templates and registers; Big 4 operational-resilience advisory; software escrow (NCC Group/Escode, Iron Mountain); knowledge-capture tools (Kodesage, Hypercubic); in-house multi-vendor tower strategies; ISG and Everest at rebid.
ideas.why_they_lose: Incumbents cannot support their own exit; lock-in is their moat. Advisers write exit plans but do not run drills. Escrow covers code, not operating knowledge. Challengers cannot afford the unpaid pilots that a hot spare turns into paid ones.
ideas.moat: Two-sided network (challengers need a foothold, clients need a credible exit), the benchmark data it generates, and an evidence format supervisors recognize (cornered resource once two or three supervisors accept it).
ideas.earned_secret: The exit penalty, not price, is the incumbent's real moat, and exit plans are never tested because testing needs a second vendor who is not paid to be there. Paying the second vendor for a slice turns the plan from fiction into an operating fact.
ideas.first_90_days: Pick three regulated clients; stand up read-only ticket copies; pre-qualify two AI-native shadow vendors; run 5% shadow for a quarter; produce the first exit-test report and walk the client's supervisor-facing team through it. Legal checks: DORA wording at EUR-Lex and whether supervisors accept shadow-run as testing; MSAs restricting third-party access to vendor-written ticket notes (run on client-owned data); privacy and security of replicated tickets.

ideas.title: One Knock: the annual home check that replaces six statutory visits and fixes what it finds
ideas.one_liner: A two-ticket technician team does the gas check, electrical test, alarm test, a 29-hazard screen and small fixes in one 75-minute visit a year, so the landlord pays for one access attempt and starts no legal clock it cannot meet.
ideas.customer: Mid-size and large social landlords (housing associations, ALMOs, councils) with 10k-60k homes that tender gas, electrical, alarms, stock-condition and fire-door work as separate single-service lots.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Director of Assets / Compliance (or COO). Budget lines: gas servicing, electrical testing, alarms, stock-condition surveys and cyclical fire-safety checks, normally 4-6 separate contracts. CEO and board sign because the executive team owns the liability under the safety standard and Awaab's Law.
ideas.problem: Statutory visits are bought as separate lots, each with its own no-access rate and paperwork (a failed visit costs about GBP25-100). Mears calls UK housing compliance 'largely single service led' and 'fragmented'. Under Awaab's Law any hazard a contractor or inspector sees counts as the landlord becoming aware, which starts the 5-working-day safety-works clock. From 30 Nov 2026 phase 2 adds electrical, fire and explosion (boilers), falls, excess cold and heat, structural and hygiene hazards to the same clocks, and social landlords now owe five-yearly electrical inspections (existing tenancies by 1 Nov 2026 per one secondary source).
ideas.solution: A crew of two: a technician with Gas Safe and electrical-inspection tickets plus a hazard screener with a fix kit. One visit produces the gas safety record, the EICR when due, alarm tests and replacements, a photo-and-sensor screen against the 29 HHSRS hazards (logger left for 14 days), a stock-condition and asbestos-register refresh, and on-the-spot fixes under about GBP150 (handrail, extractor fan, door undercut, smoke alarm). Larger findings go to the landlord with evidence attached and the clock already running. One home record feeds the landlord's housing system; one access process with tenant-chosen windows and evening/weekend slots.
ideas.why_now: Phase 2 goes live 30 Nov 2026; the awareness trigger means uncoordinated visitors create unfunded clocks; the new five-yearly electrical duty has a 1 Nov 2026 deadline for existing tenancies; the 2035 Decent Homes Standard is condition-based; compliance lots come up for renewal in 2027-29.
ideas.wedge: Start as a subcontractor to a landlord's existing gas contractor for 1,500 homes: gas plus alarm test plus hazard screen. Customers 2-10 are mid-size housing associations and ALMOs (8-25k homes) whose gas and electrical lots expire in 2027-28.
ideas.path_to_100m: Visit-based compliance pool (my assumptions; no compliance-only tender price found): gas 3.0M homes x GBP85 = GBP255M; electrical 4.4M/5 x GBP200 = GBP176M; alarms GBP40M; stock condition 20% a year x 4.4M x GBP70 = GBP62M; other cyclical (fire doors, FRA, legionella, asbestos re-inspection) GBP100M. Total about GBP633M, plus on-the-spot fixes at 30% of homes x GBP120 = GBP158M, so a pool of about GBP790M. Revenue about GBP180 per home-year. GBP77M ($100M) needs about 430,000 homes a year, roughly 10% of stock and 10% of the pool, about 19 landlords of 22,000 homes. Not heroic. Reachable payers: about 200 large groups plus about 150 stock-holding councils.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Mears (bought Pennington Choices Sep 2025 for GBP9.5M, GBP17M revenue; manages about 450,000 homes); Sureserve (3,700 staff); Aspect, Gas Call, Equans and in-house teams (from memory); partial linking by Darlington and North Northamptonshire (alarms tested with gas service or EICR); Switchee and Aico sensors. Four searches found no landlord running a single multi-skilled annual visit for gas, electrical, alarms and stock condition.
ideas.why_they_lose: The primes sell compliance as per-visit, single-service lots; a combined visit cuts their visit revenue by roughly a quarter to a third and needs dual-ticket staff they do not employ. Landlords split gas, electrical, fire and survey budgets across different owners, so nobody is paid for fewer visits.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against per-visit revenue; scale economies (route density lowers cost per home); cornered resource (dual-ticket technicians, see the Guild idea); switching costs (five-year cycle plus the home record).
ideas.earned_secret: The cost of compliance is the knock on the door, not the engineering. Six separately tendered contractors each knock, fail and chase, and since Awaab's Law each knock is also an inspection that starts a legal clock the landlord has not budgeted to meet. One visit, one record, one clock.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign one mid-size landlord for a 1,500-home pilot due Jan-Mar 2027; hire and cross-train 6 technicians; measure visits per home, no-access rate, findings per visit and minutes from finding to clock start against the incumbent baseline; publish a phase-2 clock map before 30 Nov; price against the sum of the separate lots.

ideas.title: Hot-Spot Contract: capitated root-cause care for the worst 5-8% of homes
ideas.one_liner: Take a fixed annual fee per home for every repair, disrepair claim and root-cause fix on a landlord's highest-cost homes, guarantee the fix for five years, and keep the savings.
ideas.customer: Landlords with 25k+ homes and a visible disrepair or damp-and-mould problem (London boroughs, large ALMOs, large housing associations).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Finance Director and Director of Assets. Fee funded from responsive repairs plus the disrepair, compensation and legal budgets, with root-cause works moved to capital. CEO and board approve a multi-year contract.
ideas.problem: Per-visit contracts reward repeat visits: the same home is patched 5-8 times a year while the root-cause fix (ventilation, roof, leak, heating controls) is a capital item nobody proposes. Damp is in 7% of social homes (11% on a broader measure). The right to sue and legal clocks now punish patching. Lambeth's disrepair legal costs plus damages were GBP15M in 2024/25.
ideas.solution: Rank each landlord's homes by trailing three-year cost of repairs, disrepair and compensation and contract for the top 5-8%. Diagnose with sensors and a competent assessor, do the root-cause works, take over all repairs on those homes for a capitated fee of about 80% of trailing cost, and give a five-year guarantee that pays for any repeat visit, reinsuring the tail once 12-24 months of loss data exist. This is the high-cost-patient programme and accountable-care shared-savings model from managed care, moved to buildings.
ideas.why_now: The right to sue (phase 1 live, phase 2 on 30 Nov 2026) turns repeat failures into claims; fixed recoverable costs for disrepair are exempt until Oct 2028 so claimant costs stay uncapped; landlords' lenders watch interest cover.
ideas.wedge: A 500-home pilot at one mid-size housing association, then landlords already burned by disrepair claims. Data access is the gate; landlords own their job-level data.
ideas.path_to_100m: Responsive-plus-void cost is about GBP600-800 per home a year in council benchmarks (2016-21); assume hot-spot homes cost about four times that, about GBP2,800 (assumption). A 5% cohort is about 220,000 homes, a pool of about GBP616M a year. At a GBP2,200 capitated fee, GBP77M ($100M) needs about 35,000 homes: 16% of the cohort, 0.8% of all stock, about 15-20 landlords handing over 1,500-2,500 homes each. Revenue is gross of crew costs; net margin assumed 12-18% plus shared savings and guarantee premium. Kill test: if the top 5% of homes carry under about 15% of repair spend in three landlords' data, drop it.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Mobysoft RepairSense (repeat-repair analytics, 108 staff, GBP109,800 a year at Flagship); Switchee Mould iQ (monitor and treat, 92,000 homes across 3 housing associations); Aico HomeLINK; Plentific; Made Tech; the primes' own total-asset contracts. None was found taking capitated risk.
ideas.why_they_lose: Primes earn on visits and run 5.7% margins that cannot absorb outcome risk. Analytics and sensor vendors cannot do the work or carry a guarantee. Insurers exclude gradual damp as a maintenance matter and no damp-and-mould cover product was found.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (a cross-landlord loss dataset that prices building risk, which nobody has); counter-positioning against visit-based pay; 5-10 year contracts; reinsurance relationships. Legal premise to check: whether an uncapped repeat-repair guarantee is a 'contract of insurance' under FSMA; keep it a service warranty from the party doing the work and get FCA perimeter advice; multi-year capitation needs a Procurement Act 2023 route.
ideas.earned_secret: Repair spend is skewed, and the contractor who sees it earns more by patching. Root-cause fixes are capitalised, patches are revenue, and capitalising lifts the EBITDA-MRI interest-cover covenant, so the landlord's own books favour the fix that no one proposes. Evidence is partial (a 2022 case study of one housing association found heavily skewed costs; Ombudsman findings cite temporary fixes and poor diagnosis); no published Pareto split was found.
ideas.first_90_days: Get job-level data from three landlords and measure concentration (the kill test); pick one 500-home cohort and set a baseline; fix and instrument the top 100 homes; write the guarantee wording with a broker and counsel.

ideas.title: Clock Desk: pay per closed Awaab case, not per hour
ideas.one_liner: A vetted assessor network and a case desk run the entire statutory clock (intake, 10-day investigation, 3-day summary, 5-day make-safe, 12-week works, early settlement of any claim) for a fixed price per closed case, with a pooled fund behind the deadlines.
ideas.customer: About 200 large landlords and 150 councils whose in-house surveyors are overwhelmed; Lambeth's 347 cases in three weeks is the signal.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Director of Housing Services or Repairs; a new line carved from damp-and-mould, disrepair and legal budgets. The Chief Operating Officer signs.
ideas.problem: Landlords are hiring surveyors and letting damp-and-mould frameworks (Riverside's GBP657M framework across 12 regional lots). Winter brings long lead times. The right to sue makes missed clocks costly and Clyde & Co expect a 'significant increase in claims activity' from phase 2. No competent-person scheme or managed case service exists.
ideas.solution: A credentialed network of assessors (environmental health, building surveyors, damp specialists) with our own protocol, QA and professional-indemnity cover; remote-first triage using tenant video and sensors; a case desk that issues the written summary, builds the evidence file, scopes works, books crews, triggers decant and settles claims early with fixed-fee panel counsel; and a reinsured pooled fund that pays when the Desk misses a clock. Pattern transferred: outcome-priced replacement of a high-volume measurable function (Sierra) plus credentialed expertise sold to a new concentrated buyer class (Mercor, Surge).
ideas.why_now: Phase 2 on 30 Nov 2026 multiplies hazard types beyond what damp surveyors cover and phase 3 follows in 2027; Ombudsman repair complaints are up sharply; councils can fine up to GBP7,000 from 22 Jun 2026 and inspect only about one in three complaints. The duty is about a year old, so no standard exists yet.
ideas.wedge: One council or housing association with 100+ cases a month; run the clock for 60 days on the hardest 20% of cases. Customers 2-10: London boroughs and large ALMOs with disrepair pain.
ideas.path_to_100m: All assumptions mine: 8% of 4.4M homes gives about 350,000 cases a year by 2028 (Lambeth's first three weeks annualise to about 18% but include backlog). Fee GBP450 per case plus own works on 40% of cases at GBP1,100, about GBP890 per case. Claims: 25-40k a year nationally (claims against councils rose 392% 2020-24) at about GBP2,500 per claim handled. GBP77M ($100M) = 64,000 cases (GBP57M) + 8,000 claims (GBP20M): about 18% of cases and about 25% of claims. That is heroic. If case volumes are half my estimate it needs 35% and the idea fails. If Awaab's Law reaches private renting (no date; 2027+ at the earliest) the needed share halves.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Landlords' in-house surveyors (Karbon, Lewisham hiring); damp specialists such as Insite Group; frameworks (Riverside, LHC); Plentific; Alphatec ClaimControl (claims software); panel law firms (Ward Hadaway, Clyde & Co, Devonshires publish guidance); Zurich Municipal for liability cover; the primes.
ideas.why_they_lose: Panel solicitors bill by the hour, so fast resolution cuts their revenue. Primes cannot sign for deadlines that depend on landlord-controlled steps. Marketplaces carry no liability. Insurers exclude gradual damage.
ideas.moat: The protocol and registry becoming the standard if a landlord consortium or regulator adopts it; assessor supply network effects; claims data that prices the fund. Legal: the fund is insurance, so use a regulated carrier or reinsurer and act as TPA/MGA first; litigation only through SRA-regulated counsel; the credential is contractual because no statutory scheme exists.
ideas.earned_secret: The clock, not the inspection, is the product. Landlords do not lack surveyors so much as a single party accountable for every deadline from intake to works, and everyone who touches the case profits from delay (hourly lawyers, per-job contractors).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign the pilot, recruit 25 assessors, run 100 cases through the clock, publish on-time rate and cost per case, and take reinsurance quotes on the fund.

ideas.title: Home Safety Technician Guild: the scarce input behind every other idea
ideas.one_liner: A landlord- and levy-backed guild trains career changers into dual-ticket home-safety technicians (gas plus electrical plus hazard screening) and bills hours under take-or-pay offtake from landlords and primes with funded backlogs.
ideas.customer: The 20-40 landlords and primes holding phase 2/3, electrical, MEES and adaptations backlogs that cannot hire.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Director of People or COO plus Director of Assets. Budget is agency and sub-contractor labour (already paid) plus unspent apprenticeship levy.
ideas.problem: CITB's 2026-2030 outlook needs about 41,000 extra construction workers a year (206,000 over five years). Training providers estimate 27,000 extra gas engineers by 2028 and 15,000 electricians in five years (commercial sources). Single-trade routes take 3-4 years; employers train for their own contracts and lose staff to rivals.
ideas.solution: A 24-month blended route for career changers (ex-forces, retail and logistics leavers aged 25-40) covering Gas Safe, electrical inspection and testing, hazard screening and small repairs, with paid work from month 4. The guild is employer of record; landlords commit hours at about GBP48 an hour for trainees and GBP62 for qualified staff. Training is funded by levy transfers (up to 50% of unspent levy; 83% of councils in an LGA survey did not use their full allowance; from 1 Aug 2026 the 10% top-up ended and new funds expire after 12 months). Twist: landlords pay partly in housing, offering key-worker tenancies from their own stock. Pattern transferred: capex-supercycle pass-through to scarce trades.
ideas.why_now: The shortage is documented, the levy rules changed on 1 Aug 2026, and phase 2/3, MEES and the electrical duty all draw on the same technicians.
ideas.wedge: A 40-person first cohort for two landlords or primes; customers 3-10 are the same landlords' neighbours in each region.
ideas.path_to_100m: GBP77M ($100M) = about 1,250 technicians billed at about GBP62k; with 60% completion that is about 420 starters a year for three years. About 1.4% of roughly 90,000 social-housing operatives (my estimate). Gross margin about 12-18%, so revenue-rich and profit-thin; its main value is as the supply engine for One Knock, Void Clock and Falls on a Clock.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Prime-run academies (Mears, Wates, Kier, from memory); colleges; recruiters (Hays social housing); housing associations' own placements (one has launched a 20-place scheme); private Gas Safe training providers; CITB.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each employer trains for its own contracts and fears poaching; colleges teach single trades; nobody sells a multi-ticket route with guaranteed employment.
ideas.moat: Weak and honest: a trained cohort bonded to offtake lasts only while the shortage lasts. The only durable moat is an employer-group-led occupational standard, which needs an approval process of 12-18 months. Dies if the shortage eases or offtake is not take-or-pay.
ideas.earned_secret: Every phase-2 and MEES plan assumes technicians who do not exist. The real constraint is a multi-ticket worker, and the barrier for career changers in high-cost regions is housing, which landlords own and can offer.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign two take-or-pay offtakes; secure two levy transfers; contract a training provider; form the employer group for the standard; recruit the first cohort.

ideas.title: Void Clock: the one party paid for the days between tenants
ideas.one_liner: A fixed price per void, a 35-day target against today's 74, and a payment that moves with the days, with the provider owning the whole chain: certificates, asbestos, works, clear, clean, inspection, keys and lettings handover.
ideas.customer: Landlords with 10k-40k homes and 600-2,500 voids a year.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Director of Assets or Housing Operations; budget is the voids line in responsive repairs, with the rent line (about GBP105 a week, about GBP15 a day, my estimate) justifying a bonus.
ideas.problem: About 300,000 voids a year cost GBP1.6B all-in (over GBP1B repairs, GBP220M lettings). Average re-let time rose from under 30 days to 74 in five years (HouseMark via a supplier CEO). Milton Keynes loses 4-5 weeks of rent per void and spends about GBP8,590 on works; council re-let times run from a 51-day target (Anglesey) to 87 days (Cardiff).
ideas.solution: A void cell per region run as a joint P&L with the landlord: a pre-void inspection and materials order during the tenant's notice period, parallel booking of gas, electrical, asbestos and damp checks, one crew sequence, a lettable standard agreed up front, a hand-off API to lettings, and a fixed price by archetype (about GBP4,000: over GBP1B repairs / 300,000 voids = GBP3.3k plus about GBP0.7k lettings) with per-day malus and bonus. Idle void homes can feed the Decant Reserve.
ideas.why_now: Void times have more than doubled; the new electrical duty and Awaab checks add steps; rent caps and the new rent settlement make rent loss visible.
ideas.wedge: Take the tail voids (over 60 days) of one mid-size landlord as a managed pilot, then the full void flow. Customers 2-10: landlords whose repairs contract is expiring or who already run voids as a separate lot.
ideas.path_to_100m: GBP77M ($100M) / GBP4,000 = about 19,000 voids a year, about 6% of 300,000, about 14 landlords with 1,400 voids each. Landlord value: 39 days x GBP15 x 19,000 = about GBP11M of rent plus a 5-10% works saving (my estimates).
ideas.who_does_it_today: The primes' bundled voids work (Mears, Wates, Morgan Sindall, from memory); Made Tech voids prioritisation software (vendor claims GBP573 saved per void and 21% shorter re-let); councils' in-house teams. No public contract with a guaranteed turn time was found.
ideas.why_they_lose: A prime cannot sign for days it does not control and bundling voids with responsive work hides the pricing. A landlord cannot quickly restructure its allocations and compliance teams. Software vendors cannot deliver the work.
ideas.moat: Process power (cell design and step-level data); switching costs (embedded in the lettings workflow); regional purchasing scale.
ideas.earned_secret: Re-let time rose from under 30 days to 74 while the works themselves did not change. The added days are queues between 6-9 hand-offs held by different teams and contractors, and nobody is paid for fewer days.
ideas.first_90_days: One pilot landlord; log days by step for 200 voids; take 100 tail voids below 45 days; agree the price book.

ideas.title: Decant Reserve: idle void days and block-leased units as the supply landlords and councils cannot trade
ideas.one_liner: A licensed, furnished stock of void-gap homes and leased apartments that landlords call on for Awaab decants and councils call on as temporary accommodation overflow, priced under nightly-paid hotels.
ideas.customer: Housing associations needing decant capacity; councils needing temporary accommodation.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Council Director of Housing/Homelessness (TA budget); housing association Director of Assets (new Awaab alternative-accommodation line and regeneration decants).
ideas.problem: Housing associations hold idle homes (300,000 voids x 74 days / 365 is about 61,000 vacant at any moment, my arithmetic) but cannot sublet short term because of nominations agreements, tenancy law, insurance and VAT. Councils spent GBP2.84B on temporary accommodation in 2024/25 (+25%, 134,210 households). Awaab's Law now forces landlords to buy decant at short notice, yet today's decant market is tiny: the Procurement for Housing framework was tendered at GBP25M over about four years and Places for People ran a GBP2M tender.
ideas.solution: Licence void-gap homes of 4+ weeks from housing associations, furnish them and manage them under occupation licences; block-lease serviced apartments for longer decants; run a 24/7 booking desk that handles tenant support, storage, pets and moving; sell the same inventory to councils as TA overflow. Price about GBP80 a night (assumption; no decant nightly rate was found).
ideas.why_now: Phase 2 widens the hazards that can force a decant; TA spend is up 25% in a year; the government will consult on applying Awaab's Law to temporary accommodation; void times are at their worst in years.
ideas.wedge: One housing association (1,500 voids a year) and one London borough; pilot 40 units; run one Awaab decant.
ideas.path_to_100m: GBP77M ($100M) / GBP80 = about 960,000 nights, about 3,100 units at 85% occupancy; against over GBP1B of nightly-paid self-contained TA spend that is about 7.7% share. The Awaab decant market alone is far too small; only the temporary-accommodation bridge makes it big, and TA is an adjacent pool, not this one.
ideas.who_does_it_today: ICAB and the other Procurement for Housing framework suppliers; councils' own leasing schemes, hotels and B&Bs; housing associations' own TA leases and nightly-paid TA providers (from memory).
ideas.why_they_lose: Framework suppliers lease commercial stock at market cost and cannot reach void-gap supply; housing associations cannot run a hospitality-style operation; councils pay hotel rates because they have no alternative.
ideas.moat: Balance sheet (leased inventory); privileged supply (void pipelines of partner landlords); approvals as a barrier; booking data. Legal premises to verify before any pilot: short-let VAT treatment, nominations agreements, licence versus tenancy status, insurance, planning use class.
ideas.earned_secret: Many void days are not safety days: they are waiting for allocation, viewings or keys. A share of the 74 days (my guess is 10-25) is lettable but unlet, and councils pay hotel rates a few streets away. Unsourced; the first pilot tests it.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign one housing association and one borough under an MoU; get a VAT and licence opinion; furnish 10 units; run 5 Awaab-style decants and compare cost per night with hotel rates.

ideas.title: Falls on a Clock: standard adaptations delivered inside the Awaab deadline
ideas.one_liner: From 30 Nov 2026 a handrail, stair, bath or level-access failure for an older tenant is a clocked hazard (make-safe in 5 working days, fuller works within 12 weeks); a phone-based trusted-assessor protocol and standard kits replace an occupational-therapy queue that runs to 8 months.
ideas.customer: Housing associations and councils with older tenants; councils administering Disabled Facilities Grants (DFG).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Director of Assets/Housing (landlord adaptations and Awaab clock budgets); council DFG manager (DFG budget).
ideas.problem: DFG is GBP761M in 2025-26 after a late top-up, about 60,000 grants a year averaging about GBP10k. OT assessment waits reach 8 months (Salford, longest of 89 councils) and completion takes almost two years in several areas. 56% of properties needing adaptations lack them, and the share of adapted homes in the housing association sector fell by about a fifth in a decade. Phase 2 turns falls (level, stairs, between levels) into a legal clock.
ideas.solution: A phone/video trusted-assessor protocol run by OT assistants and technicians for simple works (rails, steps, ramps, toilet frames) with OT review only for complex cases (the 2022 DFG guidance allows trusted assessors; verify); standard kits (grab and stair rails, step conversions, level-access shower pods) installed by the same crews that do One Knock; a fixed price per case and a 5-day make-safe commitment.
ideas.why_now: Phase 2 on 30 Nov 2026; a one-off DFG top-up shows political pressure; Ombudsman findings on OT delays (Redbridge, 8 months).
ideas.wedge: Two mid-size housing associations (rails and handrails are the commonest adaptation) plus one council's DFG minor-works stream.
ideas.path_to_100m: In-pool social adaptations about GBP150-250M (Leicester's council stock spends about GBP1.1M a year on about 33,000 homes, about GBP33 a home, x 4.4M = about GBP145M; my extrapolation). Adjacent DFG pool GBP761M. Combined about GBP0.95B. GBP77M ($100M) = 8% of the combined pool, e.g. 15% of the in-pool market (GBP30M) plus 6% of DFG (GBP46M). In-pool alone it is too small; the DFG bridge is needed.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Millbrook Healthcare (home improvement agency for many councils; FY25 turnover GBP114M, EBITDA GBP3.8M; owned by Cairngorm Capital; a Lichfield contract drew an improvement notice); councils' own agencies; Foundations; stairlift and bathroom suppliers (Stannah, Premier Care in Bathing, from memory); housing association in-house teams. Millbrook proves a $100M-revenue adaptations business exists, at thin margin.
ideas.why_they_lose: Millbrook is paid to administer grants and supervise contractors, and the OT assessment queue belongs to the council, not to them. Landlords treat adaptations as a minor operational issue.
ideas.moat: An assessor protocol approved by councils; kit standardisation; contract position (5-7 year council contracts); case data.
ideas.earned_secret: The queue is the assessment, not the install. A handrail takes an hour to fit and eight months to approve. Phase 2 converts approval delay from a service failure into a breach of contract.
ideas.first_90_days: Agree the protocol with one OT service; run 100 rail and step cases against the 5-day clock; publish waiting-time reduction; open DFG minor-works talks with one council.

ideas.title: Whole-Home Once: one disturbance per home instead of five component programmes
ideas.one_liner: A factory-made interior service core (kitchen and bath, ventilation, electrics, heating controls, alarms, handrails) fitted in 5 working days with the tenant in place, sold at a fixed price per home archetype and capitalised.
ideas.customer: Housing associations and councils with large capitalised programmes (GBP3.9B capitalised repairs a year plus council major works).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Executive Director of Property/Assets; capital programme budget; Board approval for multi-year deals.
ideas.problem: Kitchens, heating, windows and electrics are bought as separate component programmes from separate lots, so tenants are disturbed 4-6 times in ten years and each mobilisation carries access, set-up, asbestos survey and liaison overhead (my estimate 15-25%). Deep retrofit delivery has been slow: London's retrofit partnership had 61 deep retrofits in the pipeline against a target of 65 in Jan 2024, versus over 1,800 once contracted; Mears has done about 5,000 homes of fabric and ventilation work.
ideas.solution: Factory-built kits matched to the top 8 archetypes in a landlord's stock; interior-only (no scaffolding or planning, which de-risks it); fixed price about GBP14-18k per home (assumption); a 12-year performance guarantee on ventilation and moisture; asbestos survey and tenant liaison included; capital-eligible by design; energy measures follow PAS 2035 where included.
ideas.why_now: The forced capital programme: EPC C by 2030 (government impact assessment over GBP16B), a condition-based Decent Homes Standard from 2035, phase 2 excess-cold and fire hazards, and a Warm Homes Plan with GBP4.4B of social-housing grant.
ideas.wedge: One housing association's worst 300 homes from its own damp and disrepair list (a feed from Hot-Spot), then neighbours with identical stock archetypes.
ideas.path_to_100m: GBP77M ($100M) / GBP17k = about 4,500 homes a year. If about 35% of capitalised spend (about GBP1.4B) is interior component work (my assumption), that is about 5.5% of that spend. No heroic share, but working capital and bonding needs are heavy.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Mears (about 5,000 retrofits; further 2,329 planned by 2028); Wates, Kier, Morgan Sindall, Willmott Dixon (from memory); Energiesprong UK and Melius Homes (63 Nottingham homes); London's retrofit innovation partnership; Sero and kitchen/bathroom specialists (from memory, not verified).
ideas.why_they_lose: Separate lots by component and trade, schedule-of-rates pricing per component, and asset teams that buy from sample surveys. Nobody tenders by home.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in the factory kit; process power; switching costs from the home record built by One Knock. Execution risk is high: UK deep-retrofit delivery is slow, and offsite housebuilders Ilke and Legal & General Modular failed (from memory).
ideas.earned_secret: The expensive part of a kitchen replacement is not the kitchen, it is the fifth visit to the same home. Capitalising a bundled renewal also helps the interest-cover covenant, so the landlord's own finance team prefers it.
ideas.first_90_days: Define the 8 archetypes from one landlord's stock data; prototype one kit in three real homes; test asbestos and tenant-in-situ logistics; get a capitalisation opinion from the landlord's auditor.

ideas.title: Girvi Formalizer
ideas.one_liner: Buy the books, vaults and people of retiring pawnbrokers in Tier-3 towns, re-paper their customers into one RBI-regulated NBFC at roughly half the informal rate, and run each shop as an employee-staffed branch with an XRF reader and a shared ledger.
ideas.customer: Small-ticket borrowers (INR 10,000-1.5 lakh) who pay a pawnbroker 24-48% a year, and the retiring pawnbroker who wants a clean exit.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Borrowers pay 18-22% interest (my price target; Muthoot's yield is about 20%). Signers: the pawnbroker (sale plus employment contract), the borrower (new loan agreement), and the bank credit committee funding the NBFC at about 10-11% (assumption).
ideas.problem: Informal lenders still hold a large share at two to five times the formal price because they are 200 metres away, accept anything and ask nothing. Formal greenfield branches need INR 20 crore or more of pipeline, so a lane with INR 4-6 crore of books never clears the hurdle. Owners are ageing and their children do not want the trade (insider claim).
ideas.solution: A conversion kit: diligence the ticket book (redemption, auctions, realised loss); buy goodwill and lease the vault premises; re-paper each live pawn ticket as a new NBFC loan that pays off the pawn ticket the same day so gold never leaves the room; the pawnbroker becomes a salaried branch head with equity upside (satisfies the employees-only handling rule, para 30); install XRF, scale and photo capture so every pledge gets a para 27 certificate; shared loan system, central audit, bank-line funding.
ideas.why_now: Licences and branches are being bought rather than built: Tata Capital is buying about 88.6% of Yogakshemam Loans (Jul 2026), Godrej took over Kanakadurga Finance, and Jefferies/HDFC Securities expect 3,000-3,700 new gold branches in FY27. Gold 23% below its January peak squeezes pawnbrokers who financed at peak prices, which should create willing sellers (assumption).
ideas.wedge: One district cluster, ten pawnbrokers in two or three adjacent towns with books of INR 3-8 crore each, using an acquired dormant small gold NBFC as the vehicle (the route Tata and Godrej took) instead of a fresh licence.
ideas.path_to_100m: About 1,000 converted shops x INR 6 crore average book (assumption) = INR 6,000 crore ($645M) of loans x about 20% yield = about $130M a year. That is 0.3% of the ~$215B stock and about 1.5% of an informal pool that is at least $42B even if informal is only 20% of today's stock (the only informal-share estimate I found is a dated 2017 KPMG/WGC figure of 60-70%). Needs about $95M equity (15% of loans) and about $550M bank debt over five years. No share above 2% needed; the constraint is execution speed (about 200 conversions a year) and capital.
ideas.who_does_it_today: No pawnshop-conversion programme found in my searches. Greenfield: Muthoot (more than 7,500 branches per one weak aggregator source), Manappuram, IIFL, Bajaj Finance (1,507 gold branches, AUM INR 17,831 crore, +115%), Aditya Birla Capital, Tata Capital, Godrej Capital. Fintech: Rupeek set out to fix the unorganised market and had AUM of only INR 1,864 crore at Sep 2024 (INR 236 crore own book); IndiaGold holds an NBFC licence (weak source).
ideas.why_they_lose: Greenfield economics skip lanes that cannot reach INR 20 crore. A formal lender cannot rent a relationship, and a compliance-first culture does not know how to take over a cash-economy owner. Rupeek's app-led attempt shows persuading the borrower alone stays small; buying the shop and the person is a different bet.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource: the sourced, vetted shops and pawnbroker-turned-branch-heads with their customers' trust can be bought only once. Scale economies in funding and audit are secondary.
ideas.earned_secret: A pawnbroker's real asset is not the gold but his memory of whom to trust and his tolerance of the long tail (stones, partial pieces, socially enforced late payment). His loss rate on gold is tiny, so the 30%+ price he charges is for liquidity and privacy, not risk. This is an insider claim to test with loan-level data; legal premise (state pawnbroker/moneylender acts, RBI change-of-control approval, off-book cash) must also be checked and kills the idea if books fail diligence.
ideas.first_90_days: Map one district's licensed pawnbrokers from the state list (Tamil Nadu licences come from the tahsildar under the 1943 Act; other states differ). Meet 30, obtain loan-level ticket books from 10 under NDA and test two claims: realised loss under 0.5% and annual redemption above 85%. Shortlist two dormant small NBFCs for acquisition and ask the RBI regional office about the change-of-control route.

ideas.title: Bullion-Bid
ideas.one_liner: A lender-neutral national bid layer that sells pledged gold when a loan goes bad, before or inside the Directions' auction, and lets stressed borrowers sell part of their gold to renew a loan instead of losing all of it.
ideas.customer: Lender heads of collections and recovery; stressed borrowers at renewal; refiners and bullion dealers who want scrap.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The lender pays a seller fee from its auction and recovery budget; the winning bidder pays a buyer premium. Signer: the NBFC or bank Head of Collections and Recovery, with the Chief Risk Officer approving the auction SOP (para 9 requires one).
ideas.problem: Para 41 forces the first auction to be physical in the branch district, so bidding is thin exactly when the lender is most exposed. Para 42 bars the lender and related parties from bidding, closing the old private sale to a group company. Reserve falls from 90% to 85% of current value after two failed auctions, so the rules bake in a 5-point haircut.
ideas.solution: (a) A para 39-compliant empanelled auction service with live remote bidding by 20+ refiners and dealers and audit-ready reports. (b) Borrower-initiated pre-auction sale: a tri-party release in one branch visit where the buyer pays the lender, the lender releases only the sold items and the borrower keeps the surplus. (c) Sell-to-renew: at renewal, sell surplus pieces to bring LTV within the cap and keep the family's best pieces. (d) Triage by item using the para 27 certificate images: melt lots to refiners, lots with maker or stone value to a jeweller marketplace intact.
ideas.why_now: The paras 37-43 auction SOP took effect in Apr 2026. Gold is about 23% below its January peak and CreditSights expects asset quality to weaken over coming quarters; the 12-month bullet cap makes maturities hard dates. Households are already selling: nearly 50 t in Apr-Jun 2026 (+43%, IBJA via ET).
ideas.wedge: Second-attempt lots, which para 41 lets move online or to an adjoining district. Pilot with a mid-size NBFC or small finance bank, add three refiners, target ten lenders in year one.
ideas.path_to_100m: Stress-year scenario (assumptions): (A) 3% of the $215B stock reaches para 37 notice stage and half is sold = about $3.2B of loans, about $4B of gold; 40% share ($1.7B) x 2.5% blended net take = $42M. (B) Borrower part-sales and sell-to-renew: $3B x 1.5% = $45M. (C) 5% of the $30-37B annual scrap flow ($1.7B) x 0.8% = $14M. Total about $100M, needing about 40% of the distress flow plus a start in scrap; in a normal year layer A is about a quarter of that. Heroic, and dependent on gold staying low.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Local auctioneers and the jewellers who bid at them (the 'ring' is industry folklore I could not verify); lenders' own staff-run auctions; refiner scrap networks and cash-for-gold shops; Tanishq-style exchange schemes (nearly 80% of Ahmedabad jewellery sales went through exchange schemes). I found no national lender-neutral bid layer.
ideas.why_they_lose: Lenders cannot bid and cannot run a national bidder pool. Local rings cannot scale beyond their town. Refiners lack local origination and lender integrations. Jeweller exchange schemes only work against a purchase of new jewellery.
ideas.moat: Network economies (more refiners raise lot prices, attracting more lenders) plus process power from audit-ready SOP evidence lenders will not rebuild.
ideas.earned_secret: A quarter or more of pledged pieces (temple sets, Kundan, polki, antique) carry maker's or stone value that a melt-priced auction hands to local bidders, and the first-auction-in-district rule guarantees those bidders face no competition. This is a hypothesis from lender and refiner practice, to be tested on 100 lots. Legal checks: auctioneer empanelment, whether remote bidders can join the physical first auction, no lender-affiliated owner (para 42), GST and AML on gold.
ideas.first_90_days: Run 100 second-attempt lots for one lender. Get at least three refiner bids per lot via a simple API, compare the clearing price with the 85-90% reserve and the lender's historical realisation, and report uplift by lot type.

ideas.title: Karat Ledger
ideas.one_liner: An independent verification and record layer for pledged gold: instrument-backed assay evidence at the counter, surprise re-assay for the lender's own audit team, a shared appraiser track record, and a live collateral ledger that holds each pledge's LTV through its tenor (Persona/Socure-style per-event rail created by a liability-shifting mandate).
ideas.customer: Chief Compliance Officers, heads of internal audit and gold-loan business heads at NBFCs and banks; funders of NBFCs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The lender pays per pledge and per active loan per year from its compliance and fraud-loss budget; signer is the Head of Internal Audit or Chief Compliance Officer, with the Gold Loan Business Head co-signing. At public-sector banks the borrower already pays 'appraiser charges' per pledge (I believe about 0.25% of the loan; not verified), an unverified extra pool.
ideas.problem: Para 21 demands a uniform assay procedure, para 27 an assay certificate with image, para 34 periodic surprise verification, para 20 ongoing LTV. The audited party (branch or appraiser) writes the evidence. In 2026 fraud cases the unit of damage was the appraiser, not the gold: 44, 96, 159 and 683 accounts per case. Appraiser panels are growing fast (Indian Bank +982 in six months to 3,538) and nobody tracks an appraiser fired by one lender and empanelled by another.
ideas.solution: (1) Handheld XRF, scale and camera kit with an app that writes and signs the para 27 certificate. (2) Surprise verification as a service for the lender's own audit employees (devices stay in lender hands, consistent with para 30). (3) Appraiser registry with outcome scores. (4) Collateral ledger holding weight, purity, images and LTV per pledge on the para 17 price rule, with margin-call and release workflows. (5) Later, a fraud warranty backed by reinsurance.
ideas.why_now: The Directions turned assay evidence from a branch habit into a regulated record. RBI's Sept 2024 notice flagged third-party sourcing and appraisal as a deficiency, and a string of 2026 frauds followed (ICICI Nagpur over INR 23 crore, NBFC Delhi INR 3.81 crore, Bank of Baroda about INR 10 crore).
ideas.wedge: Sell para 34 surprise verification to the internal audit head of one NBFC or small finance bank: audit has a mandate and no tool and needs no IT sign-off. Add the ledger as the second product.
ideas.path_to_100m: Per pledge INR 60 ($0.65) x about 158M pledges a year = $102M at 100% share. Per active loan INR 100 ($1.08) x 90M accounts = $97M at 100%. A fraud warranty at 5 bps of about INR 26 lakh crore of originations = $140M at 100%. $100M needs roughly 35% of all three modules together or 50% of the first two. Heroic, so this is a wedge to the co-lending idea, not a stand-alone $100M business. Pricing per account is capped by small tickets (INR 76,500 average up to INR 2.5 lakh).
ideas.who_does_it_today: In-house systems at Muthoot and others; core-banking vendors (weak on item-level images); XRF makers selling hardware; Rupeek and IndiaGold claim AI-assisted assessment (their claims, untested). Credit bureaus cover the borrower, not the appraiser or collateral. I found no lender-neutral appraiser registry or independent assay-evidence company.
ideas.why_they_lose: The auditee writes the evidence. Each lender keeps its fraud data private. Public-sector core systems cannot store spectra and images per item. Bureaus do not touch collateral.
ideas.moat: Switching costs once the ledger is the system of record, plus a cornered data asset: cross-lender spectra and appraiser outcomes no single lender can assemble.
ideas.earned_secret: Gold-loan fraud is mostly collusion with a handful of appraisers who originate dozens of accounts each, not clever fake gold; catching one appraiser's pattern is worth more than a better assay on every pledge. The borrower-present, image-certificate rule (paras 23, 27) means every pledge now yields structured evidence a neutral party can score. Legal checks: para 30 (our people never touch gold), DPDP Act and competition law on pooling appraiser data, an insurer fronting any warranty.
ideas.first_90_days: Rent five handheld XRF units. With one internal audit head, re-assay a 2% sample of packets in 20 branches, compare to the certificates, and deliver an appraiser-level anomaly report; price per branch from that.

ideas.title: Gold Float
ideas.one_liner: A revolving credit line on UPI secured by gold already in a lender's vault, charging interest only on days money is used and sweeping UPI inflows to repay it (Fuliza-style auto-overdraft plus control of the repayment channel).
ideas.customer: Lumpy-cash-flow gold borrowers (shopkeepers, farmers, traders) who today take a lump sum and pay 10-20% on idle money, and banks and small finance banks that want gold assets without more branches.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The lender shares interest on the drawn balance with the program manager (my assumption: 150 bps). Signer: the bank's Head of Digital Lending or Chief Business Officer. The borrower pays interest on use only.
ideas.problem: Gold loans are priced and built as bullet lumps. NBFC revenue depends on interest on the full balance, so pay-on-use cuts their own income; public-sector systems cannot run a limit.
ideas.solution: A white-label line manager: limit from LTV on the para 17 value, daily revaluation to keep LTV within para 20, UPI draw and auto-repay from inflows, partial top-up and release flows.
ideas.why_now: Axis Bank and Freecharge proved the product in Sept 2025 under NPCI's secured-credit-line framework, and tiered LTV up to 85% for small tickets raised limits.
ideas.wedge: One small finance bank or private bank already live on UPI credit lines: pre-approve 5,000 existing gold borrowers by collateral headroom and measure draw frequency.
ideas.path_to_100m: 5% of the 9.03 crore active accounts = 4.5M lines x INR 1.4 lakh average drawn (assumption) = $6.8B drawn x 150 bps = $102M. That is 5% of all gold borrowers on a line with this platform as program manager on every one, or 10% of borrowers if the platform has half. Heroic.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Axis Bank with Freecharge (existing Axis customers, MSME and self-employed focus); banks' gold overdrafts for MSMEs (from memory). No NBFC or multi-lender manager found.
ideas.why_they_lose: NBFCs cannot cannibalise lump-sum interest. Public-sector systems cannot run a limit. Axis's line is a closed product for its own customers.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against NBFC lump pricing; switching costs are low, so the position is weak.
ideas.earned_secret: Fuliza worked because wallet inflows repaid the overdraft automatically; gold has no such rail yet, and the unlock is sweeping UPI merchant and wage inflows. The collateral is already locked, so the line needs no new vault visit. Make-or-break legal premise: I found no RBI statement permitting revolving consumption lines against gold, the Directions cap bullet consumption loans at 12 months, and NBFC access to UPI credit lines is unverified. If not permitted, only the MSME/income-generating version survives, which cuts the pool.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign one live UPI-credit-line bank, build the gold limit adapter, run 5,000 pre-approved borrowers, and compare their effective interest cost with a bullet loan.

ideas.title: Switch Desk
ideas.one_liner: A lender-neutral desk that moves gold borrowers from 20-48% lenders to 9-12% banks at the moment their loan matures, paid by the bank per completed switch plus a share of the borrower's first-year saving.
ideas.customer: Borrowers with loans of about INR 1 lakh or more at an NBFC or pawnbroker; banks and small finance banks that want gold assets.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The bank pays a sourcing fee of 0.75% of switched principal from its customer-acquisition budget (net 90+ delinquency is only 0.2%); the borrower pays 10% of verified first-year savings. Signer: the bank's Head of Gold Loans or Retail Assets.
ideas.problem: Repeat borrowers are about 75% of new sourcing; they renew where they are. Rates: small/regional NBFCs 18-24%, large NBFCs 9-14% on big tickets, banks about 8.4-12%, informal 25-50% (mixed-quality sources). Muthoot earns about 20% on roughly INR 1.65 lakh crore, so one point of yield is about INR 1,650 crore ($177M): it cannot cut the price for its installed base. Banks cannot hunt customers (sales incentives, appraiser capacity) and aggregators are paid for new borrowers, not for moving an existing one.
ideas.solution: Use the 12-month bullet cap, which gives every consumption loan a hard maturity date. Reach the borrower 14-20 days before it (consented bureau or Account Aggregator triggers plus lead partners), show a bank quote and an itemised comparison using each lender's published net-weight method (para 22), book the bank assay, arrange a bridge so the old lender is paid off the same day, and co-schedule two branches in the same town so the borrower collects gold at one (same-day release, para 35, INR 5,000 a day as leverage) and pledges it at the other. No doorstep, no outsourced gold handling.
ideas.why_now: Paras 22, 23 and 27 force price and valuation transparency. The bank gold book is growing 105% a year (INR 5.1 lakh crore, May 2026) and wants volume. Para 35 gives the borrower leverage on release.
ideas.wedge: Two or three towns in Tamil Nadu or Kerala (southern states hold over 75% of the market), one partner bank, borrowers of INR 1-3 lakh at regional NBFCs and pawnbrokers.
ideas.path_to_100m: Per switch: bank fee 0.75% x INR 1.2 lakh = INR 900 ($9.7), plus 10% of year-1 saving (informal-to-bank, a 20-point gap, INR 24,000 saved, fee INR 2,400 = $26; NBFC-to-bank, 10 points, fee INR 1,200 = $13). Blended about $30. 3.3M switches a year = $100M; that is $4.3B of principal, about 2% of the $215B stock or about 5% of a high-rate pool of ~$82B (NBFC book $40B plus at least $42B informal, assumption). If borrowers will not pay the success fee, revenue is $9.7 a switch and 10M switches ($13B, 6% of stock) are needed: heroic. Base-rate warning: Rupeek's informal-to-formal thesis produced under INR 2,000 crore of AUM in nine years.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Lender-run 'balance transfer' pages (Shriram, L&T and others); Rupeek as business correspondent for Federal, South Indian and Axis; lead-gen sites (from memory). I found no outcome-priced, lender-neutral switch desk.
ideas.why_they_lose: NBFCs cannot match the bank price without repricing their whole book. Banks cannot run proactive outbound sales and have appraiser limits. Aggregators are paid on new customers and do not coordinate two-branch settlement.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against NBFC repricing; process power in the same-day two-branch choreography; modest.
ideas.earned_secret: Switchers are not price-shoppers, they are deadline-driven: the maturity date is the only moment they decide, and the only party speaking to them then is the renewal desk of the lender they are leaving. Be the second voice with a signed quote. Legal checks: DPDP consent for using bureau/AA data to time outreach, a lender-funded (not unregulated) bridge, and RBI outsourcing and digital-lending rules.
ideas.first_90_days: With one bank, attempt 500 switches in three towns using maturity-targeted leads. Measure contact-to-pledge conversion, incumbent counter-offers, and whether borrowers accept the success fee.

ideas.title: Co-Lend Exchange
ideas.one_liner: A neutral trust layer that lets banks fund gold loans originated and vaulted by NBFCs: independent collateral attestation, a shared ledger, the payment waterfall and LTV monitoring in one place.
ideas.customer: Bank heads of co-lending and treasury; NBFC CFOs, especially new entrants growing 5x (Tata Capital, ABCL, Godrej, Bajaj).
ideas.payer_and_signer: The funding bank pays an attestation and monitoring fee from its origination-cost line; the NBFC pays for faster, cheaper funding. Signers: the bank's Head of Co-lending and the NBFC CFO.
ideas.problem: NBFCs borrow from banks at about 10% to lend at about 20%; banks lend directly at 9-10% but are capacity-bound. The funder cannot see the gold in the NBFC's vault (paras 30-31). After RBI barred IIFL Finance from fresh gold loans in Mar 2024, its partners reviewed their exposure, so funders know originator risk is real.
ideas.solution: Karat Ledger evidence shared with both lenders in real time, monthly independent attestation on the co-lent pool (para 34 sample), LTV monitoring on the para 17 price, escrow and reconciliation for the waterfall, and a standard co-lending data tape.
ideas.why_now: New entrants with large targets need cheap funding, banks need volume, and the Directions require documented evidence.
ideas.wedge: One new-entrant NBFC plus two banks on a pilot pool.
ideas.path_to_100m: The addressable base is the NBFC book only: INR 3.41 lakh crore ($37B) at Jun 2026, growing about 35% a year (ICRA) to roughly $60-65B by FY28 (assumption). At 35 bps of co-lent balance, $100M needs $28.6B co-lent, about 45% of the FY28 NBFC book. Thin and heroic. Honest verdict: dead as a stand-alone; keep as a module and channel for Karat Ledger.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Bilateral deals: Rupeek with Indian Bank and Federal, Finkurve with Godrej Finance (Mar 2026), Indel with IndusInd, IIFL with Canara, DCB and DBS (older). Generic co-lending software platforms exist (from memory, not verified).
ideas.why_they_lose: Each NBFC deals bilaterally with one to three banks on its own systems and no neutral party is trusted by both. Muthoot prefers its own balance sheet at 20%.
ideas.moat: Network economies if several banks and NBFCs share one ledger; switching costs once settlement runs through it.
ideas.earned_secret: A bank credit committee will lend at 9.5% against gold all day, but it will not fund a pool whose gold it cannot inspect and whose originator can be debarred overnight; the product is the proof, not the platform. Legal check: I did not confirm how the 2025 co-lending directions treat gold or the 80:20 split.
ideas.first_90_days: Run one independent attestation on a live co-lent pool and measure how much faster a second bank approves because of it.

ideas.title: Renewal Wall Cure Desk
ideas.one_liner: An outcome-priced desk that gets lenders' borrowers through the renewal LTV test with the cheapest cure (pay-down, part-sale, transfer) instead of an auction, aimed at the dated cohort of peak-priced loans maturing in early 2027.
ideas.customer: Lender Chief Risk Officers and heads of collections at NBFCs and banks.
