ideas.moat: Process power (state-by-state title playbooks) and scale economies (a directory of lienholder payoff contacts and e-lien connections that improves with every file).
ideas.earned_secret: Valuation is not what makes a TL slow. The twelve days between 'owner accepts' and 'lien paid' are, because the lien lives in a payoff department and the owner is missing one signature. A desk that owns lienholder relationships by name wins days, not accuracy, and carriers measure the wrong thing so nobody manages it.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign one regional carrier on the lien-and-title leg. Time-stamp 1,000 files end to end for the baseline. Build the top-200 lender directory and ELT state coverage. Settle adjuster licensing and E&O (this is claims adjusting in every state).

ideas.title: Same-Day: delivery-hour parts network with total-cost sourcing and tariff price-lock
ideas.one_liner: A collision-parts network that promises a delivery hour per part from pooled dismantler, distributor and dealer stock, picks the source on total repair cost (price plus rental days plus comeback risk), locks quotes for 48 hours against tariff swings, and funds shops net-45 against the insurer-approved estimate.
ideas.customer: MSO procurement teams and independent shops buying about $15B of collision parts a year (my arithmetic: 8.5M repaired vehicles x $4,818 x an assumed 38% parts share).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Shop or MSO pays a fulfilment fee and financing spread; suppliers pay a listing fee; insurers can be charged a success fee for rental days saved. Signer: MSO VP of procurement or shop owner.
ideas.problem: A repair waits for its slowest part: OEM parts take about 9 days, aftermarket and recycled about 3. OEM is 52% of orders and OEM prices are up 4.3% since the tariffs while aftermarket stayed under 1% (PartsTrader). At about 15 rental days per claim (Enterprise Q2 2026: 15.1) and tens of dollars a day, extra parts days can outweigh the price gap, but estimating and procurement tools rank by unit price. Tariffs add about $100 of parts per repair order; prices move between estimate and order and surface as supplements.
ideas.solution: (1) Delivery-hour promise on the top 300 fast-moving parts (bumper covers, lamps, grilles, mirrors) from pooled stock with couriers. (2) A total-cost selector showing price, delivery days, estimated comeback rate by supplier. (3) A 48-hour price lock backed by a small pooled inventory. (4) Net-45 terms secured on the approved estimate, repaid by direction to pay; this financing leg is a hypothesis since I found no data on shop payables terms or insurer payment timing.
ideas.why_now: The tariff divergence means the cheapest part and the fastest part are now different parts for most orders, and insurers are pushing alternative parts to cut cost (LKQ: alt-parts usage at a record).
ideas.wedge: 40 shops of one MSO in one metro, 4-hour delivery on 200 part numbers with a measured cycle-time result. First 10 customers: PE-platform MSOs with central purchasing.
ideas.path_to_100m: Parts flow about $15.6B (my arithmetic). Revenue per dollar of flow: delivery/fulfilment 3% + credit and price-lock spread 1.5% + supplier listing 1% = 5.5%, or $860M at 100% of flow. $100M needs about 11.6% of all collision parts flow (about $1.8B GMV): heroic but not absurd for a logistics network.
ideas.who_does_it_today: LKQ/Keystone (largest distributor, couriers, own recycled and aftermarket parts), PartsTrader (insurer-aligned RFQ marketplace, supplier-paid), OEConnection CollisionLink (OE parts from dealers), dealer parts counters, insurer price-matched OEM programs (18% of orders).
ideas.why_they_lose: PartsTrader is supplier-paid and run to insurer program rules, so it optimises price. LKQ cannot be neutral about source because it sells the parts and owns the recyclers. OEConnection is OE-only. None carries a delivery-hour promise or shop financing.
ideas.moat: Network economies (more stock sources and shops raise same-day hit rate) and scale economies in last-mile logistics density.
ideas.earned_secret: A parts manager knows the price on screen is the smallest number in the decision. The supplier's ETA is a guess, a wrong part comes back with a restocking fee, and the bay sits empty. They already phone three suppliers and trust none, so a verified hour promise is worth more than a 5% discount.
ideas.first_90_days: Instrument 1,000 recent orders for promised versus actual delivery. Sign 6 dismantlers and 2 couriers in one metro. Build the total-cost selector. Run the 4-hour pilot on 200 part numbers and report days saved per repair.

ideas.title: Open Yard: asset-light salvage sales from the tow yard where the car already sits
ideas.one_liner: A salvage network that lists a totaled car the day it is declared, from the tow yard or shop where it already sits, and ships it once, straight to the buyer, so the insurer skips the second tow, yard intake and dwell time.
ideas.customer: Insurers' salvage/vendor-management teams (start with regional carriers and MGAs with little leverage in a duopoly) and the existing buyer base of rebuilders, dismantlers and exporters.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The insurer pays a per-unit seller fee lower than today's tow-in, intake, loading and storage stack; buyers pay a buyer fee. Signer: director of salvage or VP of claims vendor management.
ideas.problem: Copart and IAA hold about 80% of US salvage (one investor write-up; other sources split 40-45% / 30-35%); insurers supply 80-85% of units; Copart owns 275+ yards. A totaled car moves crash site -> tow yard or shop -> auction yard -> buyer (general industry practice). Record TL volume fills yards and storage bills; an insurer moved volume between Copart and IAA in 2025, so contracts are not sticky.
ideas.solution: Certify tow yards and shops as pickup points with a standard photo and VIN/title capture; sell online to the same rebuilders, exporters and dismantlers plus dealer wholesale buyers; release the car from the yard to the buyer's carrier; pay the insurer net of a lower fee. Buyers get escrowed payment and a misdescription guarantee, so the platform prices condition risk it does not hold on a lot.
ideas.why_now: TL volume is up while Copart's US insurance units are down (-9.5% Q1 2026, -10.7% Q2). IAA is now a division of RB Global, so insurers want a third option. Vehicles are older and cheaper (72% of valuations on cars 7+ years old), which makes the second tow a bigger share of value.
ideas.wedge: One state, two regional carriers, 30 tow yards, only cars already sitting in a yard waiting for paperwork; recruit 40 regional buyers from exporters and dismantlers who already bid on Copart. First 10 customers: regional mutuals and MGAs.
ideas.path_to_100m: About 3.5M TLs a year (my arithmetic). Platform take of $300 a unit (assumed: about $100 seller-side plus $200 buyer fee; I did not find either incumbent's fee schedule) means $100M is about 333,000 units: about 9.5% of all TLs, or about 12% of Copart plus IAA volume. A plausible share but a heroic execution problem, because proceeds depend on bidder depth, which only comes with volume.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Copart, IAA (RB Global), small regional dismantler auctions. I searched for ACV Auctions or a startup running in-place insurer salvage and found nothing; could not rule it out.
ideas.why_they_lose: Copart's returns are tied to owned yards and yard-centred fees, so a car that never enters a lot is revenue they do not earn and an asset they cannot redeploy; they cannot tell an insurer not to send it to them. Their moat (275+ permitted yards) is exactly what Open Yard does not need.
ideas.moat: Network economies (more buyers raise proceeds, which pulls more insurers) and counter-positioning against yard-heavy incumbents.
ideas.earned_secret: The second tow exists to serve the auction company's yard, not the buyer. Most of a salvage unit's dwell time is waiting for title and lien paperwork, which a yard does not speed up, and a shop or tow yard can hold the car as well as a Copart lot. (general industry practice, not re-verified)
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 30 yards to the capture standard. Pilot 300 TL cars with one regional carrier. Recruit 40 buyers. Set up escrow and the misdescription guarantee. Compare net proceeds per car with matched cars sold through Copart or IAA.

ideas.title: Dent Plan: prepaid repair membership priced off shop slack, not insurance risk
ideas.one_liner: A prepaid repair membership sold through collision chains, dealers and credit unions to drivers who dropped or never had collision cover: a monthly fee buys a yearly repair credit at fixed menu prices at network shops.
ideas.customer: Owners of older, cheaper vehicles who cut collision as premiums rose, and owners who now skip small claims ('keep the dent and pay the rent', PartsTrader Spring 2026).
ideas.payer_and_signer: The driver pays $19-29 a month. Distribution partners sign: MSO VP of marketing, dealer F&I director, credit-union VP. The MSO pays a platform fee on the work it receives.
ideas.problem: Premiums rose about 46% from 2022 to 2024 (Insurify, via a secondary summary); CCC's 2026 report (via a secondary summary) found 29% of consumers cancelled or downgraded an insurance product. Repairable claims fell about 10%; personal-auto claim volume fell 5% (2024) and 3% (2025). Customer-pay is only about 20% of shop repair orders yet the best-margin work. An insurer cannot sell sub-$1,000 cover without wrecking its loss ratio, and surcharges exist to discourage small claims. The only subscription I found (Deductify, Sep 2025, $10.99/month for $1,000) pays after an insurance claim.
ideas.solution: A 12-item fixed-price menu (bumper scuff, paintless dent repair, headlamp restoration, windshield chip, mirror, wheel, trim, minor panel) using recycled or aftermarket parts, scheduled into slack days, with about $1,500 a year of credit. No claim, deductible or surcharge. A stop-loss layer covers the tail. Structured as a service contract, or as insurance where a state requires it.
ideas.why_now: Coverage drop-off and claim avoidance coincide with falling shop volume. PE-backed MSOs (130+ firms) want volume insurers do not steer and that is not capped by labour-rate contracts.
ideas.wedge: One MSO of 30-80 shops in one metro; sell $19.99 a month to its own past customer list and to 10 dealers' F&I menus; add 5 credit unions' auto-loan members. First 10 customers: MSO marketing heads and credit-union product managers.
ideas.path_to_100m: Gross membership revenue at about $290 a year means 345,000 members for $100M. If about a quarter of roughly 250M registered vehicles lack collision cover (my assumption; no figure found), that is about 60M vehicles, so 345,000 is 0.6%. At half a claim per member that is about 175,000 repair orders, about 8% of customer-pay orders (about 2.2M, my arithmetic). Contribution after repair cost is about 25-30% (my assumption), so the revenue is gross and the profit pool a quarter of it.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Deductify (deductible reimbursement), dealer-sold dent-and-ding / tire-and-wheel / appearance protection (F&I, one-off, at dealer margin), Fidelis PPM (prepaid maintenance with deductible reimbursement, 2018, status unchecked), credit-union plans reimbursing deductibles up to $500. I found no MSO selling a prepaid collision repair plan.
ideas.why_they_lose: Insurers cannot price small claims at frequency and their products are built around the claim. Deductify and credit-union plans depend on a paid claim. Dealer plans are product-by-product at dealer margin. MSOs have capacity but not compliance, distribution or a pricing engine; nobody has joined the two.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (shop network density lowers marginal cost) and brand in the customer-pay segment; counter-positioning against claim-based insurance pricing.
ideas.earned_secret: A shop's only perishable inventory is bay and paint-booth time. Tuesday's empty booth costs the same as Friday's full one. Retail-priced customer work is the best margin in the building but few drivers can afford it, so a fixed-price plan that fills slack days at marginal cost builds a customer list insurers cannot steer.
ideas.first_90_days: Pick one MSO. Price the 12 items from six months of slack-hour data. Sell to 5,000 past customers. Sign 3 dealers. Get legal opinions on insurance versus service contract in CA, TX, FL, NY and IL before selling outside the pilot state.

ideas.title: Proof Plate: neutral ADAS repair plan and completion record
ideas.one_liner: A vendor-neutral layer that fixes the list of OEM-required scans and calibrations on the estimate before repair, so insurer approval and shop duty are one document, then issues a tamper-evident completion record the shop can produce in court and the insurer can pay against without review; sublet calibration work routes through the same record.
ideas.customer: MSOs, glass chains, alignment/mechanical shops; insurers' DRP and quality teams; garage-liability underwriters.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Shop/MSO pays per vehicle for the record; insurer pays a small fee per auto-approved calibration (desk review saved); calibrators pay a dispatch fee on routed sublet work; garage-liability carriers can credit the shop's premium. Signer: MSO general counsel/risk manager; insurer VP of claims quality.
ideas.problem: Calibrations are on 28.3% of repairable estimates (21.8% a year earlier). Missed/improper-calibration suits went from 3 (2018) to 61 (2024) per an analyst; an attorney says sublet does not shield the shop and plaintiffs request OEM procedures, scan logs, calibration reports and customer communications; analysts put settlements at $200k-$1M and say nearly half of shops miss required calibrations (estimates). Laws are arriving (MD glass 2023, UT, AZ, NY signed 19 Dec 2025; IL HB 4373 and a MD anti-denial bill pending). 70% of collision shops lack in-house capability (KPMG) and each tool brand logs differently.
ideas.solution: (1) Map OEM position statements to repair operations per VIN so the plan is generated at estimate time and attached to the claim. (2) Ingest scan and calibration logs from the main tool brands regardless of who did the work. (3) Issue the signed record including customer notice. (4) Auto-approval rules for insurers on pre-agreed operations. (5) Dispatch to qualified calibrators on sublet jobs, with the record as the acceptance test.
ideas.why_now: Calibration frequency is up about 30% a year, tort exposure is rising with it and the first state laws have landed. Calibration revenue is forecast to grow from $1.2B (2024) to about $3.0B in the US by 2030 (KPMG), so whoever holds the plan holds the dispatch.
ideas.wedge: MSOs with 8+ shops in NY, MD, UT or AZ, starting with sublet calibration jobs (worst documented) and one garage-liability underwriter giving a verified-record credit. First 10 customers: those MSOs' general counsel or risk managers.
ideas.path_to_100m: About 8M calibration events a year (my arithmetic: 28.3% of ~11.5M repairable claims = 3.3M collision, plus AutoBolt's 3.8M glass-related in 2022, plus alignment/mechanical). $9 record + $4 insurer auto-approval = $13 on in-house events; sublet events (assume 40%) add an 8% dispatch fee on ~$350 = $28, so $41. Blended about $24, or $190M at 100% coverage. $100M needs about 53% of all events: heroic. It only reaches $100M if dispatch on sublet work becomes the engine (8% of the $3.0B 2030 forecast is $240M).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Repairify asTech (remote OEM scans and reports), Opus IVS (ADAS MAP platform for multi-shop operators; licensed Protech ID3 tech Nov 2024), AirPro Diagnostics, Caliber's Protech, Safelite (TruRoad), LKQ's Elitek, equipment makers (Bosch, Hunter, Autel, Mahle, TEXA), I-CAR training, free OEM position statements (OEM1Stop). The pool file's 'nothing funded here' is wrong.
ideas.why_they_lose: Every competitor is a calibrator or tool vendor, so its proof covers its own jobs; none is neutral across providers and tool brands, and insurers will not accept a calibrator's self-certification as pre-approval. They earn on jobs, not on dispute reduction.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (the record sits in the shop's legal file) and a cornered resource (OEM requirements mapped to repair lines and VINs).
ideas.earned_secret: A calibration can pass and still be wrong; the only truth is the log, and most shops cannot produce it in discovery. A calibration technician who drove 90 minutes to a job knows which ones fail first time (alignment, ride height, tyre pressure, battery voltage, an uncleared DTC) and the customer was told it was done.
ideas.first_90_days: Map OEM requirements for the 50 best-selling vehicle lines to repair operations. Get one garage-liability underwriter to price a verified-record credit. Run 500 sublet calibrations through the record with two MSOs in NY or MD. Build an auto-approval rule with one carrier's DRP team.

ideas.title: Ground Truth: independent audit and sold-price data for total-loss valuations and claims AI
ideas.one_liner: An audit and data service that recalculates each total loss and AI damage decision under the state's rules using actual sold prices, flags the drift that cost Progressive $15-48M a case, and gives the carrier a file it can hand to a regulator or a judge.
ideas.customer: Personal-auto carriers (tier-2/3 first) and valuation/estimating vendors (CCC, Mitchell, Audatex, J.D. Power) needing independent accuracy evidence.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Chief claims officer plus general counsel or chief compliance officer; budget is compliance, model risk and litigation reserves.
ideas.problem: Fixed-amount adjustments win class certification (Progressive CO projected-sold adjustment $15.24M, opt-out deadline 5 Nov 2026; Progressive NY $48M; State Farm AR $15.6M for a 9% 'typical negotiation adjustment') while condition-adjustment classes keep failing on appeal. The NAIC's 12-state examination covers TL thresholds, damage assessment and parts valuation; insurers answer for vendor AI regardless of who makes the decision; a vote on nationwide adoption is at the Nov 2026 meeting. 72% of TL valuations are on vehicles 7+ years old, where comps are thin.
ideas.solution: (1) Shadow-recalculate each TL from raw comps, state tax/fee rules and actual sold prices (dealer retail sold data, wholesale auction results). (2) Test configuration drift between state rules and vendor settings. (3) Test damage-AI calls (TL thresholds, stripped operations) against final repair invoices and late totals. (4) Produce an exam-ready file per carrier for the NAIC's four areas.
ideas.why_now: The NAIC pilot ends Sep 2026 and the vote is in Nov; trade groups already objected to penalties on an unfinished tool (Dec 2025 letter); Pennsylvania rulings show courts separate provable adjustments from judgement calls.
ideas.wedge: Five tier-2/3 carriers writing in the 12 pilot states (CA, CO, CT, FL, IA, LA, MD, PA, RI, VT, VA, WI), sold as a 12-month exam-readiness plus shadow audit at $250-500k. First 10 customers: those carriers' general counsel.
ideas.path_to_100m: My arithmetic: 40 carriers with $20M+ of TL litigation exposure at $750k ($30M), 60 mid-size at $250k ($15M), 5 vendors at $2M ($10M) = about $55M. I think this is a $40-60M company at best; as a stand-alone it fails the $100M test and I would call it dead. The only route above $100M is becoming a second-source valuation or sold-price reference for older vehicles that also sells to lenders and dealers, a head-on fight with Cox (KBB, Manheim), J.D. Power and Black Book that I have not sized.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Carriers' compliance and model-risk teams; plaintiff and defence experts hired per case; the valuation vendors themselves (CCC, Mitchell, Audatex, J.D. Power); consultancies selling AI-governance reviews. No dedicated TL-audit product found.
ideas.why_they_lose: CCC and peers cannot audit their own engine for their own customers and still sell it. Consultancies are bespoke and costly per carrier. Carriers lack raw sold-price data.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (a matched dataset of valuations to actual sold prices and repair outcomes) and a neutral brand with regulators.
ideas.earned_secret: The exposure is rarely a bad valuation model; it is configuration drift: thousands of per-state tax, fee and deduction settings in a vendor engine, one wrong for years. A litigator knows the provable ones (a fixed-percentage adjustment) get certified and the judgement-based ones (condition) do not.
ideas.first_90_days: Build the sold-price match for older vehicles in three states. Audit one carrier's last 5,000 TLs for drift. Draft the exam-readiness file against the NAIC four areas. Get a privilege opinion on whether an audit report is discoverable (a round-1 killer: selling a 'privileged' number that defeats its own privilege).
