ideas.title: Intercompany Reconciler
ideas.one_liner: Software plus a licensed filer that sets, documents and reconciles the intercompany price on every related-party import, so customs duty, income tax and the year-end transfer-pricing true-up stop contradicting each other.
ideas.customer: US subsidiaries and parents of multinational groups with more than $250M a year of related-party imports. Related-party goods are 49.0% ($1,663B) of 2025 US imports (Census, primary).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Group head of tax or VP Tax and Trade, with the US entity CFO. Budget: tax/transfer-pricing advisory and the customs duty line itself; fee is a share of verified duty saved, so no new budget line is needed.
ideas.problem: For related-party imports the customs value is usually the intercompany price (accepted via circumstances of sale or test values, 19 USC 1401a). The tax team sets it under IRC 482 and trues it up after year end; those true-ups almost never reach customs. A downward adjustment is a lost refund unless entries were flagged for CBP Reconciliation (21 months, needs a formula that existed in advance) or fixed by post-summary correction (~300 days) or protest (180 days after liquidation). An upward adjustment is unpaid duty with penalty exposure (one customs firm quotes 200-800% of lost revenue). Section 1059A caps US tax basis at customs value (IRS PLR 202552012, Dec 2025, loosened it in a deductive-value case). NY Fed: weighted statutory rate 2.6% at start of 2025, 13% by Dec 2025, so each 1% of customs value is worth about 5x.
ideas.solution: Ingest the ERP intercompany price file, the transfer-pricing model and ACE entries (power of attorney to a licensed broker partner, later own licence). Compute SKU-family price corridors inside both the tax arm's-length range and customs test values; write the formula documentation before goods enter; set Reconciliation flags at entry; track the 21-month deadline; file reconciliations, corrections and protests; match year-end true-ups to entries; produce the circumstances-of-sale binder. For parents in countries taxed above the US a lower import price also cuts global tax.
ideas.why_now: Tariffs are 5x higher, groups are renegotiating who bears the tariff and the instrument is the transfer price. The Dec 2025 PLR shows the tax side moving. DOJ trade-fraud push (Perfectus $549.5M FCA settlement May 2026; Task Force passed $1B Jul 2026) makes sloppy under-declaration costly, so the upward direction needs control too.
ideas.wedge: US distribution subsidiaries of Japanese, Korean and German industrial and auto-parts groups with $200M-$2B of related-party imports and limited-risk-distributor models (US margin fixed, so tariff cost flows into the price corridor). First 10: free diagnostic on 12 months of ACE entry data plus the intercompany price file, sold through mid-tier trade counsel and transfer-pricing boutiques.
ideas.path_to_100m: Related-party imports $1,663B x 6.3% collected rate (214/3,391) = ~$105B of duty on those goods [derivation, assumes average rate]. Target 300 groups averaging $1.2B related-party imports = $360B (22% of the pool). A defensible 2% customs-value reduction at a 7% blended duty saves $504M/yr; 20% fee = $101M. At a 1% reduction it takes 600 groups. HEROIC: needs >20% of related-party value, about half of the top ~600 groups. Group concentration is an unsourced assumption (verify with Census LFTTD or ACE data).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Big Four customs and transfer-pricing practices (EY, KPMG, PwC, Deloitte publish on it), Forvis Mazars, EisnerAmper, trade counsel; generic transfer-pricing software (Supernomial t0, Thomson Reuters ONESOURCE) with no customs link; customs software (SAP GTS, Descartes, Thomson Reuters) with no transfer-pricing link. I searched for a vendor reconciling the two and found none.
ideas.why_they_lose: Big Four split tax and customs, bill hourly, and are barred from contingent fees on audit clients (17 CFR 210.2-01(c)(5), primary). TP tools have no ACE connection; customs tools never see the ERP price file; brokers file entries but never see the group's pricing policy; nobody owns the 21-month reconciliation calendar.
ideas.moat: Switching costs: embedded in the ERP intercompany price file, the year-end close and ACE reconciliation flags that run 21 months. Counter-positioning against hourly advisers is secondary.
ideas.earned_secret: Customs and tax each treat the intercompany price as the other team's input. CBP recognises a downward adjustment only if entries were flagged for Reconciliation, or fixed inside a correction window, under a formula that existed beforehand, and almost nobody writes the formula before goods enter. For parents in higher-tax countries (Japan, Germany; memory) a lower import price is rarely a trade-off: it cuts duty and global tax together.
ideas.first_90_days: Hire two former customs-valuation partners and engage a licensed broker as responsible supervisor. Get a trade-counsel opinion on circumstances of sale, test values and 1059A. Run free diagnostics on five US subsidiaries to find true-ups that never reached customs in either direction. Sign three on a capped savings share. Build the flag-and-formula pack for Japan-parented distributors first.

ideas.title: Rights Ledger
ideas.one_liner: A standard rights notice and shared ledger that lets a distributor that paid duty on imported goods pass the drawback right down the sales chain to the customer who exports the same goods, with insurance for the importer's liability.
ideas.customer: US manufacturers and exporters that buy imported inputs from US distributors/importers (the claimants), and those distributors, who hold the entries.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The claimant: Controller or VP Tax of the exporting manufacturer pays a contingent 15% of the refund. The distributor gets a revenue share and the indemnity; its CFO signs.
ideas.problem: Under 19 USC 1313(j)(2) (primary) the claimant need only have received same-HTS8 goods directly or indirectly from the importer, and ordinary invoices prove the transfer; drawback is 99%, 5-year window. But the exporter does not know which entries a supplier several hops upstream paid duty on, and the importer is liable for the claimant up to the lesser of duties claimed or authorized, (k)(2), while gaining nothing, so distributors refuse. The right goes unclaimed. Paid drawback ran ~$0.9-1B/yr (GAO avg $896M 2011-18, secondary); vendor claims of 80% unclaimed are marketing and not relied on.
ideas.solution: Machine-readable rights notice generated from the importer's ERP and attached to each B2B sale (HTS8, quantity, entry number, duty paid, MFN or 301 flag). Claimant side aggregates notices, matches its exports at HTS8 and files through a licensed drawback broker partner. Platform supplies standard contracts and an insurer-backed indemnity for the (k)(2) liability and pays the importer a share.
ideas.why_now: The Jul 24 2026 Section 301 duties reach inputs from the EU, Japan, India and 60 economies, far beyond China, and vendor summaries say they are drawback-eligible after an August CBP Chapter 99 fix (verify the CSMS). 5-year lookback makes 2021-26 imports claimable. IEEPA duties are out (CAPE) and Section 232 is mostly barred, so the base is MFN plus 301.
ideas.wedge: MRO, fastener, bearing, chemical and electrical distributors importing >$20M and selling to export-heavy OEMs. First 10: three distributors plus seven of their exporter customers, sold bottom-up through exporter controllers.
ideas.path_to_100m: US goods exports $2,179.9B in 2025 (domestic $1,759.1B, Census primary). Assume manufactured domestic exports $1.2T, imported-input content 12% ($144B), blended MFN+301 rate 6% = ~$8.6B/yr eligible duty [assumption chain] vs ~$1B actually paid. $100M at a 15% fee = $667M of claims filed per year = ~8% of the eligible base or ~10% of the unclaimed part. Verify by matching Census export HTS8 to import HTS8 per firm.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Drawback specialists (Sandler & Travis, Livingston, UPS, Kuehne+Nagel; memory); vendors Pax, Consyn, Lightsource, GingerControl, Passport (e-commerce), Tariff Refund HQ, Zollback; Flexport tariff-refund automation; CBP's free ACE drawback module. All serve one claimant company at a time. I found no cross-company rights ledger and no drawback marketplace.
ideas.why_they_lose: A single-claimant vendor cannot get the importer (the supplier's supplier) to cooperate; the importer's broker is paid by the importer and gains nothing; the importer carries (k)(2) risk. So vendors claim only on the client's own imports.
ideas.moat: Network economies: each distributor on the ledger makes every exporter's claim cheaper and each exporter makes joining worth more to the distributor. Counter-positioning against per-client vendors.
ideas.earned_secret: The drawback right travels with the goods, not with the importer. A manufacturer can claim on duty a distributor three hops upstream paid, matching only at the 8-digit HTS, and ordinary invoices prove the chain. What kills claims is the distributor's fear of the importer-liability clause, not the law.
ideas.first_90_days: Write the rights-notice schema. Get an insurer quote for the (k)(2) indemnity. Recruit five distributors and replay 2021-26 ACE data against ten exporters' export files to show dollars. Hire a licensed drawback broker. File one pilot claim. Risks: GAO has reported CBP not manually checking some claims (incorrect refunds), so expect tighter scrutiny; build fraud controls first.

ideas.title: Origin Rail
ideas.one_liner: A certified third-party attestation per shipment of where goods were last substantially transformed, where the metal was smelted and the metal weight fraction, paid per shipment by the importer and by a yearly verified profile bought by the foreign factory (age-verification and e-invoicing rails, transferred to customs).
ideas.customer: Importers of industrial goods from Asia, the EU and Mexico whose duty depends on origin and composition, plus the foreign factories supplying them.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Importer's VP Trade Compliance or General Counsel pays $15-30 per shipment from the legal-risk/compliance budget; the factory's export sales director pays $1.5-3k a year to keep the US customer.
ideas.problem: Origin now sets the rate (10% vs 12.5% under the new Section 301; legacy China 301 on top; Russian-smelted aluminum 200%; Section 232 on full value). The importer carries the proof: a CBP request for information or EAPA case gives ~30 days to produce factory records, and DOJ is converting origin errors into False Claims Act cases (Ceratizit $54.4M for 301 origin, Perfectus $549.5M). The weak link is a foreign factory that does not answer email.
ideas.solution: A rail anchored by a licensed broker. Factories onboard once (documents, partner audit or video plus scale/XRF checks). Each shipment carries a signed statement referenced by the entry data. Exports go out as a CBP-format evidence binder under a counsel-directed structure (privilege matters; a vault of bad facts is discoverable). Billed per API call.
ideas.why_now: FCA wave and DOJ Trade Fraud Task Force; Section 232 full-value cliff; country-specific 301 rates; and CBP ruling HQ H350722 (Jan 16 2026, primary), which stops unlicensed vendors preparing entry data and so pushes the anchor onto a licensed entity.
ideas.wedge: Importers of aluminum and steel derivatives from Vietnam, Malaysia, Taiwan and Thailand. First 10: mid-size HVAC, electrical and machinery component importers plus each one's top 20 suppliers.
ideas.path_to_100m: 25,000 verified factories x $2,000 = $50M, plus 2.5M attested shipments x $20 = $50M. 2.5M is ~7% of ~35M entries [derivation] or ~25% of an assumed 10M evidence-sensitive entries [assumption]. Factory count is unverified (CBP manufacturer-ID counts not found). $20 is 0.2% of duty on a $50k shipment at 25%; the age-check analogue (Yoti) earns ~10 cents a check, so per-check price must be justified by duty at stake. Needs ~25% share of evidence-sensitive entries: heroic.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Altana (Product Passports; ~$322M raised; CBP two-year contract Oct 2025; bought Cervo AI Jul 24 2026); Sayari, Sourcemap, Everstream, Resilinc, Interos (mapping/risk; memory); SGS, Intertek, Bureau Veritas (factory audits; memory); Oritain, Applied DNA (forensic origin; memory).
ideas.why_they_lose: Altana sells to CBP (its WTO case study describes importers opting in to share compliance data with CBP), so importers hesitate to hand it adverse evidence. Mapping vendors sell dashboards, not signed per-shipment attestations. Audit firms visit factories, not shipments, taking weeks at $1-5k a visit. None anchors a licensed filer.
ideas.moat: Network economies (a factory is verified once and every US customer reuses it) plus a cornered resource: the verified factory file.
ideas.earned_secret: Importers lose CBP evidence requests because a factory in another time zone does not answer within 30 days, not because the law is against them. Factories answer when an order depends on it, so the party the factory must please (its US customer) should require the rail and the factory should pay for it.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign three importers that have already had a CBP request for information. Onboard 30 of their suppliers and assemble one full evidence binder. Settle the privilege structure with FCA counsel. Define the attestation schema around CF-28 and Section 232 Annex IV. Choose a licensed-broker anchor.

ideas.title: Licence Bank
ideas.one_liner: Buy licensed customs brokerages for their licences, licensed supervisors and importer powers of attorney, run them on one AI filing stack priced per clean entry with a correction warranty, and rent the licensed chassis to the software vendors that CBP ruling H350722 now locks out.
ideas.customer: Mid-market importers using three to five small brokers; and AI/software vendors (audit tools, classification tools, marketplaces) needing a licensed back end.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Importers' logistics director or CFO from the existing brokerage-fee line (~$5.48B/yr US market, Mordor, secondary); vendors' COO from cost of revenue.
ideas.problem: The only legal way to run AI over entries is inside a licensed broker: H350722 (Jan 16 2026, primary) treats unlicensed OCR extraction of entry data, 10-digit AI classification tied to a prospective entry, Form 5106 filing and power-of-attorney pass-through as customs business. Licensed supply is capped (14,454 active licence holders; pass rate ~15%). Most brokerages are small and owner-run, and entries got harder with stacked Chapter 99 lines.
ideas.solution: Acquire 30-60 owner-operated brokerages with earn-outs; move them onto one stack where licensed brokers supervise AI-prepared entries; price per clean entry with a warranty covering corrections and penalties up to a cap (outcome pricing); sell the licensed chassis to vendors at a wholesale per-entry fee.
ideas.why_now: H350722. AI-native entrants are unlicensed or small: Alchemize (YC S26), Amari ($4.5M seed Feb 2026, serves 30+ brokerages), Altana with Cervo AI (Jul 2026). Flexport's standalone brokerage grew 86% in a year (secondary). Owners are ageing.
ideas.wedge: Five brokerages in one port cluster (Houston, Los Angeles) bought from retiring owners; their importers are the first customers; first two vendors sign for the chassis.
ideas.path_to_100m: $100M = 1.8% of a $5.48B pool [derivation]: ~35 firms at $2.9M revenue or ~110 at the $0.88M average ($5.48B / ~6,200 firms; firm count unverified). No price data found; assume 0.5-1.0x revenue = $50-100M of capital [assumption]. Revenue is bought, not organic.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Flexport Customs LLC (national permit); Livingston (Platinum Equity, 2019); Expeditors, UPS, DHL, Kuehne+Nagel, DSV; Southfield-backed Alba Wheels Up (bought Steer and others); ~6,200 small firms (unverified); tool vendors Amari, Digicust, Nabu, Alchemize.
ideas.why_they_lose: Forwarders bundle customs with freight at low prices and cannot sell outcome pricing (inference). PE roll-ups bought brokers without rebuilding the stack. Tool vendors that sell to brokers do not own the customer. Flexport competes with every forwarder it would serve.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (licences, licensed supervisors, powers of attorney) plus scale economies in cost per entry.
ideas.earned_secret: The licence is the cap. A licensed individual must exercise responsible supervision and control, so entries filed are limited by licensed headcount, not clerks (my reading of 19 CFR Part 111, not verified). AI removes the clerk limit and leaves the licence as the scarce asset. Caveat: an AI roll-up is on the cliche list; it survives only because the licence is scarce and H350722 is new.
ideas.first_90_days: Pull the CBP broker list. Shortlist 40 firms with owners over 60. Sign letters of intent with three. Hire a chief licensed broker. Decide build versus buy for the filing engine. Line up seed capital and an acquisition facility. Sign two vendors for the chassis.

ideas.title: Second Filer
ideas.one_liner: An independent, licensed post-entry auditor that works only for a share of recovered duty and delivers CBP-ready workpapers, aimed at large importers whose Big Four auditors are barred from contingent fees.
ideas.customer: About 2,000 large US importers: public companies and PE-backed groups with $20M or more of annual duty.
ideas.payer_and_signer: VP Tax or Director of Global Trade; the CFO approves the savings share. No budget line needed because the fee comes out of recoveries.
ideas.problem: CBP liquidates almost every entry as entered without checking whether the importer overpaid (memory). Recoveries need post-summary corrections (~300 days), protests (180 days after liquidation), drawback, FTA claims, valuation fixes (freight, assists, royalties) and classification corrections. Tarifflo reports 1 in 8 of 1M+ entries audited was overpaid (self-reported). The Big Four are barred from contingent fees on audit clients (17 CFR 210.2-01(c)(5), primary). Law firms bill hourly and cannot share fees with non-lawyers (memory). Brokers cannot audit their own filings. Unlicensed software cannot file corrections (H350722).
ideas.solution: A licensed broker entity working under counsel. Ingest five years of ACE entry-summary line data; AI plus human review of classification, valuation, origin, FTA eligibility, 301 exclusions and MPF caps; file corrections, protests and drawback through the licensed entity; underpayments found go to counsel under privilege for the prior-disclosure decision. Fee 25-30% of cash recovered plus a prevention subscription.
ideas.why_now: Duty is six times higher. DOJ's task force and the qui tam surge make underpayment findings urgent. Tarifflo (YC S26) has shown demand at the small end. Big Four customs teams are swamped.
ideas.wedge: Big-Four-audited mid-cap manufacturers and distributors with $20-150M of annual duty. First 10: introductions from PE operating partners.
ideas.path_to_100m: Top 1% of trading firms hold ~80% of trade value (Bernard-Jensen-Redding-Schott, memory), so ~2,000 importers hold ~$170B of duty [assumption]. Target 600 at an average $80M = $48B. Recoveries of 0.6% (12.5% of entries overpaid x ~5% of entry duty, from Tarifflo's self-reported rate) = $288M; 30% fee = $86M, plus $30M from 300 prevention subscriptions at $100k = ~$116M. HEROIC: needs 30% of the top 2,000, and the 0.6% rate is unverified.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Big Four customs practices (EY, KPMG, PwC, Deloitte); Sandler & Travis, Livingston; Tarifflo (YC S26, ~$520k raised, small/mid importers, broker arrangement unclear); GingerControl; Pax; Flexport tariff-refund automation; brokers' own correction services.
ideas.why_they_lose: Big Four: barred from contingent fees on audit clients, and hourly. Law firms: hourly and cannot scale. Brokers: an audit exposes their own errors and E&O claims. Software: not licensed. A licensed, independent, contingent, counsel-supervised entrant has no conflict.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (the conflict-free contingent model), plus process power from audit playbooks and cross-client benchmarks.
ideas.earned_secret: CBP liquidates by operation of law, as entered, so nobody inside government checks for overpayment; the only quality control on duty paid is whoever audits. For audit-client importers the firm that knows the files best is legally barred from sharing in the recovery.
ideas.first_90_days: Stand up the licensed entity and a counsel arrangement. Run three free sample audits on mid-cap importers. Write the privilege protocol for underpayment findings. Measure recovered dollars per dollar of duty. Sign the first three contingent contracts. Map post-summary-correction and protest limitation periods.

ideas.title: Peer Ledger
ideas.one_liner: An importer-controlled, firewalled pool of how real importers classify, value and document the same parts, giving each member an outlier score before CBP or a whistleblower finds it, and giving sureties, lenders, insurers and big buyers a compliance-risk score on consent.
ideas.customer: Importers with $250k+ of annual duty, and the institutions that carry importer risk (sureties, asset-based lenders, PE buyers, large retailers).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Importers: director of trade compliance or GC, $3-10k a year. Risk buyers: head of surety underwriting, lender credit officer or PE operating partner, $100-200k a year for a data feed.
ideas.problem: Classification is defended by consistency and records (reasonable care). Each broker sees only its own clients, CBP sees everything, importers see nothing. Public manifest data (Panjiva, ImportGenius) shows what shipped, not what was declared. Supply-chain graph vendors sell to CBP, so importers do not feed them adverse facts. Sureties, lenders and PE buyers now carry ~6x the duty exposure and price it blind.
ideas.solution: With the importer's consent, pull its entry-summary line data via ACE Reports and a power of attorney to a licensed broker partner; encrypt it into a pool governed by members; score each part's classification, valuation and origin against peer ranges; keep a reasonable-care file; release scores to third parties only on member consent.
ideas.why_now: FY2025 CBP completed audits revised up to 465 (secondary); FCA cases surging; CAPE proved ACE data can be handled in volume; error cost has risen fivefold; H350722 pushes any data vendor toward a licensed anchor.
ideas.wedge: One trade association (HVAC, hardware, furniture components). First 10: ten importers pull their ACE reports and see their outliers across a million lines.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assume 40,000 importers with $250k+ of duty [unsourced assumption]. 11,000 at $5k = $55M, plus 300 institutional feeds at $150k = $45M, total $100M. That is 27% of importers: HEROIC. CBP importer counts by duty band would settle it.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Altana (supply-chain graph; Product Passports; CBP contract; est. $37.5M ARR for 2024 per Latka, which is unreliable); S&P Panjiva, ImportGenius, Descartes Datamyne (manifest data); Thomson Reuters ONESOURCE (rules); Zonos Classify; Tarifflo; Flexport.
ideas.why_they_lose: Altana cannot promise a CBP-blind vault. Manifest vendors do not hold declarations. Brokers each hold one slice and owe client confidentiality. The Big Four are siloed by client.
ideas.moat: Network economies (more members sharpen every peer range) plus a cornered resource in consented declared-data.
ideas.earned_secret: Classification is not decided by a rule; it is defended by consistency and records, and the only party that sees every declaration for a part is CBP. A pool lets importers see their own file the way CBP does. (I found no primary source on CBP peer-outlier targeting; this is inference.)
ideas.first_90_days: Sponsor with one trade association. Pull ACE reports from ten importers. Build an outlier score on a million lines. Get an antitrust and confidentiality opinion. Pitch two customs sureties.

ideas.title: Weight Line
ideas.one_liner: A bill-of-materials-to-weight engine and evidence file that tells importers of Section 232 derivatives which SKUs sit within reach of the 15% metal-weight line (below it the duty is zero, above it 25-50% of full value) or the 10% US-metal lane, and does the redesign, supplier change and documentation to cross it.
ideas.customer: Importers of annex-listed derivative goods: machinery, electrical equipment, appliances, fittings, vehicle parts.
ideas.payer_and_signer: VP Supply Chain with VP Engineering; COO or CFO signs. Budget is the tariff line in cost of goods; the fee is a share of avoided duty.
ideas.problem: Since 2026-04-06 duty falls on the full customs value of annex goods (Annex I-A 50%, I-B 25%, Annex III transitional 15%), but goods outside Chapters 72-76 with under 15% metal by aggregate weight are exempt (CBP CSMS 68253075, secondary). Articles made entirely with US-melted/smelted metal pay 10%; Russian-smelted aluminum content 200%. A two-point change in weight fraction can move 25-50 points of price, yet BOM weights sit in design engineers' files and factory records: brokers never ask and engineers do not know the tariff.
ideas.solution: PLM/ERP connectors; supplier BOM weight collection with spot-check scales or XRF at partner labs; weight fractions by SKU; a heat map of distance to the line; redesign options (material substitution, separate entry of the metal component, US assembly where lawful); an evidence file; a mill-certificate chain for the US-metal lane; refreshed as inclusions change. Entries go through a licensed partner.
ideas.why_now: April 2 2026 proclamation (effective Apr 6), Annex IV technical corrections of May 6, the new rolling inclusion authority, and DOJ trade-fraud enforcement that punishes wrong weights.
ideas.wedge: HVAC, electrical gear and small-machinery makers/importers with $20-200M of annex imports from Chinese, Vietnamese and Mexican factories. First 10: referrals from brokers who see the new duty on every entry.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assume $150B of annex-listed imports at a 25% blended rate = $37.5B of duty [assumption; one-day check: Census import value for the annex HTS lines]. A 10% fee on $1B of avoided duty = $100M, i.e. 2.7% of that base. Equivalent: $60k software x 600 importers = $36M plus $64M of success fees.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Trade counsel/consultants (tariff-engineering advice); SGS, Intertek, Bureau Veritas (composition testing; memory); PLM vendors Siemens, PTC, Dassault (no tariff module; memory); mapping vendors Sourcemap and Altana; classification tools from Thomson Reuters, Descartes, TariffLens AI. I searched for a tool computing distance to the weight line and found none.
ideas.why_they_lose: Brokers and classification tools stop at the HTS number. PLM vendors do not know the tariff. Testing firms sell one-off tests per sample. Consultants bill hourly. Each side lacks the other side's data.
ideas.moat: Process power and switching costs (BOM integration, evidence files); cornered resource in supplier weight data.
ideas.earned_secret: The 15% line is a weight fraction on the aggregate of the applicable metals, and the proof is records, not a lab test. The people who hold the records have never been asked by a broker. Tariff engineering is lawful, and here two points of weight can buy 25-50 points of price.
ideas.first_90_days: Build the weight-fraction calculator on five real BOMs. Pull Census import value for the annex lines to size the pool. Pilot with three importers. Get a counsel memo on the documentation standard and how CBP verifies (unknown today). Sign a lab partner. Risks: CBP could require certificates or change the threshold or lists; Section 232 is statutory and has been durable, unlike IEEPA.

ideas.title: Pass-Through
ideas.one_liner: A buyer-side recovery-audit firm for tariff surcharges: it finds every explicit surcharge on a customer's supplier invoices, matches it to the supplier's refund and contract clause, recovers the buyer's share of IEEPA refunds on contingency, then audits every future Section 232 and 301 surcharge against the duty actually owed.
ideas.customer: B2B buyers (contractors, OEMs, distributors, retailers) that paid separately listed tariff surcharges to suppliers.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Controller or CFO, with the chief procurement officer. Contingent 20-25% of recovered dollars; no budget line needed.
ideas.problem: IEEPA duties (~$170B) were struck down 2026-02-20 and refunds go only to the importer of record (CAPE had accepted 25.1M entries by Jul 31). Customers that paid itemised surcharges (e.g. a 12% temporary tariff surcharge) have contract and equity claims; law-firm alerts (Jones Walker Feb 2026, Carter Ledyard Jul 2026, Legal500 Aug 2026) say B2B buyers with explicit surcharges have stronger claims than consumers. Importers that hold refunds book them (Fastenal Q3-2026 gross margin cites tariff refunds, primary 8-K via the pool file). Suppliers will not volunteer; accounts payable cannot parse the claims. Going forward 232/301 surcharges are unverifiable and change monthly.
ideas.solution: Ingest accounts-payable and invoice data and detect surcharge lines; a clause engine reads supplier terms; send demands with refund-evidence requests supplier by supplier, negotiate, take recoveries as credits. Then run a standing audit of surcharges against actual rate stacks, annex treatment and exemptions, and pass future refunds (Section 122 and 301, if struck) through the same way. Legal advice stays with a partner law firm.
ideas.why_now: Refunds are flowing now, claims doctrine is forming, and the buyer's position is strongest while the supplier still holds the cash. Pending cases on Section 122 and the new 301 could repeat the pattern.
ideas.wedge: Mid-size contractors and industrial buyers with $50M+ a year of purchases from distributors that added surcharges (construction, HVAC, electrical). First 10: design partners via contractor associations.
ideas.path_to_100m: Take $170B of IEEPA duty. If 10% reached B2B customers as explicit surcharges ($17B; range 5-20%; unsourced) and 35% is recovered ($6B), a 22% fee pool is ~$1.3B, so $100M is ~8% of it. The standing audit of ongoing surcharges is smaller (~$15B/yr x 5% overbilling x 25% = ~$190M), so $100M there would need about half. This is a 2-3 year spike unless refund events recur: HONEST WEAKNESS.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Law firms (Jones Walker, Carter Ledyard & Milburn, Arnall Golden Gregory); One Eagle Advisory (sells tariff-refund recovery for downstream buyers); consumer class-action firms; accounts-payable recovery auditors (PRGX; memory); Big Four.
ideas.why_they_lose: Law firms bill hourly and cannot process thousands of supplier relationships. Recovery auditors lack ACE and tariff-stack knowledge. The distributors that hold the refunds cannot volunteer them without giving up margin.
ideas.moat: Weak: process power from clause and settlement data, and counter-positioning. I would not call this defensible beyond the window.
ideas.earned_secret: The refund goes to one legal name on the entry, but the loss sat on invoice lines in other companies' payables. The invoice with surcharge text is the evidence, and only the buyer holds it.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign five buyers. Pull 24 months of accounts-payable data for surcharge text. Build clause matching. Send demands to each buyer's top 20 suppliers through a partner law firm. Track response and settlement rates. Confirm that non-lawyer demand letters stay on the right side of the unauthorized-practice line.

verdicts.title: Lot-Lender

competitors_found.name: Zippy
competitors_found.what_they_do: Digital chattel lender and servicer with community, retail and wholesale channels. Pitches park operators to convert renters, lease-to-own customers and rent-credit holders into owners, with a dedicated partner and tag/title handling. No lot-rent data or three-party agreement mentioned.
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $20M Series C from Saluda Grade announced 14 Oct 2026; 27 states; more than $600M capital commitments; Forum Markets up to $150M loan purchases

competitors_found.name: 21st Mortgage / Vanderbilt (Clayton, Berkshire)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Largest chattel lender and floor-plan lender; runs a park-approval program (park and owner approved, homes placed with $0 out of pocket, 12 months before payments, 21st originates and services the buyer notes)
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Berkshire FY2025 10-K data tags show $31.3B manufactured-housing loans before allowances (tagged extract, not cross-checked); cheapest funding in the industry

competitors_found.name: Cascade Financial Services (Pretium)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Chattel and real-estate manufactured-home lender; bought to expand Pretium's manufactured-home lending
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Acquired by Pretium announced 10 Sep 2026 (price undisclosed, Centerbridge seller); Fitch-rated $162.7M ABS deal with 36.6% credit enhancement

competitors_found.name: Triad Financial Services
competitors_found.what_they_do: Chattel loans and floor plan sold through retailers, brokers, community managers and credit unions
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Private; Champion JV per the pitch (not verified)

competitors_found.name: UMH Properties (in-house lending)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Operator finances its own home sales with installment loans inside its communities
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $100.0M of notes receivable at about 7.0% weighted rate, about 6-year maturity, year-end 2025

verdicts.substitutes: Operator seller-financing (UMH holds its own paper at about 7%), contract for deed, personal loans, credit-union chattel programs (PremierOne, San Antonio FCU), and a written lot-rent agreement between lender and park, which lender advice already recommends as standard practice.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $1.0B average book x about 10% gross yield = about $100M of interest revenue, but that needs about $150M of equity plus $850M of warehouse debt. Zippy, five years in, has $600M of commitments, so funding is the binding constraint, as the pitch admits. Revenue is not profit: funding 6-7%, opex 2%, losses 2-4% leave little unless park data really cuts losses. Median: a $250-350M book by year 6-7 is $25-35M of revenue.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) 60-day lot-rent history predicts default materially better than FICO: unproven, perhaps 25% likely. (2) $150M equity and an $850M warehouse available: plausible, since Saluda, Pretium, Apollo and Forum money is flowing. (3) Exclusive agreements covering 100+ communities from operators who today also work with Zippy and 21st Mortgage: about 40% plausible. (4) Funding cost close to Clayton's: not plausible, so the edge must come from losses and approval rates.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Premise 'no incumbent has a contract with the park' is false in part: 21st Mortgage has a park-approval program and Zippy a community partner channel. FHFA numbers confirmed (65.6% vs 8.8% denial, 9.24% vs 6.63% rate, 91 FR 37848, comments closed 24 Jul 2026, final expected effective by 1 Jan 2028). Park lien and repossession rules vary by state and were not surveyed.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Park-lender contracts and a lender community channel already exist (21st Mortgage, Zippy), capital is flooding in (Pretium/Cascade, Saluda/Zippy), and the one new claim, that rent ledgers beat FICO, is untested.

verdicts.title: Open Lot

competitors_found.name: Champion Homes
competitors_found.what_they_do: Manufacturer buying retail: agreed May 2026 to acquire 11 Homes Direct stores, the largest independent manufactured and modular dealer in the West
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: NYSE-listed; deal expected to close in fiscal Q2 2027; terms not disclosed

competitors_found.name: Cavco (American Homestar)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Bought a builder with 19 retail locations and 2 plants, which also writes some loans and acts as insurance agent
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $190M cash, closed Sep 2025; earlier Solitaire deal $93M with 22 stores

competitors_found.name: Clayton Homes retail with 21st Mortgage
competitors_found.what_they_do: Integrated retail, manufacturing and captive lending; 21st Mortgage also says it serves almost all independent retailers, so independents already shop lenders
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: 21st Mortgage originated nearly $3.3B in 2023 (company release via search)

competitors_found.name: Legacy Housing
competitors_found.what_they_do: Builder and financier selling through independent dealers plus company-owned stores
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Public; profile cites 176 independent and 13 company-owned locations (may be dated)

verdicts.substitutes: The independent dealer as it exists today, using 21st Mortgage, Triad and other lenders and floor plan; dealer-to-dealer sales; OEM-owned retail.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $11B / about 1,200 dealers = about $9M each, so 11 dealers = about $100M of revenue: the arithmetic holds. But dealer counts conflict (about 1,200 per VerticaliQ, 2,438 per IBISWorld, 4,077 retailers and distributors receiving shipments per MHI Q1 2026) and I found no dealer gross margin source. My assumption is low-teens gross margin and mid-single-digit EBITDA, so $100M of revenue is perhaps $5M of EBITDA. Revenue is easy; value creation is not.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) 25+ dealers bought at 0.3x sales or less while shipments are down 7.3% YTD: plausible in a downturn. (2) Multi-brand wholesale terms from plants that prefer their own stores: uncertain. (3) F&I reserve retained under state law: varies by state. (4) Four-lender waterfall raises approvals: weak, since independents already use several lenders. Revenue upside is plausible, profit upside is not.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: No legal blocker found. The F&I reserve captive structure and dealer licensing are state-specific and were not checked. Premise that independents are locked to their biggest competitor's lender is overstated: 21st Mortgage serves nearly all independents, but so do Triad and others.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Revenue is easy but the moat is not: manufacturers with captive plants, lenders and cash are already buying the same independents, and independents already shop lenders. A distribution roll-up with thin margins.

verdicts.title: Park Shield

competitors_found.name: MSI (The Baldwin Group)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Embedded insurance plus LeaseTrack compliance tracking for manufactured-housing communities, nationwide, announced 30 Sep 2026
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Extends a renters program that reached over 1 million residents; Baldwin Group is public

competitors_found.name: Triad Financial Services community insurance program
competitors_found.what_they_do: Insurance added to the lease and paid with rent for community-owned rental homes
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $156 a year per the 2017 post; underwriter not named

competitors_found.name: CoverTree
competitors_found.what_they_do: MGA for manufactured homes (Markel paper) with Maple resident-insurance management software for property managers and Bonsai for agents and lenders
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $23M raised ($10M seed 2022, $13M Series A May 2024)

competitors_found.name: Complete Markets Mobile Home Parks Program
competitors_found.what_they_do: Program insurance for mobile home parks
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Not disclosed

competitors_found.name: Foremost (Farmers) and American Modern (Munich Re)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Individual manufactured-home policies, roughly $700-1,600 a year per consumer guides
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: No policy counts or market share found

verdicts.substitutes: Standard individual policies already required by lenders and many leases; the park's own master policy; going uninsured, which is why parks care.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: As an MGA at 15-20% commission, $100M of revenue needs $500-650M of premium, 13-17% of the pitch's own $3.9B pool, and that pool rests on assumed home counts and consumer-site premiums that I could not verify. As a risk-bearing carrier it needs $50M+ of surplus. Premium counted as revenue only works for a carrier.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Both large REIT owners plus several regionals sign a default-enrollment addendum (about 60,000 policies at $1,100 = $65M premium), a fronting carrier and reinsurer agree to community-specific rating, and regulators accept mitigation credits. The REIT assumption is the weak link: they have in-house risk managers and are already being courted by MSI.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: A park collecting premium risks acting as an unlicensed agent; referral-fee limits and opt-out enrollment rules vary by state. A commercial-lease case shows disputes over insurance billed beyond what the lease allows. The pitch only checked Oregon. The 'only the operator can sign the lease addendum' claim is already exploited by MSI and Triad.
verdicts.deciding_reason: MSI, backed by Baldwin Group, launched park-lease embedded insurance 18 days ago, Triad and others already sell it, and MGA commission cannot reach $100M of revenue.

verdicts.title: Park Utility Co

competitors_found.name: Cooperative Development Institute, Water Infrastructure Support Program
competitors_found.what_they_do: Free technical and managerial help for resident- and nonprofit-owned parks to win water and wastewater grants
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $41.7M of grant funding awarded to 64 communities since March 2023

competitors_found.name: ROC USA
competitors_found.what_they_do: Nonprofit that finances and supports resident-owned communities including infrastructure
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $38.1M HUD PRICE award (Dec 2024); $47M acquisition loan pool

competitors_found.name: American Water / Nexus Water Group
competitors_found.what_they_do: Consolidating scaled small water and wastewater systems; Nexus is selling non-core systems
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $315M for 47,000 connections (closed 1 Jun 2026); Cal Water buying Nexus Nevada and Oregon systems for $218M

competitors_found.name: State grant programs (Minnesota Housing, Vermont)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Fund park infrastructure directly to owners, co-ops and nonprofits
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Minnesota $16M appropriated 2023; 2024 cycle $13.3M requested, $2.7M funded; Vermont $13.3M to 46 communities

verdicts.substitutes: Park owners and their own contractors; RUBS billing firms; municipal annexation; free technical assistance from CDI and ROC USA; state programs.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Route 1 (design-build): $2.5M per 100-site park x 40 parks = $100M a year, against visible grant pools of roughly $13-34M of requests a year in Minnesota, a one-time $225M federal PRICE round in FY2023, and zero new PRICE money in FY2026. Capturing a third of every visible grant dollar gives about $50M. Route 2 (utility): 92,600 sites x $90 x 12 = $100M, but a $2.3B rate base that only an infrastructure sponsor could carry.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: A national program appears (PRICE appropriated at $225M a year, authorized to 2033 by Sec. 304 of P.L. 119-101 but proposed for elimination in FY2027) AND the firm wins a third of all park infrastructure grants AND moves into rate-based ownership with an infrastructure fund. The first condition is currently going the wrong way.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Need is real (AP/EPA: nearly 70% of parks running their own water systems violated rules in five years, vs 48% for cities). But regulation is patchy: California AB 604 exempts compliant submetering parks from PUC regulation, and most states do not regulate park systems; selling the pipes would likely create a regulated utility with PUC approval cycles. ARPA money is one-time and ending.
verdicts.deciding_reason: The payer is one-time grants that are shrinking, a utility charge is a rent increase by another name, and even a third of visible grant money is about $50M.

verdicts.title: Covenant Parks

competitors_found.name: ROC USA
competitors_found.what_they_do: Nonprofit that helps residents buy and run their parks as cooperatives, financed by a CDFI arm
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $47M National Acquisition Loan Pool; $38.1M HUD PRICE award; capital-constrained

competitors_found.name: New York MHAP
competitors_found.what_they_do: Low-interest state loans for mission-driven acquisitions with a rent-increase cap (3% over current rent) and a regulatory agreement
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: State program; used for Lake Placid at $4.7M

competitors_found.name: Fannie Mae MHC tenant site lease protections
competitors_found.what_they_do: Mission pricing for communities adopting one-year renewable leases and notice rules; no rent cap
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: 2024: 122 properties, 19,808 pads, $943.4M mission-adjusted UPB; $1.9B total MH volume in 2025

competitors_found.name: Public REITs and private-equity funds (ELS, Sun, UMH; Havenpark, Apollo, OZ Impact Funds)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Acquire and operate communities underwriting 5-6% rent growth; none offers a recorded cap
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Apollo $850M first close of a manufactured-housing fund; OZ Impact Funds bought 21 communities for $100M; Sun same-property base rent $766 a site a month, ELS $956

competitors_found.name: Minnesota Manufactured Home Community Redevelopment grants
competitors_found.what_they_do: Infrastructure grants whose recipients record a 25-year covenant limiting rent increases to 5% without state permission
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $16M appropriated in 2023

verdicts.substitutes: Owner sells to the highest bidder (REIT, fund or flipper); resident-led cooperative purchase with ROC USA under right-of-first-refusal laws; state rent regulation; doing nothing.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Pitch used $9.0-9.4k a site, which is REIT-level (Sun $766 a month = $9.2k, ELS $956 = $11.5k). Small independent parks run $350-500 a month, institutional comparables $550-750 (vendor claim). At $7,000 a site-year, $100M = about 14,300 sites = about 143 communities = 0.33% of 4.3M homesites. At Northmarq's Q1 2026 median of $58,400 a space that is about $835M of assets and $290M of equity at 65% LTV, about 22 parks a year over 6-7 years. The pitch's 10,700-11,100 sites and $230-270M of equity were about a third too low. Share is trivial; capital and seller price expectations are the constraints.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) An anchor pension or insurer commits $200M+ at roughly 7-8% levered returns: unproven but the buyer pool exists, about 40% plausible. (2) Sellers aged 65+ in right-of-first-refusal states accept a covenant bid within about 5% of market for a clean closing: untested, 50% plausible. (3) Agency debt prices the covenant at least as well as tenant protections: likely. (4) 22 parks a year of sourcing: Havenpark-style roll-ups have done it with PE capital: plausible. Combined perhaps 15% for the upside.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Right-of-first-refusal laws confirmed: New York (signed 25 Oct 2023: 60 days to indicate intent, 140 days to close, per press coverage) and Maine LD 1145 (effective 24 Sep 2025; first use in Jay in 2026). Recorded rent covenants are lawful private contracts in principle. Delaware's CPI-linked cap produced large increases in 2022, so a fixed ceiling is needed. The resident equity glide path may raise securities, tax and Fannie-lease-term issues (Fannie leases of 2+ years cannot contain a site purchase option), so structure it as an option at a formula price, with counsel. H.R. 2461 is only introduced.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Real gap with no scaled for-profit covenant owner found, counter-positioned against REIT rent growth, tailwinds intensifying, and the $100M path survives at corrected numbers. Price-to-return is the open risk.

verdicts.title: Deposit Bridge

competitors_found.name: Triad Financial Services (credit-union programs)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Markets chattel programs and loan-portfolio advice to credit unions, plus retailer and broker products
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Private; flyers show 550 minimum FICO, $10,000 minimum loan

competitors_found.name: PremierOne Credit Union
competitors_found.what_they_do: Launched a chattel-style program for HUD-label homes on leased land, up to $800,000 and 25 years
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Program start Jul/Aug 2025

competitors_found.name: San Antonio Federal Credit Union
competitors_found.what_they_do: One of five lenders NCLC estimated hold over 52% of chattel lending
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: About $1B of chattel (NCLC 2022 estimate)

competitors_found.name: America's Credit Unions
competitors_found.what_they_do: Trade body lobbying for GSE chattel pilot guidelines (24 Jul 2026 letter)
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Says chattel is 0.50% of credit-union loan originations

verdicts.substitutes: Triad-style vendor programs, individual credit-union chattel desks, 21st Mortgage and Vanderbilt directly, and doing nothing (chattel is half a percent of credit-union originations).
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Managed book $6B is called 10% of an inferred $45-65B stock that has no source. The pitch itself says $6B needs 11-24% of annual originations ($5-11B) within about eight years. Servicing 0.55% x $6B = $33M, origination 1.25% x $1.2B = $15M, retained 10% slice $57M of gross interest: the biggest piece is interest on the credit union's own balance sheet, not CUSO revenue. A realistic $3B managed book is about $55M.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Hundreds of credit unions each clear ALCO and board approval, commit capital to the CUSO, and shift chattel from half a percent to a large share of originations within about eight years. Credit unions are slow and have little chattel appetite today, so this is implausible.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: CUSO structure under NCUA rules (12 CFR Part 712, from memory) limits federal credit-union investment and permitted services; I found no manufactured-housing CUSO, but could not confirm one does not exist. Repossession and title rules still vary by state.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Credit unions already have a top-five chattel lender and Triad markets to them; the $6B managed book is unsourced and heroic. Even a $3B book yields about $55M.

verdicts.title: Title I Reborn

competitors_found.name: Ginnie Mae manufactured-housing MBS (existing program)
competitors_found.what_they_do: MH pool type for FHA Title I loans, already exists
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $92M outstanding April 2026, $94M March, $131M April 2024; falling every month

competitors_found.name: HUD Title I Manufactured Home Loan Program
competitors_found.what_they_do: The insurance program the pitch would build on; dormant (Pew 2024: no loans made in recent years)
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Limits $105,532 single-section and $193,719 multi-section (Mar 2024); raised again in P.L. 119-101

competitors_found.name: Private-label chattel ABS (Cascade, Clayton, Cavco)
competitors_found.what_they_do: The funding substitute lenders use today
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Cascade Fitch-rated deal $162.7M, 36.6% credit enhancement, 637 average FICO

verdicts.substitutes: Private chattel ABS, warehouse lines, bank and credit-union deposits, Berkshire's balance sheet for Clayton.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $2.0B a year of issuance x 2-3% gain on sale is about $50M, plus a $6B servicing book x 0.6%. But the existing Ginnie MH program is $92M outstanding and shrinking, and $2.0B a year would be 20-40% of chattel originations. The 'Treasury-linked spread' economics fail because Title I coverage is capped at 10% of the lender's portfolio, not guaranteed per loan.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Would need Congress or HUD to remove the 10% portfolio cap and pay full-loss claims, FHA premiums low enough to price below 8.5%, and non-Berkshire lenders to switch en masse. The enacted P.L. 119-101 Title I changes (higher limits, 30-year max term, lease flexibility) do not appear to touch the cap in the bill text I read, so none of this is in motion.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: FALSE PREMISE. 24 CFR Part 201 (via secondary summaries; confirm on ecfr.gov): coverage is limited to 10% of the lender's insured portfolio through a reserve account, pays at most 90% of loss up to the reserve, claim is reduced by appraised value, and FHA can contest a claim for two years. The pitch's 'all pending items are not law' is stale: Title I modernization was enacted in P.L. 119-101 on 11 Jul 2026 (Sec. 303), though I read H.R. 7792 as introduced, not the enrolled text.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Premise is false on primary data: Ginnie manufactured-housing MBS is only $92M and shrinking, and Title I cover is capped at 10% of a lender's portfolio, so it does not convert chattel into a Treasury-linked asset.

verdicts.title: Keyring

competitors_found.name: UMH Properties
competitors_found.what_they_do: Owns and rents about 11,400 homes inside its own communities
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: 95% occupancy; 202 new rentals in the latest quarter; rental homes 44.8% of occupied sites (Jun 2026 10-Q)

competitors_found.name: 21st Mortgage park program
competitors_found.what_they_do: Places homes in approved parks at $0 out of pocket with 12 months before payments, then originates and services buyer notes, solving the park owner's capital problem
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Clayton/Berkshire balance sheet

competitors_found.name: Zippy
competitors_found.what_they_do: Converts community renters, lease-to-own customers and rent-credit holders into homeowners
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $20M Series C Oct 2026; 27 states

competitors_found.name: Sun Communities and Equity LifeStyle (rental programs in own parks)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Rent homes in their own parks; third-party placement not found at scale
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Sun 97.9% combined occupancy Jun 2026; rental counts not retrieved

verdicts.substitutes: Park owners buying homes with 21st Mortgage's program or wholesale financing from builders such as Legacy; local rent-to-own operators; seller financing; used homes.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $1,000 a month x 8,300 homes = $100M checks, but $95k per home gives $12k gross, about 12.6% before vacancy, repairs, insurance, tax, servicing and credit losses. At an assumed 35-40% of rent, net yield is 7.5-8%, close to the cost of 70-75% debt, before depreciation of a personal-property asset. A resident paying $1,000 plus lot rent needs roughly $64k of income at one-third of income, above the typical denied-chattel profile (assumption). No data found on actual rent-to-own default rates.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) About 6,500 homes ($620M of assets) financed with 70-75% debt in a market without agency debt for scattered-site fleets: uncertain. (2) Fleet pricing meaningfully below Census retail prices ($88-91k single-section): plausible with underused plants. (3) Residents denied chattel credit can carry $1,000 plus lot rent: doubtful. (4) Parks agree to remit home rent: possible but adds counterparty risk.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: New York's 2019 law requires written rent-to-own contracts and refund of payments if the park terminates tenancy. North Carolina Chapter 47H treats disguised installment arrangements on manufactured homes as contracts for deed, and Rodriguez v. Riverstone (2022 NCLC class action) alleged a park operator's used-home installment contracts were disguised; outcome not found. General rent-to-own statutes often exclude manufactured homes. A true-lease structure helps but gives up the equity feature that sells it.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Works inside REIT parks; outside them it adds park-remittance risk, rent-to-own law exposure and a thin spread, and 21st Mortgage already funds infill for park owners.

picks.title: Covenant Parks
picks.one_liner: A for-profit owner-operator of small and mid-size land-lease communities that records a rent-growth covenant and a resident buy option at closing, financed by agency tenant-protection debt and pension or insurer equity.
picks.sharpened_pitch: Covenant Parks is the first scaled for-profit owner-operator of small and mid-size land-lease communities that records a rent covenant at closing: increases capped at the lesser of CPI or 4% for 10 years, with documented capital-cost pass-through reviewed by a residents' association, plus a pre-agreed formula price and 90-day path for residents to buy, structured as an option that recycles our capital rather than an obligation. Delaware's CPI-linked cap produced large increases in 2022, so the ceiling is fixed. It is sold to three audiences. Sellers aged 65+ in right-of-first-refusal states (New York since Oct 2023, Maine since Sep 2025) get a clean, litigation-proof closing. Agency lenders get tenant-protection compliance built in; Fannie financed 19,808 pads with those protections in 2024. Pension and insurer capital gets stable lot-rent cash flow, no rent-gouging label, and a hedge against rent regulation. The $100M path is not shrunk: at $7,000 a site-year it needs about 14,300 sites (about 143 communities, 0.33% of 4.3M homesites), roughly $835M of assets and $290M of equity over 6-7 years, about 22 parks a year. The original pitch's $9.0-9.4k a site understated the sites needed by a third. Seller trust and the capital pool are the moat, not a limit on scale.
picks.payer_and_signer: Residents pay lot rent every month (existing budget line, about $7,000 a site-year in small parks). Signers: the selling owner or broker (right-of-first-refusal states), the investment committee of a pension, insurer or impact fund, and a Fannie or Freddie MHC lender for the debt.
picks.path_to_100m: $100M / $7,000 = about 14,300 sites = about 143 communities of 100 sites = 0.33% of 4.3M homesites. At Northmarq's Q1 2026 median of $58,400 a space that is about $835M of assets, about $290M of equity at 65% LTV, about 22 parks (about $125M) a year over 6-7 years. Median case $25M: about $75-80M of equity and 3,500 sites. Correction to the pitch: $9.0-9.4k a site is REIT-level rent (Sun $766 a month, ELS $956); small independent parks run $350-500 a month.
picks.competitors_and_edge: ROC USA (nonprofit, resident-led only, capital-constrained: $47M pool, $38.1M PRICE); NY MHAP (3% cap, subsidized debt for mission buyers); Minnesota grant covenants (5% cap, grants only); Fannie tenant protections (no cap); REITs and funds (Sun, ELS, UMH, Havenpark, Apollo $850M, OZ Impact) underwrite 5-6% rent growth and cannot promise caps. No for-profit covenant platform at scale found. Edge is counter-positioning plus seller trust in right-of-first-refusal states.
picks.why_now: Right-of-first-refusal laws in New York (Oct 2023) and Maine (Sep 2025, first use in Jay in 2026), a Pennsylvania 4% CPI-tied cap bill and a federal tenant bill pending, 2025 transaction volume up 47% (Berkadia), REIT rent growth of 5.2-5.6% fueling backlash, and agencies already pricing tenant protections.
picks.moat: Counter-positioning (REITs cannot match a cap without cutting guided rent growth), cornered resource (seller and resident trust in right-of-first-refusal states), and pre-compliance if states cap rents. Thin until sellers are shown to accept a covenant bid.
picks.biggest_open_risk: Price-to-return: a buyer capped near 4% bids against REITs and funds underwriting 5-6% growth at about a 6% cap rate, and impact capital that accepts below-market returns already goes to ROC USA near 1%. Whether a pension and insurer pool accepts about 7-8% levered returns at $290M scale is unproven.
picks.cheapest_next_test: Within 30 days: underwrite five live New York and Maine listings with and without the cap and compute the bid gap to market; get written answers from a Fannie or Freddie MHC lender on covenant pricing and from three pension or insurer allocators on a 7-8% target at $50M+ tickets; ask 20 sellers aged 65+ via brokers whether a covenant bid within 5% of market with a clean closing wins. Success: three LOIs and one allocator term sheet. Cost under $30k.

result.pool_note: Real money (about $13.6B of homes, roughly $40B of lot rent) but every finance and insurance wedge is occupied or freshly funded: Zippy, Pretium/Cascade, Apollo, MSI. Government-guarantee ideas are dead (Ginnie manufactured-housing MBS is $92M). The one open gap is owner-operator positioning against REIT rent growth.

verdicts.title: National ESA provider network (Forage + CAQH + Headway for ESA vendors)

competitors_found.name: ClassWallet vendor pay and marketplace
competitors_found.what_they_do: Runs ESA wallets and vendor onboarding for AZ, AL, AR, NC, NH, SC, IN; vendors register per state after state approval
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $7.5B+ distributed, 38 states, about $102.6M raised

competitors_found.name: Odyssey (TEFA Marketplace and state vendor programs)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Runs TX, UT, IA, LA, WY, GA, MO programs, each with its own vendor list; Texas marketplace launched with nearly 2,400 vendors and 54,000 products
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $74M Series B (Sep 2026), 13 programs, $2B+ state funds a year

competitors_found.name: Student First Technologies and Step Up For Students (MyScholarShop)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Vendor approval and payment for WV and TN, and Florida, per program
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Step Up runs Florida's roughly $3.7B program

verdicts.substitutes: The state platforms' own statutory vendor onboarding and marketplaces; states will not accept a third-party credential without statute or contract change. Iowa pays vendors in 2-5 business days and Alabama in 2-10, so the payout pain is mostly solved. Texas says vendors are not charged to list or sell.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: The $100M path needs 40,000 providers paying $2,500 a year, a 5% take on about $50k of billings each, while platforms already pay in days and states bar or shift fees (NC statute up to 2.5%, TN up to 2%, charged to the account holder). Honest build: 40,000 x $60 a month ($29M) + fast-pay premium on a quarter of $2B billed ($7.5M) + $10-25 credential checks ($2M) = about $40M ceiling. $100M needs about 37% of the idea's own $270M pool.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Two or more large states accept the network credential as a pre-check: low-to-moderate, no ESA precedent (closest analog is the FSMB Uniform Application for physicians, which works because boards agreed). (2) A large share of about 40,000 providers pay $60 a month: moderate. (3) A fast-pay premium sells even though platforms pay in 2-10 days: low.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Vendor approval is per program by statute, so portability needs state buy-in. The 7-30 day payment baseline (EdChoice) is stale against current 2-5 and 2-10 day state figures. Texas bars listing fees; NC and TN cap fees on account holders. No national credential or directory found.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Payers own vendor lists by statute, payout is already 2-10 days, and the realistic ceiling is about $40M even if states cooperate.

verdicts.title: School payments and capital OS (Toast for private schools and microschools)

competitors_found.name: FACTS / Nelnet
competitors_found.what_they_do: Tuition payment plans, payment processing and now FACTS Compass for SGOs; sells school information systems
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Nearly 12,000 K-12 schools; Nelnet education technology and payments segment about $147M revenue a quarter (Q1 2025); Nelnet owns a lending balance sheet

competitors_found.name: Building Hope Lending Lab
competitors_found.what_they_do: ESA bridge loans, lines of credit and partial lease guarantees for microschools and small schools up to 100 students
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Pilot; original $675k Stand Together/Curry loan fund; volumes undisclosed

competitors_found.name: Charter School Capital
competitors_found.what_they_do: Receivable sales and working capital for charter schools
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Established charter-school lender; not ESA-specific

verdicts.substitutes: Existing tuition payment plans from FACTS, school-owned reserves, local bank lines of credit, and philanthropic bridge loans. Texas pays 25% on Jul 1 and Oct 1 and 50% on Feb 1, so half the year's money is in by Oct 1.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: The $114M total rests on advances earning 14% on $500M average outstanding ($70M). State-backed, front-loaded payments would more plausibly price at 7-9% ($35-45M), and the $500M must be raised. ESA money sits in a family-controlled account, so there is no assignable state receivable to lend against. Still needs 6,000 schools and about 30% of choice-funded tuition volume. The 'six months late' framing is overstated.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) A wallet platform grants payment-direction or sweep rights: low-to-moderate, platforms sell to states and may refuse. (2) A $300M+ cost-of-funds facility at around 8% appears: moderate. (3) 4,000-6,000 schools adopt a non-FACTS payment stack: low, FACTS owns the school relationship. (4) FACTS/Nelnet does not copy it despite having the schools and balance sheet: low.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Texas installment schedule confirmed on Odyssey's support page (25% Jul 1, 25% Oct 1, 50% Feb 1). Lending against ESA payments depends on family-controlled accounts and clawback rules; assignment of payments is untested. Lending licences and usury rules not checked.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Real pain but half the cash is front-loaded, no assignable receivable, and FACTS/Nelnet owns the schools and a balance sheet. Upside depends on platforms' cooperation.

competitors_found.name: ACE Scholarships EmpowerEd
competitors_found.what_they_do: End-to-end SGO administration including digital wallets, donor management and compliance
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: 25+ year national SGO

competitors_found.name: Odyssey
competitors_found.what_they_do: State ESA platform, ACH after proof of delivery, marketplace; SGO suite

verdicts.substitutes: ABF desks buy directly from originators (forward flow described as 'an option for just about any lender', Morgan Lewis, Jan 2026); Carlyle/KKR (Discover) and Apollo/Blackstone (Wells) hold legacy books and need origination; originators use bank partners or their own ABS; credit unions fund on balance sheet.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: The $100M is GROSS interest: $1B balance x 10%, funded with ~$0.9B of notes. Net of ~6-7% funding cost and losses, $1B yields ~$35-40M plus fees. Median: ~$300M balance by year 6-7 = ~$30M gross, ~$12M net. Top-decile: ~$1.5B balance (about 8% of a ~$9.4B private grad market) = ~$150M gross, ~$55M net. $100M net needs ~$3B, not a 5-7 year outcome. College Ave took ~8 years to reach $1B a year of originations.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Raise ~$100M+ first-loss capital for an unproven conduit (low to moderate). (2) Sign 8-10 originators who would otherwise sell to KKR or Nelnet and keep brand and servicing (low to moderate). (3) Insurers take ~$0.9B of 10-15 year notes (moderate). (4) Outcome-based loans perform; Ascent's own ABS shows higher-than-expected losses (unknown). Gross interest of $150M is reachable; net is the honest number.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Premise 'no multi-originator aggregator, First Marblehead is the only precedent' is wrong (Nelnet-CommonBond, Nelnet ABS of Truist/Cognition loans, CU Student Choice, Ascent ABS). Reg B final rule (effective 21 Jul 2026) dropped the federal disparate-impact test but state AGs keep enforcement (Earnest paid MA AG $2.5M), so program-level pricing grids carry state-law risk. First Marblehead/TERI lessons (single guarantor, chain-of-title) are valid design advice.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Best of pool and a genuine capital-and-data gap, but no verified edge over Nelnet, KKR and Ascent's own ABS, and net revenue upside (~$55M) is about half the bar. First-loss capital is a precondition, not an outcome.

A pledge with no recourse is not credit enhancement; a binding one is the stay-or-pay structure the laws target. IRC 127 student-loan repayment is permanent but capped at $5,250 a year. No lender found that underwrites off a job offer.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Carrot-only employer design is a real insight, but the lending half rests on an unsupported credit claim, the employer half belongs to funded incumbent Clasp, and volumes are unsourced.

verdicts.substitutes: Price-per-property repair contracts (Tamworth moved from schedule of rates); landlords' own damp teams; damp-proofing insurance-backed guarantees (from memory); disrepair panel law firms; sensor and analytics tools.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 35,000 homes x GBP2,200 = GBP77M (about $100M) = about 16% of the 5% cohort (220,000 homes), 0.8% of stock, roughly three Mears-Thurrock-sized annual contract values. Procurement Act 2023: registered providers are generally contracting authorities so multi-year capitation needs a competitive route or framework call-off. FRC exemption for housing disrepair runs to Oct 2028. Weightmans: most housing-condition claims are not insured; no damp-and-mould cover product found.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Only idea where no one was found taking capitated risk on the costliest homes; budget lines exist, skew is plausible, and a data/reinsurance asset gives a scale route; kill test still open.

picks.from_title: Hot-Spot Contract: capitated root-cause care for the worst 5-8% of homes
picks.title: Hot-Spot Contract: capitated root-cause care for the costliest homes
picks.one_liner: Take a fixed annual fee per home for every repair, disrepair-defence cost share and root-cause fix on a landlord's costliest 5-8% of homes, buy stop-loss cover on the tail, and keep the savings.
picks.sharpened_pitch: Sell it as a capitated service contract, not an insurance-style guarantee. For the costliest 5-8% of a landlord's homes (ranked by three-year trailing cost of repairs, disrepair and compensation), the contractor takes every repair, a share of disrepair defence cost and the root-cause works (ventilation, roof, leak, heating controls) for a fixed fee of about 80% of trailing cost. The 'five-year guarantee' is simply the capitation running five years; the contractor buys its own stop-loss reinsurance, which keeps it outside the FSMA insurance perimeter. The landlord stays the duty holder for Awaab clocks, so the contractor runs them under delegation and claims-defence savings are shared, not guaranteed. Enter through a framework call-off or a below-threshold pilot, because registered providers are generally contracting authorities under the Procurement Act 2023 and a standalone multi-year tender takes 12-18 months. Make the cross-landlord loss dataset (job-level cost, cause, recurrence) the scaling asset: after 12-24 months it prices building risk better than any single landlord can, which supports reinsurance and later a carrier-fronted product. Use two payer lines: repairs spend plus the disrepair legal budget, with root-cause works capitalised. Do not narrow to damp only; the cohort is defined by cost, whatever the cause.
picks.payer_and_signer: Finance Director and Director of Assets sign; funded from responsive repairs plus disrepair, compensation and legal budgets, with root-cause works capitalised. CEO and board approve the multi-year contract.
picks.path_to_100m: 35,000 homes x GBP2,200 capitated fee = GBP77M (about $100M). That is about 16% of a 220,000-home cohort (5% of 4.4M homes), 0.8% of all stock, roughly 15-20 landlords at 1,500-2,500 homes each, or about three Mears-Thurrock-sized annual contract values (GBP24M a year each; Thurrock home count unverified). If skew follows the old 80/20 record, cohort cost per home is above the GBP2,800 assumed and fewer homes are needed. Net margin 12-18% plus shared savings.
picks.competitors_and_edge: Mobysoft RepairSense and Switchee sell analytics/sensors and take no risk; primes (Mears, Osborne, Wates) sell whole-stock price-per-property or total-asset contracts, not a worst-homes carve-out with repeat-repair accountability. Edge: outcome pay on the cohort where patching is most profitable for incumbents, plus a cross-landlord loss dataset and reinsurance relationships no one else holds.
picks.why_now: Awaab's Law phase 2 goes live 30 Nov 2026 and makes repeat failures a s.10A breach with County Court damages; fixed recoverable costs stay off disrepair until at least Oct 2028; Ombudsman findings cite temporary fixes and poor diagnosis; landlords' interest-cover covenants favour capitalised fixes over revenue patches.
picks.moat: Cornered data asset (job-level cost, cause and recurrence across landlords that prices building risk), reinsurance relationships, 5-year contracts with switching costs, and counter-positioning against visit-based pay. Honest limit: none exists until three or more cohorts have 12-24 months of data.
picks.biggest_open_risk: The skew premise is unproven at cost level (only an old KPMG 80/20 via Oxford and Leicester repeat-repair counts), landlords may refuse job-level data or a carve-out from existing total-asset contracts, and a five-year uncapped guarantee could be treated as insurance if not structured as a service contract.
picks.cheapest_next_test: In 6-8 weeks at analyst cost only: obtain three years of job-level repair and disrepair cost data from three landlords (direct, or FOI to councils with in-house records) and measure the share of spend carried by the top 5% of homes. Stop if the top 5% carry under 15% in two of three, or if no landlord will release job-level data. Then ask two landlords whether their current repairs contract permits a cohort carve-out.

result.pool_note: Awaab's Law is real and dated, but the budgets it touches are already locked in frameworks and total-asset contracts, and several "nobody does this" claims (one-visit checks, bundled voids, void decants) were already done. Only the capitated worst-homes carve-out survived.
